10010-the-eulogies-of-howard-a-vision:
Published in 1791, this vision offers eulogies of John Howard, the benevolent and indefatigable prison reformer, after news of his death first afflicted the country. The writer had been talking with a friend of Howard's, and their first surprise and sorrow turned to serious, affectionate reflection on his gentle character and sublime pursuits.

On Howard's worth they agreed entirely, but one point divided them, though both were equally sincere and ardent in regret. The vision that follows praises deeds above heroic. Readers get an eighteenth-century tribute to a reformer, in the dream form that suited solemn praise.
10044-the-father-of-british-canada-a-chr:
William Wood's chronicle, volume twelve of the Chronicles of Canada edited by Wrong and Langton, tells the life of Guy Carleton, the father of British Canada. It opens with Carleton from 1724 to 1759, then General Murray's years, and Carleton as governor from 1766 to 1774.

Later chapters cover the invasion and beleaguerment of 1775 to 1776, deliverance, the counterstroke, guarding the loyalists, and founding modern Canada from 1786 to 1796. Wood writes clear narrative history. Readers get the making of Canada through the man who held it for Britain and shaped its laws. Wood's chronicle remains a clear introduction to Canada's founding generation.
10059-aunt-jane-s-nieces-on-vacation:
Edith Van Dyne's 1912 girls' book sends Aunt Jane's nieces on vacation to Millville, opening with a hobo at Chazy Junction and an invasion of the town. The dawn of a great enterprise follows, as the girls find a way into print and divide responsibilities.

Mr. Skeelty of the mill, a sketch artist, trouble, Thursday Smith, the Honorable Ojoy Boglin, and Molly Sizer's party fill the summer, with Bob West interfering and a dancer's signal. Van Dyne writes cheerful, busy adventure. Young readers get a holiday story where girls run a newspaper and save a town's summer.
10100-byron:
John Nichol's life of Byron traces the poet from ancestry and family through early years and school life from 1788 to 1808. Cambridge and a first period of authorship follow, with Hours of Idleness and the satire English Bards and Scotch Reviewers in 1808 to 1809.

Two years of travel from 1809 to 1811 precede life in London, correspondence with Scott and Moore, and a second period of authorship with Harold's first cantos and the romances, to 1815. Marriage and separation, and farewell to England in 1815 to 1816, close the arc. Readers get Byron's youth and fame in compact, scholarly form.
102-the-tragedy-of-pudd-nhead-wilson:
A lawyer mocked as a fool keeps a calendar of maxims and a secret science of fingerprints. Mark Twain's Pudd'nhead Wilson, published in 1894, opens in Dawson's Landing, where a slave woman swaps her baby with her master's child. The switch shapes two lives in opposite directions.

Roxy's son grows up as the heir Tom Driscoll, while the true heir grows up enslaved. Italian twins, a murder, and a courtroom fingerprint test unravel the fraud. Twain uses the plot to attack slavery, race law, and nature-versus-nurture claims. The novel's bitter humor still cuts deep.
10375-england-s-antiphon:
George MacDonald published this literary history in 1868, tracing sacred poetry in England from the thirteenth century onward. MacDonald, better known as a novelist, writes here as a critic and anthologist, choosing poems that sing back to God like an antiphon in church. His aim is to show a living thread of faith in verse.

Chapters move from medieval lyrics and miracle plays through Spenser, Donne, Herbert, Herrick, and later poets. MacDonald quotes freely and comments with warmth. Readers get a rich, devout survey of English religious poetry, useful for students of hymns, lyrics, and church history.
10392-the-reminiscences-of-sir-henry-haw:
Richard Harris edited these reminiscences of Sir Henry Hawkins, Baron Brampton, from talks and manuscript notes, with a preface dated Harrogate, August 1904. Hawkins, a famous Victorian judge, doubted his own words were worth print, but Harris shaped them into a lively book. The volume follows a long legal life without strict date order.

Hawkins recalls trials, advocates, and courtroom scenes, including the long Tichborne case that made his name. Wit, anecdote, and judgment fill the pages. Readers get a vivid, first-hand view of Victorian law, told by a judge who loved a good story and a sharp cross-question.
10421-the-life-of-lord-byron:
This life of Lord Byron, transcribed for Project Gutenberg from a nineteenth-century text, traces the poet from ancient descent to fame and exile. The Byron family came to England with William the Conqueror, held manors in York and Lincoln, and took its name under Henry II. The book follows pedigree, birth, and early troubles with care.

Chapters treat Byron's mother, early education, accession to the title, and the wars of the Edwards in which his forebears fought. Later parts will follow his poetry, loves, and death in Greece. Readers get a detailed, period biography of a romantic hero, rich in family and social history.
1043-the-story-of-evolution:
Joseph McCabe, a former priest turned popular science writer, tells how life on earth rose from simple forms to man. He starts with the early seas, traces fins, scales, and fur through the ages, and ends with the rise of human mind and tool use, all in plain language for general readers.

McCabe leans on Darwin and on the fossil record, and he writes with a rationalist's zeal to push back priestly accounts of creation. Charts of time and chapters on apes, ice, and early man keep the tale clear. The book is a time capsule of early twentieth-century science, lucid and confident in its day.
10430-trips-to-the-moon:
Lucian of Samosata, a Syrian satirist born about 120 AD, wrote these trips to the moon, translated here from Greek by Thomas Francklin. Henry Morley's introduction traces Lucian from a boy sculptor's apprentice, beaten by his uncle, to a traveler and teacher of rhetoric in Greece, Italy, and Gaul. The book joins satire to fantasy.

The True History sends travelers to the moon by storm and whale, while Icaro-Menippus flies there on wings to mock gods and men. Instructions for writing history add a sharp, comic preface. Readers get a witty, ancient science-fiction satire, still fresh in its jokes on pride and belief.
10431-thirty-years-a-slave-from-bondage-:
Louis Hughes published this autobiography of thirty years in slavery, from bondage to freedom, with a preface defending its plain truth. Hughes was born in Virginia in 1832 and sold in a Richmond slave pen. He writes not for literary show, but to add accurate knowledge of an institution that shaped America for two hundred years.

Chapters treat life on a cotton plantation, the planter's home, work, punishment, and the long road to freedom. Hughes shows slavery's effect on families, labor, and the nation that finally went to civil war over it. Readers get a vital, first-hand record of slavery and survival.
10437-pulpit-and-press-6th-edition:
Mary Baker Eddy, founder of Christian Science, issued this sixth edition of Pulpit and Press in 1897. The book gathers a dedicatory sermon, hymns for laying a corner stone, and her text-book notes, with long press clippings that show how newspapers received her movement. Its tone is devout and public, meant for followers and curious readers alike.

Clippings from the Boston Herald, New York Tribune, Chicago Inter-Ocean, and many other papers fill much of the volume. They praise, question, and report on Christian Science churches and healing claims. Readers get a contemporary record of a new American faith as the press first saw it.
10443-the-rayner-slade-amalgamation:
J. S. Fletcher published this detective novel in 1922, opening with a midnight ride, a dead man, and a shoe buckle. Fletcher, a master of English mystery, builds the plot through jewels, portraits, and Russian bank notes, with murders mounting as the tale goes on. The tone is brisk, clear, and full of clues.

Mr. Franklin Fullaway, the Nastirsevitch jewels, a frantic impresario, and a Bayswater boarding house fill the middle chapters. Fifty thousand pounds reward, thick fog, and a possible death warrant push toward solution. Readers get a classic, well-plotted mystery of London crime and high finance.
10509-the-bars-of-iron:
Ethel M. Dell published this romance in 1916, dedicating it to her brother Reginald. Its mottoes from Psalm 107 and Revelation promise broken gates of brass and bars of iron smitten apart, and heaven opened. Dell, a best-selling romance writer, builds the tale in parts. It starts with gates of brass.

A jug of water, fools, discipline, a mother's help, life on a chain, and a race fill early chapters. A friend in need, a ticket of leave, and a star of hope come later. Love, suffering, and faith drive the plot. Readers get a passionate, old-style romance of hardship, pride, and redemption.
10543-norwegian-life-an-account-of-past-:
Ethlyn T. Clough edited and arranged this account of past and present life in Norway and Sweden, covering history, literature, government, and daily custom. The book moves from prehistoric times through the nineteenth century to the new king Haakon VII of Norway and the Swedish royal family. Its scope is wide and factual.

Chapters treat religion of the Northmen, literature, army and navy, schools, charities, railways, manners, health, newspapers, folk songs, and women of both lands. Material conditions and highways complete the survey. Readers get a useful, early twentieth-century guide to Scandinavian life and progress.
10573-ship-s-company-the-entire-collecti:
W. W. Jacobs gathered his Ship's Company tales in this full collection. Twelve stories are told by sailors and a night-watchman. They are Fine Feathers, Friends in Need, Good Intentions, Fairy Gold, and Watch-Dogs. The Bequest, The Guardian Angel, Dual Control, and Skilled Assistance follow. For Better or Worse, The Old Man of the Sea, and Manners Makyth Man close the set.

Each tale turns on a comic trick, a jealous wife, a false uncle, or a kind act gone wrong. Jacobs tells them in his salty, Thames-side voice. The collection shows his range, from domestic farce to sailor yarns. Readers get the complete, best-loved Jacobs company in one volume, ideal for browsing.
10584-air-service-boys-over-the-atlantic:
Charles Amory Beach wrote the Air Service Boys series during the First World War, and this 1920 volume sends Tom and Jack on a daring flight across the Atlantic. The two young American fliers start from war service in France, take on a bold plan, and face air raids, a submarine attack, and a forced landing far from help.

Later chapters strand them on an ice floe, bring a polar bear and a rolling iceberg, and carry them through to a surprise return home. Beach writes brisk, patriotic adventure, with courage and friendship at its center. Boys' adventure fans get a fast wartime flying story from the age when crossing an ocean by air still seemed almost impossible.
10643-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton edited The World's Greatest Books as a guide for busy readers, and this second volume, dated 1910, covers fiction. It retells and appraises famous novels in short summaries, from Cervantes's Don Quixote and Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress to Jane Eyre, Wuthering Heights, and Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. Each entry names its author and gives the story's heart.

The volume lets a reader survey the great novels of Europe and America without reading each one whole. Its judgments reflect Edwardian taste, earnest and wide. Modern readers can use it as a map of the classic novel, and as a record of which books an earlier age counted greatest.
10704-the-history-of-rome-book-iv-the-re:
Theodor Mommsen's fourth book of his History of Rome, titled The Revolution, covers the crisis that broke the Roman republic. In Dickson's sanctioned translation, Mommsen follows the Gracchi, Marius, Sulla, and the civil wars that turned a republic of laws into a stage for generals. The narrative moves from reform attempts to proscription, dictatorship, and collapse.

Mommsen writes with a lawyer's eye for institutions and a storyteller's pace, showing how old forms failed under new pressures of empire and wealth. The book remains a landmark of Roman history. Readers get the republic's fall told by the scholar who defined the subject for generations.
10710-problems-of-poverty-an-inquiry-int:
John A. Hobson, an English economist, first published Problems of Poverty in April 1891, and this sixth edition dates from 1906. The book asks how poverty should be measured and what industrial life does to the poor. Chapters take up machinery, the rush into large towns, the "sweating system" of low-paid homework, and the state of women workers.

Hobson weighs causes and remedies, including laws to protect labor, and closes with the outlook for low-skilled workers. His tone is factual and reform-minded, grounded in reports and figures of his day. Readers get a serious Victorian study of poverty that still frames debates about wages, work, and welfare.
10748-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton's third fiction volume of The World's Greatest Books, dated 1910, surveys novelists from Daudet to Dumas. Its summaries run from Tartarin of Tarascon and Sandford and Merton through Defoe's Robinson Crusoe to fourteen novels of Dickens, from Oliver Twist to A Tale of Two Cities. Disraeli, and Dumas with Monte Cristo and the Musketeers, close the range.

Each entry retells the plot and judges the book, so a busy reader can grasp a classic quickly. The choices show Edwardian taste at its widest. Modern readers can use the volume as a map of nineteenth-century fiction, and as a guide to which novels to read whole.
10793-sailors-knots-entire-collection:
W. W. Jacobs's Sailors' Knots, published in 1909, gathers twelve comic tales told by a Thames night-watchman and his riverside friends. The contents run from "Deserted" and "Homeward Bound" through "Self-Help," "Matrimonial Openings," "The Toll-House," "The Head of the Family," and "Double Dealing" to "Keeping Up Appearances." Illustrations match the jokes throughout.

Jacobs's humor rests on sailors, lodging-houses, wives, and watchmen, told in broad dialect and sharp dialogue. The collection includes his famous ghost story alongside domestic farces. Readers get the whole book in one place, the best single introduction to Jacobs's comic world.
10880-teddy-s-button:
Amy Le Feuvre, author of Probable Sons, published Teddy's Button in 1896 as a children's story. It opens with a slim, delicate lad with golden curls and blue eyes, standing bareheaded in blazing sun among village boys, spellbinding them with an oration. His whole frame quivers with enthusiasm, hand, foot, and tongue in motion, while he fingers a large brass button.

The button gives the tale its title and its thread, as Teddy's talk and deeds unfold around it. Le Feuvre writes for young readers with warmth and moral purpose. Children get a charming period story of a boy orator and his treasured button.
10921-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton's fourth fiction volume of The World's Greatest Books surveys novelists from Ebers to Grant. Its summaries include Edgeworth's Belinda and Castle Rackrent, Eliot's Adam Bede, Romola, Silas Marner, and The Mill on the Floss, and Fielding's Tom Jones, Joseph Andrews, and Jonathan Wild. Goethe's Werther, Goldsmith's Vicar of Wakefield, and Gaskell's Cranford and Mary Barton appear as well.

Each entry retells the story and judges the book, for readers short of time. The volume reflects Edwardian taste at its broadest. Modern readers can use it as a map of classic fiction, and a guide to novels worth reading whole.
10968-a-century-of-negro-migration:
Carter G. Woodson, founder of Black history study in America, wrote this history of African American migration from about 1815 to the First World War. Chapters follow the search for refuge, transplantation to the North, fighting it out on free soil, colonisation schemes, the successful migrant, the exodus to the West, the migration of the talented tenth.

Woodson connects the wartime movement north with earlier periodic movements, arguing that differing state policies made one section more congenial than another. Maps show Black population shares by state in 1910 and the growth of northern cities. The book remains a foundational work, treating migration as a long, deliberate search for freedom and opportunity, not a sudden flight.
1097-mrs-warren-s-profession:
Vivie Warren, a clever young woman fresh from Cambridge, learns that her mother's wealth came from running brothels across Europe. George Bernard Shaw turns their clash into a fierce debate: Vivie, who wants honest work, against Mrs. Warren, who says the trade beat starvation and a bad marriage. The play shocked London in its day.

Shaw refuses easy villains: mother and daughter both argue well, and the men around them profit or preach as it suits them. The ending is cold and unsparing. The play still bites as a case against a society that gives poor women few honest roads.
10993-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton edited this fifth volume of The World's Greatest Books, devoted to fiction from Gray to Kingsley. Each novel gets a short life of its author and a condensed retelling: Maxwell Gray's Silence of Dean Maitland, Hawthorne's Scarlet Letter, Hugo's Les Miserables and Notre Dame, and Kingsley's Alton Locke.

The retellings keep plot and problem clear, so readers can sample famous novels quickly and choose which to read whole. Hugo's Man Who Laughs appears with Ursus the philosopher and the child he shelters in his caravan. The volume works as a guide to classic fiction, useful for students and for readers building a reading list from a century of novels.
10994-the-good-resolution:
A Sunday-school tale revised by D. P. Kidder for the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1831, this short book follows Isabella Gardner on her fourteenth birthday. Waking unhappy despite sunshine and roses, Isabella traces her misery to her own fretful temper. She has spoken angrily to her sister Mary and parted in displeasure from her brother Edward, letting the sun go down upon her wrath.

Isabella resolves to check her impatience, apologises to Mary, and learns that patience pleases both God and family. The story teaches children to own faults, seek forgiveness, and practise self-control daily. Short and direct, it shows early American Sunday-school literature at work, using one girl's birthday to press a moral lesson home.
11031-samuel-johnson:
Leslie Stephen wrote this 1878 life of Samuel Johnson, the great lexicographer and literary dictator. Johnson was born at Lichfield in 1709, son of Michael Johnson, a respected bookseller, magistrate, and sheriff, who sold books from a stall at Birmingham and other towns. As a child, Johnson was taken to Queen Anne to be touched for the king's evil, a superstition then dying out, without effect.

Stephen follows Johnson through childhood, literary career, friendships, and closing years, closing with his writings. Disease scarred his face and hurt his eyes, and hypochondria haunted him, eased only by hard work or company. Stephen judges Johnson's talk, his circle including Boswell, Goldsmith, and Sheridan, and his lasting influence on English letters, in a concise, readable biography.
11079-essays-in-rebellion:
Henry W. Nevinson, war correspondent and author of Ladysmith and The Dawn in Russia, published these essays in 1913 under the title Essays in Rebellion. Thirty-eight essays range from The Catfish and Rebellion to Deeds Not Words, The Burning Book, The Imperial Race, Fix Bayonets, and A Farewell to Fleet Street. Nevinson writes about suffrage, empire, war, and the press with the experience of a reporter.

One essay quotes Burke on conciliation with the American colonies in 1775, warning that force alone subdues only for a moment and that a nation perpetually conquered is not governed. Nevinson uses history to press present causes, defending rebels, natives under empire, and children of the state. The book gives a vivid portrait of Edwardian radical journalism.
11120-hurrah-for-new-england-or-the-virg:
A Virginia boy named Pidgie writes letters home from a New England vacation in 1846, collected in this book by the author of The Boy of Spirit. Pidgie once scorned little crooked Massachusetts on the map, but Marblehead wins him over, with queer houses set cornerwise on crooked streets, up hill and down.

Letters follow fitting out for a cruise, messmates, talk about great men, old Jack, a visit to a Cunard steamer, and Boston lions. Pidgie notes steamers fitted like drawing rooms, with glass fastened against rough weather, and ladies at ease in saloons. The book gives a Southern boy's cheerful discovery of New England, written for young readers of the 1840s.
11161-mary-wollaston:
Henry Kitchell Webster published this 1920 novel in twenty-eight chapters. Miss Lucile Wollaston, set to exude sympathy like an aphid awaiting an ant, cannot sympathise with her younger brother John. Lucile was born on the election day that made Buchanan president; John near Appomattox.

At a March 1919 breakfast, John orders ham and eggs and wheat cakes from Nathaniel, the old butler, while his eye falls on a letter in his daughter Mary's handwriting. Later chapters follow a picture puzzle, a clairvoyant interval, a case of necessity, the dramatist, and two women and John. Mary refuses to sing Dolores for anybody, and John compares fighting fate to the first bar of the Fifth Symphony. Webster's novel studies family duty and a young woman's will.
11171-uncle-tom-s-cabin-young-folks-edit:
Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin appears here in a Young Folks' Edition, simplified for child readers. The book opens by explaining slavery plainly: slaves were paid no wages, receiving only food and clothes, and buyers went to market for them as for horses, cows, tables, or chairs. Kind masters might make slaves happy, but cruel ones beat them.

Uncle Tom, a faithful servant of the kind Mr. Shelby, lives with his wife Aunt Chloe, the head cook, in a cottage covered with climbing roses. The saddest thing, the book tells children, is that families could be broken at any time by sale. Later chapters follow Eliza's flight, with Phineas and George rescuing the wounded slave-catcher Tom Loker. The edition keeps Stowe's antislavery message in language young readers can follow.
11180-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton edited this sixth volume of The World's Greatest Books, devoted to fiction and published in 1910. Contents run from Le Fanu's Uncle Silas and Lesage's Gil Blas through Lever, Lewis's Monk, Lytton's Last Days of Pompeii, Malory's Morte d'Arthur, Manzoni's Betrothed, Marryat's Mr. Midshipman Easy, Maturin's Melmoth, Mérimée's Carmen, Mitford's Our Village, and Frank Norris's Pit.

Each entry gives a brief life of the author and a summary of the novel. Le Fanu, born in Dublin in 1814, grandson of a sister of Sheridan, edited the Dublin University Magazine and wrote more than a dozen novels. In Manzoni's Betrothed, Lucia pleads with the Unnamed for mercy, promising to pray for him all her life. The volume serves as a compact guide to classic fiction for readers choosing what to read next.
11192-the-americanism-of-washington:
Henry van Dyke published this 1906 essay on the Americanism of Washington. Van Dyke warns that it is hard to say anything new about Washington, but possible to unsay things never strictly true. Washington's character, he says, passed through three media of obscuration: the mist of mythology, making him a new St. George among ever-blooming cherry-trees; the clouds of oratory, pinnacling him like a sphinx on a volcanic peak; and the fog of criticism, reducing him to a decent English country gentleman, immensely lucky.

Van Dyke rejects two claims: that Washington was a solitary phenomenon of greatness, and that he was not an American. Dignified and reserved, Washington still did his work in bonds of companionship, trusting comrades, choosing cabinet and court for service to Union rather than friendship, and risking popularity to become president. The essay restores Washington as an American hero, not a myth or an accident.
11228-the-marrow-of-tradition:
Charles W. Chesnutt's 1901 novel is set in a Southern town where Black and white families are bound by blood, secrecy, and competing claims to respectability. Two households anchor the plot: the white Carterets and the Black Millers, whose lives intersect through a shared father and a child who needs a surgeon. Around them, newspaper editors and politicians stir racial hatred toward violence.

Chesnutt builds the story toward a riot modeled on the Wilmington violence of 1898, showing how respectable citizens excuse murder as order. The novel's power comes from its refusal to soften either side's motives. It remains a central American novel about race, family, and the failure of reconciliation after slavery.
11238-the-fight-for-conservation:
Gifford Pinchot's 1910 book argues that America's prosperity rests on natural resources, and that wasting them will bring misery and failure to later generations. Chapters move from prosperity and home-building through farm life, waterways, and business to the moral issue, public spirit, and an equal chance for children. Pinchot, the first chief of the Forest Service, writes as an advocate, not a neutral observer.

His central claim is blunt: conservation is the only permanent basis of national success. The final chapter, The Present Battle, urges readers to defend public resources against private monopoly. The book helped define conservation as a political cause, and its language still echoes in debates over forests, water, and public land.
11339-aesop-s-fables-a-new-translation:
V. S. Vernon Jones's 1912 translation of Aesop's Fables, with an introduction by G. K. Chesterton and illustrations by Arthur Rackham, retells the classic animal tales in fresh English. Contents run from the Fox and the Grapes, the Goose that Laid the Golden Eggs, and the Wolf and the Lamb through the Lion and the Mouse. the North Wind and the Sun, the Boy who cried wolf in shepherd's dress, and the Ass in the Lion's Skin. Rackham's drawings accompany the text.

Chesterton's introduction defends the fables as democratic wisdom, plain morals told through beasts. Jones's versions are short and direct, suited to children and adults alike. The edition remains one of the most attractive Aesop collections, pairing a fine translator with a celebrated illustrator.
1142-typhoon:
Joseph Conrad's novella follows Captain MacWhirr, a stolid, unimaginative seaman, as he steams his ship straight into a typhoon in the China Sea rather than waste coal going around it. Below decks, Chinese coolies riot over their scattered silver while the storm tears at the ship.

MacWhirr's dull calm proves a kind of heroism: he reads no poetry and fears no storm, and his plain sense brings the ship through. Conrad writes the sea with dread and awe, and the tale ends with a wry joke about the captain's report. It stands as a masterclass in short fiction.
11469-boy-scouts-on-motorcycles-or-with-:
G. Harvey Ralphson's adventure tale sends Ned Nestor of the Wolf Patrol, Jack Bosworth, and Jimmie McGraw far from their New York clubroom into a strange land. Jimmie, freckled and homesick, longs for Broadway and the Bowery while his friends take in the smells and sights around them.

Motorcycles, a flying squadron, and a run of close scrapes drive the plot, with Taoist priests and local guides crossing the boys' path. The book is boys' adventure of its period: fast talk, loyal friends, and danger met with jokes rather than fear.
11483-the-life-and-letters-of-lewis-carr:
Stuart Dodgson Collingwood's 1898 life of his cousin Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, known as Lewis Carroll, runs from his forebears and boyhood at Daresbury and Croft through Rugby and Christ Church, Oxford. Early chapters cover school magazines, Latin verse, and the first use of the pen name.

Later chapters follow the making of Alice, the Tenniel drawings, the Tennyson friendship, and Carroll's letters to child friends. The book pairs a family memoir with a full set of letters, and it remains a first source for how Alice's Adventures in Wonderland came to be.
11499-an-essence-of-the-dusk-5th-edition:
F. W. Bain's An Essence of the Dusk, translated from the original manuscript and dedicated to the other sex, retells Hindu legend in romantic prose. Its preface explains the demon Rahu, who devoured sun and moon and causes eclipses: after stealing nectar among the gods. Vishnu's discus cut his body from his head, leaving an immortal head that grips sun and moon in revenge, prompting the doleful shout chor do at eclipses. The title means a digit of the moon in the demon's grip.

Chapters include a haunted beauty, a total eclipse, and a fatal kiss. Bain, writing in the manner of an oriental tale-teller, frames myth as philosophy. Readers of early twentieth-century oriental romance will find its Suez Canal moon-watching passage characteristic of its dreamy style.
11517-out-of-doors-california-and-oregon:
J. A. Graves's 1912 Out of Doors: California and Oregon, profusely illustrated and dedicated to his nature-loving sons Selwyn and Jackson, collects outdoor essays: a motor trip in San Diego's back country. a hunting trip in the long ago, Professor Lo philosopher, a great day's sport on Warner's Ranch. boyhood days in early California, a last quail shoot of 1911, and an auto trip through the Sierras. Illustrations range from Mount Pitt and Cuyamaca Lake to Klamath Lake, Santa Cruz Island, and Yosemite Falls.

Graves writes as a Californian who watched the state change from frontier to motor age. His essays mix hunting, motoring, and memory. Readers of western outdoor writing will enjoy its affection for San Diego County, the Sierras, and Oregon waters.
11527-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, the seventh volume of The World's Greatest Books, dated 1910, retells famous fiction in short form. Peacock, Jane Porter, Pushkin, Rabelais, Charles Reade, and Samuel Richardson open the list, with Pamela, Clarissa, and Sir Charles Grandison among Richardson's titles.

Later entries cover Richter, Rosegger, Rousseau's New Heloise, George Sand, Michael Scott, and Walter Scott, whose novels continue into volume eight. Each retelling gives plot and character in brief, so a reader can meet a long novel in a few pages before turning to the full text.
11609-the-golden-canyon:
G A Henty's 1899 volume binds two boys' tales together. The Golden Canyon follows Dick and his friends. They face a run ashore, an escape, and a search for a canyon. Gold seekers hope to strike it rich there. Water runs short on the trail.

A tree on a peak marks a place, and rifles sound in a ravine. The party turns home at last. The Stone Chest opens with a mystery in a storm. Bob goes north among icebergs to an Arctic island. A madman, a volcano of ice, and a polar bear follow. A chest found at last closes the tale.
11610-madam-crowl-s-ghost-and-the-dead-s:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu pairs two ghost tales, both first published in 1871. Madam Crowl's Ghost opens with Mrs. Jolliffe, now past seventy, her hair white as snow, still straight in figure and light in step, nursing adult invalids after years with babies.

The Dead Sexton follows, with a preacher, Dolly Jenner, and a husband who preaches to the poor in a simple style. Le Fanu tells both stories through a narrator who knows the tellers, and the dread grows from houses, churches, and old women who remember too much. The pair is a compact sample of Victorian ghost fiction.
11614-the-second-generation:
David Graham Phillips opens his 1906 novel in the Ranger-Whitney flour mills, where seven hundred workmen labour, with two hundred and fifty more in the cooperage next door. The noon whistle is six minutes off, yet every man and boy works as hard as if dinner were hours away.

Chapters follow a shattered colossus, a will, a jilting, and a long farewell, with Mrs. Whitney stepping in to negotiate. Arthur falls among lawyers, is rescued, and learns a prentice trade. Madelene, Lorry, and Hiram's son carry the second generation's story, as wealth, love, and duty collide.
11659-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Edited by Arthur Mee and J A Hammerton, the eighth volume of The World's Greatest Books, dated 1910, continues Scott with Quentin Durward, Rob Roy, and The Talisman. Mary Shelley, Philip Sidney, Smollett, Madame de Staël, and Stendhal follow in the contents list.

Later entries cover Sterne's Tristram Shandy, Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin, Sue's Mysteries of Paris, Swift's Gulliver, and Thackeray's Vanity Fair. Tolstoy, Trollope, Turgenev, Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues, Walpole, and Zola close the list. Each novel is retold in brief, for readers who want the story and the characters before turning to the full book itself.
11668-the-gold-hunters-a-story-of-life-a:
James Oliver Curwood's 1909 story, The Gold Hunters, opens at noon in a Canadian forest, where moose and caribou rest, a lynx waits in rocks, and a fox sleeps. An old hunter takes off his pack, gathers wood, eats dinner, and smokes his pipe.

Chapters follow the pursuit of the Hudson Bay mail, with Rod, Wabi, and Mukoki on the trail. A shot that missed Mukoki's head by two inches, marked by a fresh hole in a tree, shows the danger close at hand. The book is a Hudson Bay adventure of gold, pursuit, and friendship in the northern wilds.
11676-the-balkan-wars-1912-1913-third-ed:
Jacob Gould Schurman's Balkan Wars, third edition dated 1916, opens with a postscript on Romania joining the Allies and declaring war on Austria-Hungary. Greece, he notes, may soon follow, after King Constantine's opposition delayed both countries.

The main text looks back to the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913, with Austria-Hungary seeking an outlet through Macedonia to Saloniki and Serbia seeking the Adriatic. Self-interest, Schurman argues, controls politics, though it is not the only force. The book is a wartime history by a university president, written as the larger war widened.
11713-the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-0:
Grenville Kleiser's third volume of The World's Great Sermons, covering Massillon to Mason, opens with Massillon, born at Hyères in 1663, famed for funeral sermons that won him preferment from Meaux. His sermon on the small number of the elect leads the set.

Later preachers include Saurin on Paul before Felix and Drusilla, Edwards on spiritual light, Wesley on God's love to fallen man, and Whitefield on the method of grace. Blair, Dwight, Hall, Evans, Schleiermacher, and Mason close the volume. A passage on Isaac, David, the brazen serpent, and the smitten rock reads them all as types of Christ's death.
11748-french-conversation-and-compositio:
Harry Vincent Wann wrote French Conversation and Composition as a school book. He was a teacher of Romance tongues at Indiana State Normal School. The book joins short tales with drills in grammar, lesson by lesson.

Lesson one covers the definite and indefinite articles, plain questions, and short forms of de and à with the definite article. Later lessons take up possessive adjectives and the place of adjectives. Future and conditional tenses come next, with the pointing adjective. Voici, voilà, and il y a follow, with phrases using avoir. Tales include honesty rewarded and a visit returned, with Triboulet pleading to François the First.
11860-black-beauty-young-folks-edition:
Anna Sewell's Black Beauty, in this 1902 young folks' edition, tells the life of a horse in the horse's own voice, beginning with an early home the narrator remembers well. The opening chapter sets a gentle, pastoral tone before the story moves through kindness, cruelty, hard work, and changing owners.

Written to teach humane treatment of animals, the novel lets Black Beauty observe grooms, cab drivers, and ladies with a moral clarity children could grasp. Its enduring appeal rests on that simple device: a working animal's point of view. That view argues that patience and kindness are duties, not favors, toward creatures that cannot speak for themselves.
11892-gardening-for-the-million:
Alfred Pink's Gardening for the Million, by the author of Recipes for the Million, aims to stimulate the cultivation of gardens more beautiful than those generally met with. Published by T. Fisher Unwin, it offers practical entries for ordinary gardeners rather than a treatise for experts, and it does not repeat flowering times in every case.

Entries give soil, water, and position in plain terms: clivias, or Caffre lilies, need leaf-mould, loam. Sand, with liberal water in full growth and restraint from September to February, while homerias, little South African plants, want bulbs three inches deep in rich, light, well-drained soil. The book's value is its density of usable detail, plant by plant, for small gardens.
11978-brave-tom-or-the-battle-that-won:
Edward S. Ellis's Brave Tom, or The Battle That Won, first in the Brave and Honest Series, appeared in 1894 with illustrations. It opens on a summer day in Briggsville, Pennsylvania, where a village is thrown into excitement. An illustration shows a boy calling, pull up, I am all right.

Later episodes turn on lost money, a duke and his captive. A boy of education hired to write letters, keep accounts, and make himself generally useful aboard a small coasting schooner. Ellis writes for young readers who liked pluck rewarded: Tom's honesty and steadiness, tested in village scrapes and seafaring work, win the battle of the title without grand heroics.
12025-english-prose-a-series-of-related-:
English Prose, a series of related essays for the discussion and practice of the art of writing, appeared in 1913. It was selected and edited by Frederick William Roe of the University of Wisconsin and George Roy Elliott of Bowdoin College. Its first section, The Personal Life, opens with Emerson's Self-Reliance, Ruskin's Early Education at Herne Hill, and a crisis in mental history.

The anthology arranges essays so students can study how writers think on the page, not merely what they say. By grouping personal, descriptive, and argumentative prose together, Roe and Elliott made a textbook for composition classes, one that treats reading good prose as the first step toward writing it.
12084-revelations-of-a-wife-the-story-of:
Adele Garrison published this novel in 1915 as the story of a honeymoon and the marriage that follows it. Told in the first person by the young wife, it follows the couple from wedding day through early quarrels, travel, and the slow work of learning each other.

Chapters move through jealousy, money worries, in-laws, illness, and old lovers who reappear at bad moments. The heroine narrates with candor about her own faults as well as her husband, and the book treats marriage as a daily negotiation rather than a romance ending. Popular in its day, it now reads as a frank record of what middle-class American wives were expected to bear, and what they quietly questioned.
12172-alone-in-london:
Hesba Stretton wrote this Victorian tale of street children in London, first published in the 1860s and long popular as a Sunday-school story. Stretton, known for Jessica First Prayer, aimed to stir pity and charity among middle-class readers.

The plot follows Tony, a crossing sweeper, and Dolly, a small girl left alone after loss and illness separate them from kin. Through hunger, hospital stays, theft, and small acts of kindness, the children cling to each other across the city. The ending turns on faith and reunion rather than realism. Modern readers may find the moral plain, but the street scenes give a vivid sense of poor London childhood.
12186-the-principles-of-masonic-law-a-tr:
Albert G. Mackey, grand lecturer and grand secretary of the Grand Lodge of South Carolina, wrote this treatise on Masonic law. Mackey, author of the Lexicon of Freemasonry, aimed to set out the constitutional laws, usages, and landmarks of the order.

The book explains lodge government, officers duties, balloting, and appeals. One passage shows how a ballot box is prepared, placed on the altar, and put to a roll call from master to youngest member. It weighs ancient landmarks against modern custom and local rule. Written for Masons who governed lodges, the treatise became a standard reference in American Freemasonry, prized for its order and its claim to speak from the craft own law.
12240-the-lady-and-sada-san-a-sequel-to-:
Frances Little published The Lady and Sada San in 1912 as a sequel to The Lady of the Decoration. Told in letters from aboard ship and from Japan, the book follows an American woman traveling in the Orient with friends.

The narrator writes to a mate back in Kentucky. She describes leaving home after years abroad, crossing the seas in June 1911, and meeting Sada San, a Japanese companion whose story gives the book its heart. Letters mix travel detail, humor, and observation of Japanese manners, schools, and homes. Little writes for readers who enjoyed the first book gentle exoticism. The sequel is lighter than a guidebook and warmer than a report, a friendly account of East meeting West.
12261-balder-the-beautiful-volume-i-a-st:
J. G. Frazer published Balder the Beautiful, volume one, in 1913 as part seven of The Golden Bough, his study in magic and religion. Frazer, fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, treats the Norse god Balder through the fire festivals of Europe and the doctrine of the external soul.

Chapters move between heaven and earth, sacred kings, and the priest of Aricia. Then come midsummer bonfires: a girl who danced round nine bonfires would marry within the year, and leaping over fire purified and kept off sickness. The volume treats Balder myth as preserving old rites of kingship and seasonal death. The volume is dense with folklore, and its comparative method shaped anthropology for decades, even where later scholars dispute its conclusions.
12265-the-flying-legion:
George Allan England published The Flying Legion in July 1920, a pulp adventure novel of aviators, lost worlds, and secret masters. England, a popular science fiction writer, fills the book with airships, storms, and desert perils.

Chapters run from a spirit caged and a gathering of legionaries through the nest of the great bird. Later come the eagle of the sky, eastward ho, a masked recruit, and a captain stands revealed. A mid-book scene has Rrisa save a man from the jinnee of the desert, amid a hail of slugs bombarding a vast airship. The novel mixes aviation thrills with Arabian Nights fantasy. It reads as pure 1920s pulp, fast, colorful, and unashamed.
12302-all-in-it-k-1-carries-on:
Ian Hay published All In It in 1917, a wartime novel about K (1), a young second lieutenant, and his battalion in France. Hay dedicated the book to all second lieutenants, and in particular to the memory of one.

The story follows K (1) from training through trench warfare, with chapters on getting together, the first hundred thousand, and carrying on under shell fire. Hay, who served himself, writes with humor about officers mess life and with gravity about attacks that depend on artillery lifting its curtain at the right moment. The novel was popular with soldiers and civilians alike. It reads now as a humane, unsentimental record of junior officers at war.
12364-the-united-states-in-the-light-of-:
Uriah Smith's 1874 exposition reads Revelation 13:11-17 as a prophecy about the United States. The two-horned beast of the passage, he argues, fits a young republic rising in a new land, speaking with lamb-like professions while gaining power. Smith writes for readers who believe the signs of their own age point toward closing events.

Step by step he matches symbols to American history, law and religion, and warns that liberty may give way to coercion. The book belongs to Adventist prophecy writing of its time, earnest in tone and close in its handling of text. Its interest now lies in that reading itself: how one nineteenth-century faith community saw its own nation inside Scripture.
12386-samantha-at-the-st-louis-expositio:
Marietta Holley, writing as Josiah Allen wife, published Samantha at the St. Louis Exposition in 1904, illustrated by Ch. Grunwald. Holley Samantha books, in rural dialect, sent a commonsense farm wife to confront modern America.

Samantha and Josiah travel to the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, marveling at crowds surging through the Pike and at fifteen dollars shown carelessly in cash. Josiah good nature returns with every mouthful he takes, while Samantha judges exhibits, foreigners, and new inventions with moral clarity. The humor lies in dialect and in Samantha shrewd eye. The book is a folk record of the 1904 fair, as seen by small-town America.
12387-paul-faber-surgeon:
George MacDonald's novel follows Paul Faber, a surgeon in the country town of Glaston, and the rector, Mr. Bevis, whose carriage Faber meets with a bold jump over a hedge in the opening lane scene. Around them gather manor house, rectory, chapel and cottage, with Juliet, a minister and a circle of neighbours whose lives cross in love, doubt and duty.

Faber, a man of science with a stern manner and a kind eye, argues with faith while tending bodies, and the novel tests conscience, prayer and moral choice through village crises. MacDonald writes at length, in a Victorian manner, letting talk and inward struggle carry the story. The book stands as a study of belief under pressure, set in ordinary parish life.
12454-france-at-war-on-the-frontier-of-c:
Rudyard Kipling's 1915 book, France at War, reports France in the first year of the Great War. A poem to France opens the volume, praising a nation broke to every mischance yet lifted by a sane joy of life. Chapters follow: the frontier of civilisation, the nation's spirit, battle spectacle, the spirit of the people, life in mountain trenches and the common task.

Kipling writes as an admiring witness, not a soldier, honouring French endurance and sacrifice. His prose is vivid and rhetorical, shaped for British readers who needed to believe in an ally. The book stands as wartime propaganda of a high literary kind, and as a record of how France looked to an English friend in 1915.
12539-observations-upon-the-windward-coa:
Joseph Corry's 1807 observations, made on the Windward Coast of Africa in 1805 and 1806, describe the religion, character and customs of native peoples. An illustration shows a Mandingo chief and his headman in costume, with other natives. Corry also proposes a system by which those peoples might be civilised, and the interior better known.

Natural and commercial resources of the country fill later pages, with an appendix containing a letter to Lord Howick on the simplest means of abolishing the slave trade. Corry writes as a reforming observer, earnest about trade, missions and abolition. The book is a period document, valuable for its detail and revealing in its assumptions about empire.
12540-george-washington:
William Roscoe Thayer's 1922 life of George Washington, in the Riverside Library, moves from origins and youth through marriage and plantation life to war and presidency. Chapters cover the first gun, Boston freed, Trenton and Valley Forge, aid from France, traitors, return to peace, welding the nation and the Jay Treaty.

Thayer draws on Channing, Fiske and Ford's writings of Washington, listed in his abbreviations. He presents Washington as a man of character formed by duty, patience and command. The biography reads as an early twentieth-century American life, respectful and narrative, suited to general readers who wanted the founder whole, from planter to president.
1263-the-glimpses-of-the-moon:
Edith Wharton tells of Nick Lansing and Susy Branch, two poor young people of good society who marry on a bargain. They will live on wedding gifts and rich friends' houses for a year, then part if love fails. The novel follows them through Paris, Venice, and Rome as the bargain frays.

Wharton writes the marriage market with irony and pity, and the pair's slow discovery of real love gives the tale its ache. The book, from her later years, shows her craft at full polish. It suits readers who like Wharton on wealth, manners, and the price of freedom.
12700-ralph-waldo-emerson:
Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote this 1891 life of Ralph Waldo Emerson for the American Men of Letters series. It follows Emerson from his Boston pastorate, through his break with his church, to Concord, lectures, and the essays that made his name. Marriage, loss, and friendship with Thoreau and Margaret Fuller shape the portrait.

Holmes stresses Emerson's role as a voice of self-trust and plain moral courage in a changing America. The Dial, his journal with friends, shows his circle at its most hopeful, despite a thin subscription list. The biography remains a warm, readable guide to a thinker more read than easily summed up.
12775-dave-darrin-s-fourth-year-at-annap:
Dave Darrin's fourth and final year at Annapolis heads toward graduation and the big cruise. First-classman Dave and Dan Dalzell face pranks, bad money, treachery from a classmate named Morton, and a search at the bottom of Chesapeake Bay. Football against West Point and a prize trip on the Dodger lighten the term.

Dan's scrapes keep landing both friends in trouble, while Dave must steady the class and speak for it when the moment comes. Graduation Day at last closes their academy years. Hancock's finale gives loyal readers the send-off his heroes earned across four volumes.
12792-the-young-captives-a-story-of-juda:
Erasmus W. Jones set this 1907 historical novel in Judah on the eve of the Babylonian captivity. A proud king feasts while a warning voice sounds in his halls, and young captives are carried to Babylon to be schooled in the conqueror's court. Questions put to the youths test their learning and their nerve.

The story follows the captives as they hold to their faith and wits under a foreign king, facing feasts, courts, and trials of knowledge. Jones writes in a earnest, Bible-coloured style for young readers. The novel aims to make the exile vivid: home lost, yet courage and learning kept alive in a strange land.
12870-the-boy-allies-on-the-firing-line-:
Clair W. Hayes set this Boy Allies tale along the Marne in 1915, during twelve days of battle. Hal Paine and Chester Crawford, guiding forty-eight British troopers ten miles ahead of the main army, reconnoitre at dawn and meet terrible odds. Riding, retreat, and night marches carry the plot.

A dusk scene finds the boys at a brook, fleeing the traitor Dersi's motorcycle pursuers and searchlight toward a clump of trees. Hayes keeps the pace brisk and the danger close. Young war readers got here a straightforward tale of pluck under fire on the Western Front.
12947-the-boy-scouts-of-the-flying-squad:
Robert Shaler's Boy Scouts of the Flying Squadron follows Hugh and Bud, Wolf Patrol boys hauling loads over frozen Stormberg mountain after a big Thanksgiving dinner. A lift from Farmer Badgely helps them toward a shanty by nightfall, and their path soon crosses aeroplanes, a mysterious explosion, and Uncle Sam's flying squadron. War monoplanes and foreign spies follow.

Bud's model aeroplane work anchors the middle: he tunes wire stays, fits a motor, and plans a rudder that will circle a field until its gasoline runs out. A cord jerk tests whether the device holds. The book blends scout hiking with early aviation wonder.
12955-consanguineous-marriages-in-the-am:
George B. Louis Arner's 1908 Columbia study examines marriages between blood relations in the American population. Arner, a university fellow in sociology, draws on genealogists, census data, and cases supplied by friends, with special thanks to Alexander Graham Bell and other scholars. Tables compare consanguineous and non-consanguineous families in Ohio and elsewhere.

The study notes its limits frankly: stock tales from isolated towns were left out as too hard to verify, and animal inbreeding results do not map neatly onto people. Selected cases from Bemiss, where nearly a third of children showed defects, skew averages. The work stands as an early, data-minded look at kin marriage.
12968-our-government-local-state-and-nat:
Our Government, Local, State, and National, by J. A. James of Northwestern University and A. H. Sanford of La Crosse, is a 1903 school textbook revised in 1913, here in the Idaho edition. It moves from local work, county rule, and city rule to the making of the Union, the Constitutional Convention, and the branches of the federal state.

Chapters explain how Congress makes laws, what powers it holds and lacks, and how the president, cabinet, and courts act. Interstate commerce, river and harbor bills, and the full texts of the Constitution and Articles of Confederation round out a plain civics course for American pupils.
12970-the-head-hunters-of-northern-luzon:
Cornélis De Witt Willcox, lieutenant-colonel of the U.S. Army, wrote The Head Hunters of Northern Luzon in 1912 from a ride through the mountains from Ifugao to Kalinga. Chapters cover Igorot trails, annual inspections, Padre Villaverde's great trail, Ilongot country, and the mountain province, with an appendix on Philippine independence. Baguio starts the journey.

A burial rite shows the book's detail: Aliguyen, killed by Kurug men, was left unwrapped to anger his spirit toward vengeance, his tomb walled with stones and an egg dashed against it. Willcox writes as soldier and observer. The book remains a vivid early account of Luzon's highland peoples.
12996-true-version-of-the-philippine-rev:
Emilio Aguinaldo, president of the Philippine Republic, wrote this account at Tarlak on September 23, 1899, and addressed it to civilized nations and above all to the United States. He presents it as a plain statement of facts about the Philippine struggle over the past three years, meant to let readers judge the justice of his cause. The tone is that of a leader pleading his case before the world.

Aguinaldo recounts dealings with American consuls, arms shipments, and broken promises, including money deposited with Consul Wildman for weapons that never came. He describes camps short of arms, commissioners asking what terms the United States would impose, and his own refusal to break a secret agreement. The book is a first-hand political plea, valuable as the voice of the revolution's leader, not as a neutral history.
13107-the-new-south-a-chronicle-of-socia:
Holland Thompson's 1919 chronicle, part of the Chronicles of America series, describes the American South after the Civil War. Thompson warns that the New South is not a wholly new land, but the old South changed by war, work, and law. Chapters cover the soldier in charge, the common man's revolt, farming, industry, labor, race, schools, and the South of his own day.

He details sharecropping, where a crop was split in thirds among land, stock and tools, and labor. He also faces the race question plainly, rejecting removal and separate states as unworkable, and pointing to education and wealth as the slow road to equal standing. The book is a sober early survey, useful for how a 1919 historian framed a region still in flux.
13138-the-forgotten-threshold-a-journal-:
The Forgotten Threshold presents itself as the journal of Arthur Middleton, given to a friend before his death. The editor says Middleton knew much in silence that he could never turn into speech, and that only the wonder in his eyes showed the dream that filled his heart. The journal is thus a fragment, transcribed in hope that beauty speaks deeper than plain words.

Entries move from bathing on dunes at Wonder Island to a sunset that felt sacramental, and to a wish that a friend share the Holy Eucharist. Later pages swell into visions of swimming through light, hearing music as divinity, and tasting the Body and Blood. The book is a short, intense work of religious mysticism, written in a private, lyrical voice.
13169-the-prose-works-of-jonathan-swift-:
Volume nine of Jonathan Swift's prose works was edited by Temple Scott. Published by George Bell and Sons in 1902, it gathers his pieces for The Tatler, The Examiner, The Spectator, and The Intelligencer. A portrait from Charles Jervas fronts the book. Swift wrote these papers in the heat of party war, and they show his pen at its sharpest.

Notes explain rivals such as Defoe's Review, which lost its spring and ended in June 1713, and the Observator of John Tutchin, once sentenced by Judge Jeffreys. One paper takes up Mr. Greenshields, prosecuted in Scotland for reading Church of England service to his own folk. The volume is a key source for Swift the journalist, not just Swift the satirist of books.
13179-the-poems-of-william-watson:
William Watson's Poems, published by Macmillan in New York and London in 1893, gathers lyrics, sonnets, and longer pieces from the early 1890s. Contents run from Autumn and World-Strangeness to poems on Landor, Tennyson, Ireland, and England and her colonies. Watson writes in a high, musical style, fond of nature, history, and public themes.

Short lyrics muse on time, spring, and the dance of life, where men start at the cold touch of eternity and cast cloaks about them. Longer verse laments a prince whose heart breaks under grief like a bitter wind, and a land left desolate when no prophet warns it. The collection shows a Victorian poet of craft and feeling, now less read than he was.
13249-our-vanishing-wild-life-its-exterm:
William T. Hornaday's Our Vanishing Wild Life, in two parts on extermination and preservation, opens with an 1857 Ohio Senate report that the passenger pigeon needed no protection. The report called the bird wonderfully prolific, with vast northern forests for breeding, and said no ordinary destruction could lessen its myriads. A photo of the last living passenger pigeon, twenty years old in 1912 at Cincinnati, answers that claim.

Hornaday also quotes laws that made a gun in an unnaturalized resident's home prima facie proof of ownership, and urges every state to act before bird life is attacked. His final chapters teach how to make a new game law, with quick action in a crisis. The book is a landmark plea for conservation, angry, factual, and practical.
13266-final-report-of-the-louisiana-purc:
Senate Document 202, from the 59th Congress, first session, gives the final report of the Louisiana Purchase Exposition Commission, printed at Washington in 1906. It was read on February 8, 1906, and referred to the Committee on Industrial Expositions. Contents include letters of transmittal, the final report, Centennial Day, Diplomatic Day, State Day, and appendices.

Appendices report accounts, receipts, salvage, foreign countries, states, and the Board of Lady Managers. One state exhibit, with stone walls of Sioux Falls jasper and Hot Springs sandstone, won a gold medal for ores, rocks, and fossils. The report is a dry official record, valuable for the fair's money, exhibits, and organization.
13276-the-mission:
Captain Marryat's Mission, or Scenes in Africa, written for young people and published by Routledge, follows Alexander Wilmot's search for his lost family. Sir Charles Wilmot doubts whether his wife and children survived the wreck of the Grosvenor, and Alexander plans a journey inland to learn their fate. His father opposes, then consents with reluctance.

On the way, hunters face elephants in a row, snorting and gaining fast, while a man reserves fire and runs for rocks fifty paces off. Lion hunting is described as a service of danger, where half the party fires first and the rest finish the beast, often at the cost of horses. Marryat's tale mixes adventure, natural history, and empire romance for young readers.
13325-sketches-of-the-natural-history-of:
Sir J. Emerson Tennent's 1861 Sketches of the Natural History of Ceylon gathers the zoological chapters of his larger work on the island, with engravings from original drawings. It covers mammals, birds, reptiles, fishes, and insects, and adds a monograph on the elephant with modes of capturing and training it. Tennent writes as a colonial governor turned naturalist.

He cites Sir Everard Home on the elephant's stomach, whose grand cul-de-sac holds ten gallons of water, and lists Ceylon's lizards and snakes in long Latin catalogues. The book mixes anecdote with anatomy, and it shows Victorian science at work in a tropical colony. Its elephant chapters remain its most famous part.
13330-the-last-reformation:
F. G. Smith argues that the church must return to its apostolic shape. He first defines the church, universal and local, and its organisation and government in the days of the apostles. Then he traces corruption, the rise of priestly power, the Reformation, and the modern sects that followed it.

A final part reads prophecy, from the apostolic age through the medieval period to the age of sects, and points toward a last reformation. Smith writes as a teacher of Scripture, using the Bible and early church writers to test later custom. His call is plain: strip away human additions and restore the faith and order of the first church.
13370-q-e-d-or-new-light-on-the-doctrine:
George McCready Price's 1917 Q.E.D., or New Light on the Doctrine of Creation, comes from a professor of chemistry and physics at Lodi Academy, California. It argues that science sets the reader square with Genesis again. Contents run from matter and its origin and the origin of energy to life only from life, the cell, what a species is, Mendelism, geology, and creation and the Creator. Price writes as a creationist critic of evolution.

He holds that the chief difference between living and not-living lies in origin, since crystals grow outside and liquids grow by intussusception, much as animals grow by eating food. Later, he claims no device has originated a single genetic factor not already latent in ancestry, and all forms left alone tend to degenerate, as sugar beet and corn prove. The book is a classic of early creationist argument.
13384-the-covered-wagon:
Emerson Hough's 1922 novel follows families who leave Missouri in covered wagons for the far West. Molly Wingate and her husband Jesse anchor one household, while Will Banion, a younger leader, drives much of the trail action. Rivalry, courtship, and a broken wedding run beside river crossings, buffalo country, quicksand, and fights at fords.

The wagon road itself is the main subject: camps, encampments, plains, the Rockies, and finally Oregon and the Sierra country. Hough mixes trail hardship with romance and frontier figures such as Jim Bridger and Kit Carson. Love, loyalty, and revenge keep pulling the travelers apart, even as the shared road forces them on together.
13432-miss-bretherton:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1888 novel Miss Bretherton opens on a private view day at the Royal Academy. With carriages crowding Burlington House and guests pressing up red-carpeted stairs past scarlet officials second only to beefeaters in glory. Inside, pictures and spring dresses fill rooms still thin before luncheon.

The heroine, an actress, picks a primrose to pieces and flings it away. Insisting she is not jealous of a great actress she refuses to see, because she cannot separate the acting from the woman. A prefatory note ties the play Elvira, in chapter seven, to a little known Romantic writer who died tragically in 1836. Ward studies art, fame, and a young woman's pride.
13436-authorised-guide-to-the-tower-of-l:
W. J. Loftie's authorised guide to the Tower of London, revised edition of 1904 and reprinted in 1907, sold at the Tower for one penny. Twelve views, two plans, and a description of the armoury by Viscount Dillon, curator of the Tower armouries, guide the visitor round the fortress.

The general sketch traces the Tower to William the Conqueror in 1078, built to protect and control the city, with two bastions of the old London wall removed to make room. Inside, the Chapel of St. John stands as the largest and most complete Norman castle chapel remaining. Armour notes weigh suits, from John of Gaunt's absent armour to the Earl of Worcester's massive plates of 1589.
13548-cambridge-essays-on-education:
Cambridge Essays on Education, edited by A. C. Benson, Master of Magdalene College, with an introduction by Viscount Bryce, gathers 1919 reflections on school reform. John Lewis Paton opens on the aim of educational reform, William Ralph Inge on training the reason, and other Cambridge writers follow on science, religion, and teaching.

Paton argues that schools, homes, and mothers hold the richest opportunity to break partition walls between Christian education and Christian life. Another essay warns that many teachers are not and can never be made scientific, so no schedule or Board order will make their work resemble science. The volume shows post-war Cambridge debating what schools should teach and why.
13583-the-correspondence-of-thomas-carly:
The correspondence of Thomas Carlyle and Ralph Waldo Emerson, 1834 to 1872, volume one, edited by Charles Eliot Norton in 1883 and revised with thirteen recovered Carlyle letters and four by Emerson. Emerson calls a letter a spiritual gift, worthy to give and receive, while Carlyle seeks what the writer actually meant, thought, and was.

Friends send kind wishes from Concord, Channing's discourse is read with estimation, and the black question of slavery lies beyond Carlyle's ken, to be settled somehow by might and right. Lord Durham's people bring golden reports of Americans, and Arthur Buller urges Carlyle to lecture across the Union. The letters show two great minds, Atlantic apart, testing each other's thought for nearly forty years.
13611-studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-v:
Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, volume two on sexual inversion, third edition of 1927. Treats homosexuality as a problem left over from the Middle Ages, when inverts were dealt with as heretics and witches were. Ellis stresses its social and humanitarian interest alongside its biological and psychological significance.

Case histories fill the volume, told in the subjects' own terms: a dreamy youth whose brother shares his tendencies. A sister of little sexual inclination, and a woman who resolved never to let her heart go out again after a friend's long illness. Ellis argues for understanding over punishment, mapping a field long clouded by law and prejudice with clinical care.
13660-the-correspondence-of-thomas-carly:
Thomas Carlyle in London and Ralph Waldo Emerson in Concord wrote to each other from 1834 to 1872. This second volume covers the middle years of that long friendship. Letters discuss books, publishers, money, travel, and the politics of their day. Each man also reports on his own writing and health with striking candour.

Emerson sends funds, news of Alcott, and plans for essays and the Dial. Carlyle answers with work on Cromwell, thoughts on Sterling, and sharp views of London life. Their tones differ: Emerson stays hopeful, while Carlyle grows darker and more impatient. Together the letters trace two major minds testing ideas across the Atlantic. They also show friendship surviving distance and disagreement.
13785-the-glory-of-english-prose-letters:
Stephen Coleridge wrote these letters to his grandson on the glory of English prose. Published in 1922, the book moves from good and bad style to the Bible, Raleigh, Hooker, and Shakespeare. Later letters treat Browne, Milton, Jeremy Taylor, and other masters. Each letter pairs a short passage with plain advice on reading.

Coleridge argues that great prose grows from clear thought and honest feeling. He warns against vague, inflated writing and praises rhythm, order, and truth. A quotation from Dr. Johnson heads the book: the glory of a people lies in its authors. The letters suit students and general readers alike. They offer a humane guide to English literature.
13840-the-sign-of-the-red-cross-a-tale-o:
Evelyn Everett-Green set The Sign of the Red Cross in London during the Great Plague. A master builder scoffs at warnings, calling plague talk an old scare. Rachel Harmer, spinning at her wheel, answers that vice and profligacy invite judgment. A warning whisper opens the tale, and the red cross soon marks infected houses.

Everett-Green follows families through fear, flight, and faith. Young lovers, nurses, and clergy face death with courage or panic. The novel teaches duty and trust in God amid disaster. Its old London setting, with streets, shops, and churches, feels vivid. The book suits young readers and fans of historical romance alike.
13888-bacon:
R. W. Church, Dean of St. Paul's, wrote this life of Francis Bacon for the English Men of Letters series, edited by John Morley. Bacon grew up among the chiefs of a rising religion at a crisis of English history. Church follows his rise at court, his philosophy, and his fall. The series sets Bacon beside Johnson, Gibbon, Scott, and Shelley.

Church weighs Bacon's genius against his moral failures with fairness. He explains the Essays, the Novum Organum, and the dream of natural knowledge. Bacon's boyhood among high places shaped his ambition. The life is short, clear, and judicious. It remains a good introduction to Bacon for general readers.
13910-a-book-of-exposition:
Homer Heath Nugent Laflin edited A Book of Exposition in 1922 for students of English at Rensselaer Polytechnic. It gathers model expositions on mechanisms, machines, processes, and ideas. Sir Arthur Keith explains levers of the human body. Philip T. Dodge describes the Mergenthaler linotype, and Fabre treats the pea weevil.

Other pieces cover modern paper-making, William James on relaxation, and Steinmetz on science and religion. A passage on head joints shows how two aims, mobility and hearing, shape design. Biographical notes aid teachers. The book teaches clear explanation through example. It suits students of writing and of early twentieth-century technology.
14016-john-knox-and-the-reformation:
This biography of John Knox, transcribed from the 1905 Longmans edition, follows the Scottish Reformer from ancestry to death. Chapter one covers birth, education, and environment from about 1513 to 1546. A burgess's diary for November 24, 1572 records Knox's death, blaming him for Scotland's sorrows since the cardinal's slaughter. The biographer weighs that charge with care.

Knox, if he sowed wild oats, stays silent as the tomb about repentance. His years as one of Baal's shaven sort, a priest, precede conversion. The book follows preaching, exile, and return to Edinburgh. It suits readers of Reformation history. Knox emerges as stern, learned, and fiercely convinced.
14094-the-suppressed-poems-of-alfred-lor:
J. C. Thomson gathered Tennyson's early and uncollected verse in this volume, covering the years 1830 to 1868. The contents range from the prize poem Timbuctoo to lyrics, sonnets, and songs first printed in magazines or annuals. Love, loss, and night skies recur, alongside war songs and national verses that show a young poet testing his voice. Greek lines and choruses hint at his classical reading.

Scholars value the book for what Tennyson left out of his collected works. Some pieces are slight, but others carry the music that later made his name: clear images, rolling rhythms, and a keen ear for vowel sound. A sonnet on eyes of black, brown, and blue shows the charm plainly. Read as a whole, the collection traces a major poet's apprenticeship, from eager student verse to the assured lyric craft of his middle years.
14104-our-changing-constitution:
Charles W. Pierson's 1922 study asks how the American Constitution changes without formal amendment. Practice, court rulings, and congressional pressure all shift the balance between nation and states. The Supreme Court holds a central place, since its power to void laws rests on moral force rather than armies. Pierson traces its role, its members, and the limits that hedge its judgments.

Concrete cases carry the argument. A tax on employers of child labor, framed under the revenue power, tests whether Congress can undo a court decision and seize a state power. Debates over excise taxes, franchises, and uniformity show lawyers wrestling with the text. Pierson warns that quiet change can remake the charter while leaving its words intact. Students of government still find the book a clear guide to amendment by usage.
14175-buffalo-roost-a-story-of-a-young-m:
F. H. Cheley, boys' work director at South Bend, wrote this 1913 YMCA story around Willis Thornton, a boy who shows pluck from the first train ride. A promise made, a mine sought, and a wilderness camp follow. Chapters trace a stage road journey, days out in camp, a glimpse of Buffalo Roost, and the discovery of a mine tied to Willis's father.

Memory drives the quest. Willis barely remembers his father except through his mother's stories and pictures, but miners praise the man as the finest young fellow who ever set a hoisting plant in the hills. An uncle, a vanished friend named Kieser, and a crooked claim complicate the trail. Cheley writes for boys who build cabins and character together, and the old cabin in Buffalo Park, with its fireplace heart, stands for the fellowship the story praises.
1419-mugby-junction:
Set at a draughty railway junction, this Christmas book follows Barbox Brothers, a lonely clerk who steps off a train into rain and wind. He finds a lodging, a kind landlady, and, in time, a purpose he had lost sight of, as the junction's comings and goings draw him back to other people.

Short linked episodes carry Barbox from a cold waiting room to a sickroom, a schoolroom, and a new household of his own making. The humour is warm and the feeling plain. It is a seasonal tale about a man stopped mid-journey who learns, almost by accident, how to live again.
14243-christopher-carson-familiarly-know:
John S. C. Abbott wrote this 1874 life of Christopher Carson, the scout known as Kit Carson. It follows him from boyhood on the edge of the settled land into the far West. Trapping, guiding, and fighting fill the tale, told in the brisk style of a boys' adventure book. Carson stands at the center as a hardy frontiersman who knew the trails and the tribes of the Rockies.

Carson leads bands over the main ridge of the Rockies to trap along the Laramie River. He bargains for furs, plans routes to Taos, and faces hostile bands on open ground. In one scene he knocks a captor down with a blow, then talks the rest of the band to a halt in their own tongue. The book praises his nerve, skill, and fair dealing. It gives a hero's view of the West and its rough code.
14295-letters-on-international-copyright:
H. C. Carey wrote these letters on international copyright, printed in an edition in 1868. They frame the fight as authors against readers, makers of books against users of facts and ideas. Carey warns that authors, having won longer terms, now want wider space: rights across the whole British Empire. He argues from the public's side, not the trade's. The letters read as a brief for cheap books and open reading.

Carey notes that the man who found a use for chloroform was never paid, while courts stay busy with men who make the goods. A house builder, he says, quarries his own stone, but a book maker builds on the common stock of thought. Press claims for more rights, he warns, may push readers to ask whether rights should stand at all. Cheap print, he adds, feeds local life. The letters still speak to debates on who owns ideas.
14298-the-art-of-interior-decoration:
Grace Wood wrote this guide to the art of interior decoration, built round plates of fine rooms. One plate shows a tea table, two chairs, and Italian vases that once held a chemist's drugs. The mirror is Italian Louis the Sixteenth, the sconces and chairs French. Wood teaches balance, repose, and line, with grace added. The book speaks to readers who want rooms that charm without show.

Bathrooms get a full chapter, with robes hung, towels dried, and mirrors set in both doors. Wood notes that Napoleon lined his Fontainebleau dressing room with mirrors, so no man need call them effeminate. A woman's bathroom of glass walls, gold trellis, and painted tin ivy shows what fancy can do. Victorian beadwork, wax flowers, and Bristol glass return as touches of color. The book urges rooms with light and shade, never one rigid type.
14326-ulster-s-stand-for-union:
Ronald McNeill wrote this 1922 history of Ulster's stand for union with Britain. It follows the Ulster Unionist Council from the Home Rule fight through the Covenant, the Curragh Incident, and the Great War. McNeill writes from the Unionist side, with pride in the movement's discipline. The book dedicates itself to the memory of the Unionist Party. It reads as both history and apologia.

Despatch riders on motor cycles freed the Council from the Post Office, which it used as little as possible. Post houses linked the chief centers, and signals along the Down and Antrim coast ran complete and effective. During the Curragh Incident, news reached Belfast two or three times a day by this route, faster than London knew it. The book shows a movement run like an army. Its strength, McNeill says, lay in order and resolve.
14381-the-roman-question:
Edmond About wrote The Roman Question in French, and H. C. Coape put it into English in 1859. About takes the Pope as a king and asks whether his temporal rule can stand. The book counts the Church at one hundred and thirty-nine millions, ruled by cardinals and priests. It moves through plebeians, middle classes, nobles, and foreigners under papal rule. About writes with wit and with scorn for priestly government.

About shows visitors won over by Roman society, between a dance and a cup of chocolate, till even bold officers swear against the Pope's foes. The government cajoles generals without loving them, and spares no effort to bend them. A state lottery nets eighty thousand pounds a year, while winners praise God and losers learn not to covet. The book argues that priestly rule fails both God and government. It stands as a liberal brief against the temporal power.
14436-military-memoirs-of-capt-george-ca:
Captain George Carleton's memoirs, printed in London in 1728, cover his soldiering from the Dutch War of 1672 to the Peace of Utrecht in 1713. Carleton served under Charles II and James II, by sea and land.

He describes campaigns in Spain, years as a prisoner among Spaniards, monasteries such as Montserrat, and the famous bull-feasts, plus the tumult when Miquelets seized a governor at Barcelona. The narrative mixes battle detail with travel observation. Long attributed to Defoe by some scholars, the memoir stands as a lively, if disputed, soldier's tale of the age.
1444-the-voice-of-the-city-further-stori:
O. Henry's collection carries on from The Four Million with more tales of New York's ordinary millions. Clerks, shopgirls, waiters, and wanderers crowd these pages, and each story turns on a small twist of fate: a lost chance, a kind lie, a gift that arrives one day too late.
