Raleigh weighs Stevenson's style, romance, and essays against time's opium, which dulls all fame. The essay treats Treasure Island, Kidnapped, and the essays with clear-eyed praise. Raleigh's lecture remains a model of honest criticism. It suits readers asking why Stevenson still matters. Raleigh's essay remains a clear guide to Stevenson's lasting appeal.
3332-the-variation-of-animals-and-plants:
Charles Darwin gathers his evidence on variation in this two-volume work, companion to the Origin of Species. A foreword, a preface to the second edition, and an introduction open it. Chapter one takes domestic dogs and cats: ancient varieties of the dog, and the resemblance of domestic dogs in various countries to native canine species.

Animals unacquainted with man at first show no fear, Darwin notes, and dogs resemble wolves and jackals in form. Barking is acquired and lost, feral dogs return to wild ways, and tan eye-spots recur across breeds. The book argues from the farmyard and the kennel to nature at large: if breeders can reshape life so fast, nature, given time, can reshape it farther.
3377-criticism-and-fiction:
William Dean Howells argues for realism in this classic of American criticism. The question of a final criterion for appreciating art, he writes, perpetually recurs to those interested in any aesthetic endeavor. John Addington Symonds supplies his example. In a chapter of The Renaissance in Italy on the Bolognese school of painting, Symonds treats a school once vaunted as the supreme exemplar of the grand style. He now believes it fallen into lasting disrepute.

Taste changes, Howells argues, and criticism must change with it, toward truth rather than grandeur. The book became the manifesto of American realism: fiction judged by its fidelity to common life, not by its height. Readers interested in how the American novel found its theory will find it here, argued with Howells's usual clarity and calm.
340-the-soul-of-the-indian-an-interpreta:
Charles Eastman, a Sioux writer known as Ohiyesa, sets out Native faith as it stood before white contact in this short book. He writes for readers who knew Indians only through war tales, and he stresses a faith that was silent, solitary, and free of priests. Prayer, he says, rose in wordless awe before a Great Mystery.

Chapters treat the family altar, rites, moral codes, unwritten lore, and the border land of spirits. Eastman contrasts this inward faith with the creeds and schools pressed on his people. The book stands as a calm, proud account of a spiritual life that valued thanks, unity, and love of neighbor.
3418-captain-brassbound-s-conversion:
George Bernard Shaw sets this play on the west coast of Morocco, where an elderly Scottish missionary tends his garden in the late afternoon. The missionary, a man of the Free Church and the North African Mission, cultivates a huge red geranium bush on a Moorish stool, calm in his faith though far from home. Into this quiet scene come travelers, a ship's captain, and questions of law and honor.

Captain Brassbound, a seafarer with a grievance against English justice, forces the party to judge him by a rougher code. Shaw turns the adventure into a debate about courts, revenge, and conscience, with wit running through the action. The play suits readers who like Shaw's blend of romance, argument, and sudden moral turns.
3451-marie-antoinette-and-her-son:
Louise Muhlbach tells the last years of Marie Antoinette in this historical novel, following the French queen from court splendor to prison and trial. Her young son, the dauphin, stands at the center of the later chapters, as revolutionaries, guards, and loyal friends struggle over his fate. The novel moves between Versailles, the Temple prison, and the streets of revolutionary Paris.

Muhlbach writes as a popular novelist of the nineteenth century, filling gaps in the record with invented scenes and dialogue. Readers should treat the book as romance built around real people, not as a scholarly life. Its value lies in its sympathy for the queen and in its vivid picture of how the Revolution felt inside a family.
3490-the-admirable-crichton:
James Matthew Barrie writes a comedy about rank turned upside down when a lord's household is shipwrecked on a desert island. At Loam House in Mayfair, the Honourable Ernest Woolley drives up smiling and thinking, as usual, mainly of himself. Once the party is stranded, the butler Crichton, practical and calm, becomes the natural leader, while his masters prove helpless without servants.

Barrie uses the island to test English class habits. Crichton can build, hunt, and govern, yet back in London he returns to his place below stairs. The play mixes wit, romance, and social satire, and it remains one of Barrie's best known comedies. It suits readers who enjoy theater that asks who is really fit to lead.
3495-the-king-of-ireland-s-son:
Padraic Colum retells Irish folk tales as a single story about the king of Ireland's son in this book for young readers. The contents name its parts. They include The King of the Cats, The Sword of Light, The Town of the Red Castle, The King of the Land of Mist, and The House of Crom Duv. The hero, one of King Connal's three sons, sets out with a boat fastened for a year and a day.

Along the way he meets a spae woman named Fedelma, an enchanter's daughter, giants, and talking beasts. Colum writes in clear, musical prose that keeps the old tales' wonder without smoothing away their strangeness. The book suits families who want Irish legend in story form, and it remains a classic of children's fantasy.
3527-the-blue-moon:
Laurence Housman writes a book of fairy tales and fanciful stories. They include The Wind, A Capful of Moonshine, The Moon Stroke, How Little Duke Jarl Saved the Castle, The White Doe, and The Blue Moon itself. The tales open on lovers named Nillywill and Hands-pansy, described as the most unimportant and happy pair the world has ever gained or lost.

Housman's stories favor moonlight, gardens, and gentle magic over battles or monsters. A peasant boy and a girl who wants to return to him anchor the longest tale, while shorter pieces play with wishes, moons, and enchanted beasts. The book suits readers who enjoy dreamy, old fashioned fairy tales written with a poet's care for language.
3534-a-complete-account-of-the-settlemen:
Watkin Tench follows his first Botany Bay narrative with a fuller account of the settlement at Port Jackson, the site of modern Sydney. Tench notes that much had already been written about New South Wales, so he offers a reason for one more book. He sailed with the fleet, stayed through anxious years, and could correct and extend earlier reports. Fresh news from the colony arrived even as his book went to press.

The account covers farming, food shortages, relations with Aboriginal peoples, and the growth of a town from tents and huts. Tench writes as a soldier and observer, clear about hardship and hopeful about the colony's future. It suits readers who want a second, deeper eyewitness view of Australia's founding years.
357-a-dream-of-john-ball-and-a-king-s-le:
William Morris frames this tale as a dream that drops a modern man into fourteenth-century Kent. There he meets John Ball, the priest whose preaching stirred the Peasants' Revolt, and watches rebels gather at a village cross. A short second piece, A King's Lesson, follows the dream tale.

The talk between dreamer and priest turns on fair work, just rule, and hope for a better world to come. Battle, supper, and hard talk with the dead fill the later chapters. Morris uses the past not as costume, but as a mirror for his own age and its own fight for change.
362-miss-billy-s-decision:
Eleanor Porter continues the story of Billy Neilson in this sequel to Miss Billy, with thirty-three chapters of Boston social life. Billy, now caught between love and duty, must choose how far to shape her own life. Around her move Aunt Hannah, the artist Bertram, the sharp-tongued Mary Jane, and old friends from the first book.

Letters, studio talk, an operetta, and a string of small crises test Billy's nerve and pride. Porter keeps the tone light, yet the choices bite: who to trust, what to give up, and when to speak plain truth. The book closes a chapter of Billy's youth with warmth and a clear sense of growth.
3654-alfred-tennyson:
Andrew Lang writes a brief life and appreciation of Alfred Tennyson, published in 1901. Lang rests his account almost entirely on the biography by Lord Tennyson, the poet's son, with the son's kind permission, and on the text of the poems themselves. He sets aside current anecdotes not given in that biography, preferring a sober sketch to gossip.

The book follows Tennyson from youth to laureate, and judges his work poem by poem, from early lyrics to In Memoriam and the Idylls. Lang writes as an admiring critic who also notes faults. The volume suits readers who want a short, reliable introduction to Tennyson's life and art.
3670-peg-woffington:
Charles Reade writes a dramatic story about Margaret Woffington, the famous eighteenth century actress. Reade inscribes the tale to her memory, saying she was falsely summed up until his day, and he draws on stage memoirs for his material. The story opens about the middle of the last century, at eight in the evening, in a large but poor apartment where a man slumbers on a rough couch.

Woffington, witty and generous, moves through London theater life, where acting, love, and reputation tangle. Reade defends her against gossip that painted her as merely a flirt. The novel suits readers interested in theater history and in a heroine who won fame by talent in an age that judged actresses harshly.
3677-on-our-selection:
Steele Rudd writes humorous stories of Australian bush life on a selection, a small farm taken up under colonial land law. The book opens twenty years after the family settled on the creek, arriving from Stanthorpe on Jerome's dray, eight people with beds, tubs, and all their goods. Rudd dedicates the stories to the pioneers who gave the country birth, whose names were never carved on tablet or tombstone.

The tales follow Dad, Dave, Joe, and the rest through drought, floods, hard work, and family quarrels, with the bush itself as a character. Rudd writes in Australian vernacular, warm and funny about hardship. The book became a classic of Australian humor and suits readers who enjoy frontier family life told from inside.
3707-the-trimmed-lamp-and-other-stories-:
O Henry gathers two dozen New York stories under the title of his most famous collection, since four million was then the city's population. Shop girls Lou and Nancy, clerks, cops, con men, and chorus girls crowd these pages, each chasing a small hope in a large town. The opening tale defends working girls against a lazy label. Later tales turn on a last leaf painted on a wall, a lost coin, and a wedding guest who counts too much.

The plots twist at the close, but the real pleasure lies in the talk, the slang, and the author's fondness for his people. New York itself acts as a character, with its flats, shops, and streetcars. Readers new to O Henry will find here the full range of his art, from jokes to pathos, in stories short enough for a single sitting.
3740-complete-project-gutenberg-collecti:
This large file binds three first hand accounts of Napoleon into a single reading text. Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne, the emperor's private secretary, gives the long official view, from the early campaigns to the fall. Constant, the premier valet de chambre, adds the private life, with mornings, moods, and household detail that no state paper shows. Stewarton closes the set with secret letters from Paris to London on the court of Saint Cloud.

Together the three memoirs let readers watch Napoleon from the desk, the bedroom, and the salon at once. Generals like Murat and Rapp pass through with their own voices, and the great events gain a human scale. The file is long, but each memoir stands alone, so readers can dip into Bourrienne for politics, Constant for character, or Stewarton for court gossip.
3812-the-mirrors-of-washington:
This anonymous volume holds up mirrors to the men who ran Washington in the Harding years, with a biographical note for each subject. Warren Harding, the Ohio newspaper man turned president, and Woodrow Wilson, the Princeton president turned war president, open the gallery. Colonel House, Wilson's close adviser, receives a long and searching portrait, with his kindheartedness, credulity, and surrender to a stronger mind all weighed.

The book argues that House, talking to Wilson, was a weaker Wilson talking to the real one, and that Wilson reached the peace conference without a capable critical adviser. The portraits are frank, partisan, and gossipy by turns. Readers who like political character sketches will find a sharp contemporary view of power, written while its subjects were still in the news.
3814-robert-louis-stevenson:
E Blantyre Simpson wrote this short life of Robert Louis Stevenson for the Spirit of the Age series. That set of little books covers men and women whose work reflects the cultivated thought of the day. The chapters follow Stevenson's apprenticeship, his Edinburgh student days, his brief career as an advocate, and his life across the seas to Samoa. Illustrations show him as an advocate in 1875, an Edinburgh student, and a teller of tales.

Anecdotes give the flavor, as when Stevenson, lured to a dinner he claimed to hate, promised to appear with temples wreathed like a victim come smiling to the altar. Simpson aims at a living personality rather than a formal record. Readers who want a brief, humane introduction to Stevenson will find a pleasant volume, short enough for an evening.
3825-pygmalion:
Bernard Shaw wrote Pygmalion around Henry Higgins, a professor of phonetics who wagers he can pass a flower girl off as a duchess by teaching her to speak. The preface argues that England needs a phonetic reformer, since no Englishman can open his mouth without making another hate or despise him. Shaw recalls the phonetic pioneers Melville Bell and Alexander Ellis, with his velvet skull cap, as the real models behind Higgins.

The play itself follows Eliza Doolittle from Covent Garden to the embassy ball, with Colonel Pickering, Mrs Pearce, and her dustman father Alfred in support. A sequel in prose tells what happens after the curtain. Readers who know the musical version will enjoy meeting the sharper original, with Shaw's wit at full stretch.
4003-androcles-and-the-lion:
Bernard Shaw's play retells the old tale of Androcles, a runaway slave who pulls a thorn from a lion's paw and later meets the same lion in the arena. Shaw sets the story among early Christians facing the lions in Rome, with a captain, Lavinia, and other prisoners arguing about courage.

Lavinia insists that a woman must be braver than a soldier, and the captain answers that what she calls courage is pride. Shaw turns the fable into witty debate about faith, pride, and mercy, with the lion's gratitude upsetting the arena's grim plan. The play mixes comedy and argument, and it suits readers who enjoy Shaw's sharp talk on stage.
4043-the-dynasts-an-epic-drama-of-the-wa:
Thomas Hardy's vast drama in verse covers the Napoleonic wars, from palace gates to battlefields, with crowds of citizens and soldiers as its chorus. Spirits watch over the action: the Spirit of the Years sends the Spirit of Rumour down to join the crowd and speak what comes into its mouth.

The Spirit Sinister will not miss another Austerlitz, and a young foreigner in disguise carries rumor into the streets. Hardy mixes history, philosophy, and stage spectacle on a grand scale. Readers who like epic drama will find a huge, strange work, part play and part poem, about nations, fate, and the men who steer them.
4239-an-essay-on-the-principle-of-popula:
Thomas Malthus published this essay in 1798. It grew from a conversation with a friend about William Godwin's ideas. Godwin had written on the future improvement of society, and Malthus answered him. His argument was stark: population tends to grow faster than the food supply.

Checks such as hardship, disease, and restraint must therefore limit growth, unless societies plan for it. Malthus wrote against hopeful thinkers such as Godwin and Condorcet. His preface admits the essay is less complete than he wished. Its single plain claim shaped debates about poverty, poor relief, and progress for a century.
4295-songs-of-action:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathered these poems of action in a volume published by John Murray in 1916, in its seventh impression. The contents range from the Song of the Bow and Cremona to the Storming Party, the Frontier Line, and Corporal Dick's Promotion. Later pieces turn to hunting, racing, and the sea.

Titles such as A Rover Chanty, A Ballad of the Ranks, and The Home-Coming of the Eurydice show Doyle's taste for stirring scenes. The poems suit readers who know Doyle for Sherlock Holmes and want his verse voice: direct, martial, and fond of soldiers, sailors, huntsmen, and the open air.
4310-will-warburton:
George Gissing opened this novel with Will Warburton bounding out of a cab near Chelsea Bridge, fresh from Alpine snows and sea wind in his hair. He pays double fare, shoulders a heavy bag, and runs up four flights to his flat. His landlady, Mrs. Hopper, greets him with a thin, cautious face at the door.

Warburton returns to London life with energy, but Gissing soon tests that energy against work, money, and love. The novel follows a young man of spirit learning the limits of his own will. It is a story of homecoming that turns, as Gissing's stories often do, into a study of character under pressure.
4315-the-life-of-sir-richard-burton:
Thomas Wright, author of a life of Edward Fitzgerald, wrote this life of Sir Richard Burton, explorer, linguist, and writer, in two volumes bound as one. Wright began fifteen years after Burton's death, and twelve years after Lady Burton's biography of her husband, which she wrote while dying of an incurable disease.

Lady Burton had asked whether she would live to tell the world how great her husband was, and to refute his enemies' calumnies. Wright takes up that task with fuller evidence, following Burton from youth through Africa, Arabia, and South America. The book gives a full Victorian life, with its quarrels, books, and journeys, in one large volume.
4327-the-valley-of-decision:
Edith Wharton set this historical novel in eighteenth-century Italy, in four books: The Old Order, The New Light, The Choice, and The Reward. It opens in a small neglected chapel, where farm noises drift through closed doors and a February light falls on a foundling child in the kitchen. The scene is quiet, poor, and watchful.

Wharton dedicated the book to her friends Paul and Minnie Bourget, in memory of Italian days together. The story follows a young Italian through old loyalties and new ideas, toward a choice that gives the book its title. It is Wharton's early large novel, rich in Italian setting and moral argument.
448-the-psychology-of-revolution:
Gustave Le Bon studies why crowds and nations turn to revolt in this early work of crowd psychology. He sorts revolutions into scientific, political, and religious kinds, and weighs how governments fail, how peoples follow, and how old habits survive new regimes. The Reformation serves as his key case for how belief moves masses.

Later parts treat the mystic mind, the part of leaders, and the slow return to order after upheaval. Le Bon writes with cool, generalizing sweep, often harsh on crowds. The book remains a landmark for readers who want to grasp revolt as a mental event, not merely a clash of armies or laws.
451-the-shadow-line-a-confession:
Joseph Conrad tells of a young seaman who takes his first command in this short novel, subtitled a confession. Bored and restless, the narrator quits a good berth, then accepts a ship in the East whose captain has died at sea. Fever, calm winds, and a crew on edge test him as he crosses into adult command.

Conrad frames the tale as a shadow line between youth and age, crossed by all in early manhood. The prose is grave and inward, tracking doubt, duty, and the slow gain of nerve. The book endures as a compact study of how a man becomes responsible when no one else can steer.
4512-gardening-without-irrigation:
Steve Solomon wrote this practical gardening book from his own experience in the maritime Northwest, where summers turn predictably dry. After moving to Lorane, Oregon, in 1978, he found that his well, first rated at fifteen gallons a minute, soon fell to about three gallons a minute in August. That failure pushed him to learn how to grow food with little or no added water.

Chapters cover water-wise science, ways to help plants need less water, year-round planning, and an alphabetical guide to crops grown with less irrigation, closing with Solomon's own garden plan. The book suits gardeners in dry-summer regions, and anyone who wants a productive plot without depending on constant watering. It is hands-on, plainspoken, and built from trial in a real garden.
4552-the-border-legion:
Zane Grey sets this western on the wild southern border of Idaho, in a year when gold rushes, vigilantes, and lawless camps had unsettled the whole region. Joan Randle, twenty years old, tall and strong, rides out on a cedar ridge regretting a quarrel with Jim Cleve. She fears he has ridden straight for the border country, and her taunt may have pushed him toward danger.

Joan follows into a world of outlaws, prospectors, and hunters, where blood and gold mix in camp talk and in real violence. Grey writes the mountains, horses, and border towns with the speed of a campfire tale. Readers get a classic western adventure about pride, regret, and rescue, in which a young woman must face the harsh country her words helped to unleash.
4599-the-small-house-at-allington:
Anthony Trollope's The Small House at Allington first ran in the Cornhill Magazine from September 1862 to April 1864. It appeared in book form in two volumes from Smith, Elder in 1864. Both serial and first edition carried eighteen full-page illustrations by John Everett Millais, with smaller vignettes at chapter heads in the serial. The contents open with the squire of Allington, the two pearls of Allington, and the widow Dale of Allington.

From the Allington household the story moves to Mrs. Roper's London boarding-house and to the wider world of suitors, cousins, and clerks. Lily Dale and her sister Bell, the two pearls, stand at the centre of a tale about love, jilting, and steady affection. Readers get a rich, humane Trollope novel, full of county life and London lodgings, and a fine entry point to his Barsetshire world.
4621-the-two-wives-or-lost-and-won:
T. S. Arthur published The Two Wives, or Lost and Won, in 1851, as the third volume in Arthur's Library for the Household. His preface states its purpose plainly. Tender, earnest, self-forgetting love can win back a husband whose steps have strayed toward ruin. By contrast, the want of those virtues under like circumstances brings sad results. The story opens in the evening, with Mrs. Wilkinson at a small work-table under a shaded lamp.

Her husband John, who has been reading, stands ready to go out, while a smile on her lips hides a cloud on her heart. From that scene grows a tale of marriage tested by temptation, pride, and forgiveness. Readers get a short, moral domestic novel of its day, written to be read in families. It shows how patience and love, rather than scolding or pride, can reclaim a life heading the wrong way.
4630-the-home-mission:
T. S. Arthur published The Home Mission at Boston and Philadelphia in 1853, gathering domestic sketches. Its contents include a vision of consolation, the step-mother, power of kindness, and bear and forbear. They go on to the social serpent, the young mother, a gentle warning, Kate's experiment, my fortune's made, and the good match. Later pieces cover a brother's temptation, the home of taste, two sisters, and an evening prayer.

Arthur's preface says good or evil impulses that become ruling affections can often be traced back to the home of childhood, where impressions last as long as existence itself. Home, he argues, is the nursery of all that is excellent in social or civil life, or of all that is deformed. Readers get a set of short, earnest tales about family influence, meant to show how early home life shapes a whole character.
4672-the-galleries-of-the-exposition:
Eugen Neuhaus, assistant professor of decorative design at the University of California, wrote The Galleries of the Exposition. It is a critical review of paintings, statuary, and graphic arts in the Palace of Fine Arts at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition. He served on the international jury of awards for fine arts, and he dedicates the book to John E. D. Trask, director of fine arts for the exposition, an untiring worker and able executive.

Contents open with an historical review and the function of art, then retrospective art and foreign nations. France, Italy, Portugal, Argentina, Uruguay, Cuba, the Philippines, Japan, China, Sweden, Holland, and Germany each receive notice. American one-man rooms follow, with Whistler, Twachtman, Tarbell, Redfield, Duveneck, Chase, Hassam, Melchers, Sargent, and Keith. Graphic arts, a conclusion, a bibliography, and an index close a useful guide for art lovers.
4774-the-merry-devil-of-edmonton:
The Merry Devil of Edmonton is an English play, opening with a list of persons mixing knights, priests, tradesmen, and spirits. Sir Arthur Clare, Sir Richard Mounchensey, and Sir Ralph Jerningham stand beside Henry, Raymond, and Frank. Sir John, a priest, Banks, the miller of Waltham, and Smug, the smith of Edmonton, join Bilbo, Blague the host, Brian, and Friar Hildersham. Coreb, a spirit, and Fabel, the merry devil himself, complete the list.

The prologue asks friends for silence and attention, so free spirits may relish the life of the active scene, calmed by invoking spells. It introduces Peter Fabell, a renowned scholar whose fame later writers forgot. Born in Middlesex not seven miles from London, he was called the merry friend of Edmonton for fame in sleights and magic. Lady Clare, Millisent, an abbess, and nuns complete the cast. Readers get an Elizabethan comedy of magic, love, and mischief.
4795-the-circassian-slave-or-the-sultan-:
Lieutenant Murray wrote The Circassian Slave, or The Sultan's Favorite, A Story of Constantinople and the Caucasus, published at Boston in 1851. A publisher's note says the novelette first appeared in The Pictorial Drawing Room Companion, as a specimen of entertaining tales gracing that journal's columns. Its contents run through fifteen chapters, from The Slave Market and The Sultan's Harem to The Bedouin Arabs and Vales of Circassia.

The Slave Ship, A Singular Meeting, and The Sultan's Prisoner follow, with Punishment of the Sack, The Lover's Stratagem, and The Serenade. The Elopement, The Struggle for Life, and The Escape from the Harem lead to The Chase and a Happy Conclusion. Its preface says the story concerns that exceedingly interesting and romantic portion of the world bordering on the Black Sea, where Circassia meets the Ottoman capital. Readers get a mid-century Oriental romance of slavery, harem intrigue, and escape.
4967-luck-or-cunning-as-the-main-means-o:
Samuel Butler's Luck or Cunning asks whether living things change mainly by luck or by intelligent design within nature itself. The second edition reprints the first of 1887, published in November 1886, with an enlarged index drawn from the author's own annotated copy, passed on by his literary executor.

Butler argues against a purely mechanical Darwinism, crediting organisms with memory, habit, and a kind of cunning in shaping their own evolution. The dedication honors the friend at whose instigation the book began. Readers get a Victorian argument about evolution that still provokes, written with Butler's combative wit and independence.
5-the-united-states-constitution:
The founding charter of the United States took shape in Philadelphia in 1787. Its preamble promises a more perfect union, justice, domestic peace, and the blessings of liberty. The articles that follow divide power among Congress, the president, and the courts.

Legislative powers come first, with a Senate and House set out in detail. Later articles cover the executive, the judiciary, relations among states, and amendment. This hosted edition presents the original articles without the later amendments. It remains the working frame of American government. Citizens still cite its articles in debates over power, rights, and the shape of government.
5002-the-rover-boys-in-business-or-the-s:
Arthur M. Winfield's Rover Boys in Business sends Sam, Tom, and Dick Rover from school themes and moonlight visits to Hope Seminary into the world of work. Sam worries over a theme due tomorrow, Tom proposes an auto trip to see the girls, and the brothers soon face a harder problem: the search for missing bonds.

Business, rather than boating, drives this volume, as the Rovers hunt for securities whose loss threatens their father's affairs. School loyalty and brotherly teasing carry them through. Readers get a boys' series novel where ledgers and offices replace rivers and camps, but the Rover spirit stays the same.
5005-journal-of-an-overland-expedition-i:
Ludwig Leichhardt's journal of an overland expedition from Moreton Bay to Port Essington records a journey into Australia's wilderness in dated chapters. The party leaves the last station, crosses the Darling Downs and Waterloo Plains, endures heavy rains on the Condamine, and loses then finds Murphy and Caleb after a frightening separation.

Later chapters reduce the party, meet friendly Aboriginal people, pass native tombs, and follow the Dawson through ranges and creeks toward the north. Leichhardt notes fossils, coal, and country with a naturalist's care. Readers get a foundational Australian exploration journal, told day by day from inside a long and perilous trek.
5218-the-satyricon-volume-01-introductio:
This first volume of W. C. Firebaugh's translation of Petronius's Satyricon opens with the translator's introduction, reflecting on the difficulties of rendering an author whose allusions were plain to his own public but obscure to later readers. Firebaugh defends a translation that honours both sense and tone, even where later hands have altered the text.

After the introduction, the volume begins the adventures of Encolpius and his companions, from the opening chapters onward. Readers starting the Satyricon here get both the translator's apology and the novel's first scenes, before the later volumes carry the story to Trimalchio's dinner and beyond.
5241-the-eye-of-zeitoon:
Talbot Mundy's Eye of Zeitoon is set among Armenians and Turks. Travellers join them in the years before the First World War, where, as one chapter says, the heart of Armenia is burning. Its chapters follow soldiers, robbers, and missionaries through mountain roads, with quotations from scripture marking a story of loyalty, faith, and rebellion.

Mundy writes of a people caught between empires, and of Westerners who must choose whether to help. The novel offers adventure with a serious edge. It gives readers a vivid, if dated, picture of Armenia on the edge of catastrophe, told by a writer who knew the region's tensions well.
5251-the-long-vacation:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Long Vacation returns to the Mohuns and Underwoods of her earlier novels, with a preface warning that its first chapters serve as a prologue for older readers. Chapters of retrospect and twaddle give way to Darby and Joan, slum, sea, or season, a happy sprite, St Andrew's Rock, and the hope of Vanderkist.

Yonge follows her characters into later life, where weary men and anxious women replace the smiling angel band of childhood. The novel offers a leisurely domestic sequel, full of moral reflection, for readers who have followed Yonge's families and want to see how their stories end.
5271-marjorie-s-vacation:
Carolyn Wells's Marjorie's Vacation follows Marjorie on a summer holiday that begins at home. It carries her to Haslemere, with chapters on the roof, a paper-doll house, interesting letters, a boat ride, a memory book, and the front stairs. Later chapters bring the Dunns, a bazaar, a birthday, Breezy Inn, a broken ladder, and firecrackers.

Wells, author of the Patty books, writes cheerful stories for girls, full of play, friendship, and small adventures. The book offers young readers a sunny vacation tale, where a long day and an old well find their place in Marjorie's summer. An eventful day joins them.
5407-the-recreations-of-a-country-parson:
A. K. H. Boyd's Recreations of a Country Parson, second series, published in Boston in 1862, gathers essays by a Scottish parish minister. Its chapters concern the parson's choice, disappointment and success, Scylla and Charybdis, churchyards, summer days, screws, solitary days, and Glasgow down the water.

Later chapters concern man and his dwelling-place, life at the water-cure, friends in council, and other parsonage topics, in the leisurely, reflective manner of Victorian essay writing. Readers get a gentle book of a clergyman's thoughts, on work, friendship, and the small pleasures of a country parish.
5436-hyperion:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote Hyperion as a romance of travel, love, and learning in Germany. The contents run from The Hero and The Christ of Andernach through Heidelberg and the Baron, Lives of Scholars, and Literary Fame. A second book adds spring, colloquies, owl-towers, and partings. A young American travels among German towns, students, and legends.

Longfellow fills the journey with talk about books, art, and the German spirit, alongside a tender love story. The novel reads as both a travel sketch and a young writer's education. Readers get an early American romance, earnest and lyrical, by a poet better known for his verse.
549-the-underdogs-a-novel-of-the-mexican:
Mariano Azuela tells of the Mexican Revolution through peasant fighters in this short, stark novel, written in El Paso in 1915. Demetrio Macias, a farmer turned rebel chief, leads his men through battles, loot, and doubt, while the cause they serve slips into self-seeking. Azuela, who served as a doctor with Pancho Villa's army, knew the war firsthand.

Azuela writes with bitter, spare prose, praising the underdogs yet mourning their betrayal. The novel, hailed in 1924 as the novel of the Revolution, endures as a classic of disillusion, where brave men fight for a better Mexico and watch it fade.
555-the-unbearable-bassington:
H. H. Munro, writing as Saki, satirizes Edwardian society in this novel of a charming, idle young man. Comus Bassington, unbearable to his mother Francesca yet loved by many, drifts through London drawing rooms, debts, and schemes. His mother, once the beautiful Miss Greech, watches his follies with cool, witty despair.

Munro writes with sharp, epigrammatic prose, and his author's note warns the tale has no moral and no remedy. The novel endures as a Saki study in wit, where a young man's charm proves both his gift and his ruin.
5588-a-question:
Georg Ebers's A Question, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, opens with a verse prelude set in the Art Palace on green Isar's strand. Before one picture, the speaker sits long, held spellbound by some magic band, unable to forget it even at home. A year passes, winter comes, and at last he plucks up courage, crying be it so, and wanders southward with those he calls his own.

The novel that follows grows from that picture's spell, carrying its characters south like birds of passage. Ebers writes art's power as a call to travel. Readers get a romantic novel about a painting, a journey, and a question that will not let go.
5617-the-bobbsey-twins-in-washington:
Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins in Washington as another adventure for the Bobbsey family. Earlier books took them to the country, the seashore, school, Snow Lodge, a houseboat, and Meadow Brook. This volume takes the twins to the nation's capital, with chapters promising a monkey trick, found money, river trips, an enemy raid, a colonel, a pursuit, and a race.

The twins form their patrol, organize, face a challenge and a defiance, while Pepper carries a message, goes missing, and becomes a quest of his own. Hope writes clean, cheerful adventure for young readers. Children get a Washington story full of twins, trouble, and teamwork.
563-the-planet-mars-and-its-inhabitants-:
A writer calling himself Eros Urides, a Martian of the city of Urid, describes Mars in this psychic revelation. Canals, double and gridironed, carry water from polar caps to reservoirs; flying ships replace trade; and a commonwealth supplies all wants without barter. Property belongs to God alone, says the author.

Chapters treat climate, economy, and spirit visions seen by a shorthand recorder. The book presents itself as dictation from Mars, not as science. It serves as a curious relic of early canal-era Mars lore, where a better world was imagined in red sands and shared goods.
5681-the-laws-of-etiquette-or-short-rule:
An unnamed gentleman author wrote this short manual of polite conduct for nineteenth-century social life. It covers good breeding, dress, salutations, and the drawing room. It also covers letters, visits, dinners, balls, funerals, and servants. Its preface disclaims literary ambition: the book claims no merit beyond correctness and fitness of application, and it hopes for a kind reception on those grounds alone. Each chapter takes one social situation and states what is expected.

Readers today gain a clear window into the manners of an age when a call, a letter, or a dinner seating carried real social weight. The advice is direct, sometimes stern, and often amusing in its care over small points. It serves social historians, novelists, and curious readers alike, since it records not just rules but the values behind them: punctuality, restraint, and respect for company.
5683-the-critique-of-practical-reason:
Immanuel Kant's Critique of Practical Reason, in the Abbott translation, examines how reason can guide action apart from desire and reward. Book one analyzes pure practical reason, its principles, its objects, and its motives, while book two turns to the dialectic that arises when reason overreaches itself. Kant defines practical principles as rules that determine the will, then separates maxims, which bind only one person, from practical laws, which bind every rational being.

The argument is dense, but its question is plain: can duty stand on reason alone, without appeal to happiness or fear? Kant answers that freedom, rightly understood, gives moral law its force, and that ideas of the soul and the world gain weight once freedom is established. Readers of ethics and philosophy will find here the core of Kant's moral system, stated with a rigor that still sets the terms of debate.
5701-the-tale-of-fatty-coon:
Arthur Scott Bailey's Tale of Fatty Coon, part of the Sleepy-Time Tales and published in 1915, follows a young raccoon through small woodland adventures. Its chapters send Fatty home, then into lessons about eggs, a turtle's secret, a mistake, fishing, and green corn. Harry Smith's illustrations accompany the text, and each chapter offers one clear incident for a young listener.

The stories teach gently, through Fatty's curiosity and its consequences, rather than through lectures. Children meet woodland neighbors, seasonal food, and the risks of taking what is not theirs, all in short, friendly scenes. Parents reading aloud will find a calm, old-fashioned animal book, and young readers will enjoy following a mischievous hero who learns, slowly, to think before he acts.
5719-janice-meredith-a-story-of-the-amer:
Paul Leicester Ford sets Janice Meredith in the American Revolution, weaving a romance through the war for independence. Ford was already known for historical fiction and studies of Washington and Franklin. He dedicates the book to George Vanderbilt. He opens with a reflection on how much of an author goes into every book. The story follows Janice among soldiers, spies, and households divided by loyalty.

Readers meet the Revolution as lived experience: roads, camps, letters, and drawing rooms where political choice becomes personal. Ford balances adventure with period detail, letting Janice's courage and judgment carry the plot. The novel suits readers of historical romance who want the founding era told through one young woman's changing fortunes.
5742-the-bird-woman-of-the-lewis-and-cla:
Katherine Chandler tells the story of the Bird Woman of the Lewis and Clark Expedition as a supplementary reader for first and second grades. The Bird Woman is Sacajawea, the young Shoshone woman who traveled with the expedition as guide and interpreter, carrying her infant son. Chandler, author of books on California plants and Pacific folk lore, writes for the youngest school readers.

The book gives children a simple, heroic account of a famous journey, stressing guidance, courage, and knowledge of the land. Its short sentences and clear scenes suit classroom reading aloud. Modern readers should note that later scholarship adds detail and corrects early accounts, but as a period school reader it shows how Sacajawea's story was first taught to American children.
5815-the-great-impersonation:
Oppenheim opens The Great Impersonation in scrub country, where Everard Dominey fights toward thin, spiral wisps of smoke. He has pushed through brush for three quarters of an hour. He urges his pony to a last despairing effort. He crashes through a great oleander shrub and pitches forward on his head into a little clearing. From that fall, a tale of identity, impersonation, and hidden pasts unfolds.

This gives a classic thriller of doubles and secrets, set between English country life and wider intrigues. Oppenheim builds suspense through mistaken identity and the fear of exposure, letting Dominey's past shadow his present. Fans of early spy and mystery fiction will enjoy a brisk, atmospheric novel where no one is quite who they seem.
5833-helping-himself-or-grant-thornton-s:
Horatio Alger follows Grant Thornton, a minister's son, in Helping Himself, opening with his mother lamenting their terrible poverty. Grant, fifteen, asks what is new, and his mother answers that nothing is new, only the old hardship grown heavier. Chapters follow Grant's business calls, a walk to Somerset, a timely rescue, his mother's pearls, unexpected trouble, and a day in Wall Street.

The book introduces a classic Alger hero whose ambition is honest work, not sudden luck. Grant takes decisive steps, makes friends, and learns business one call at a time, while family need keeps the stakes clear. The novel suits young readers who enjoy stories of effort rewarded, and it offers a clear example of Alger's hopeful, hardworking boyhood ideal.
5872-cashel-byron-s-profession:
Bernard Shaw's Cashel Byron's Profession opens at Wiltstoken Castle, a square building with circular bastions at its corners, each ending skyward in a Turkish minaret. The southwest front bears a Moorish arch fitted with glass doors, secured on occasion by gates of fantastically hammered iron, and enshrined by a Palladian portico. From that romantic castle, Shaw launches a novel about a prizefighter's profession.

Readers get Shaw's early blend of romance and social satire, as boxing, class, and love collide. Cashel's profession tests respectability, since a fighter's fame and a lady's world seldom meet. The novel suits readers of Shaw's fiction, Victorian romance with a twist, and stories where physical courage must answer to social judgment.
5951-reno-a-book-of-short-stories-and-in:
The Van-Noy Interstate Company presents Reno as a book of short stories and information. It runs in seven parts. They cover social and industrial life, Reno tragedies, Reno romance, Reno comedies, Reno and its people, Nevada divorce laws, and sons of the sagebrush. The book opens by quoting the Bible on a man putting away a wife who finds no favor in his eyes, framing Reno's famous divorce trade in scripture's own terms.

Readers also get a portrait of Reno as an up-to-date city. Electrical stores show every new device there. Stationery, candy, music, hardware, drug, and department stores stand fine as those in cities twice its size. Shops employ hundreds, and buyers travel to New York for goods, the book boasts. It suits readers curious about early twentieth-century Reno, divorce history, and booster literature that mixes stories with civic pride.
5979-japan-an-attempt-at-interpretation:
Lafcadio Hearn attempts what he admits no single work can yet fully do: picture Japan within and without, historically and socially, psychologically and ethically. His chapters move from strangeness and charm through the ancient cult, the religion of the home, and the Japanese family.

Later sections treat Shinto, Buddhism, the social order, the rise of military power, the religion of loyalty, the Jesuit peril, and feudal integration, closing with modern restraints, official education, and industrial danger. Hearn writes as an interpreter between two worlds, careful and searching. An appendix closes a patient and wide-ranging survey.
5993-walter-sherwood-s-probation:
Horatio Alger Jr. opens with a letter for Doctor Ezekiel Mack, brought by his housekeeper Nancy Sprague, once a schoolmistress. Walter Sherwood writes often to his old guardian, and Nancy praises his heart while the doctor adds a wish about his head. The doctor, near sixty, adjusts his spectacles and reads with a contracting brow.

The letter disturbs him, and its contents set the probation of the title in motion. Alger follows a young man whose money, manners, and morals are tested away from home. The tale pairs a kindly guardian's worry with a boy's effort to prove himself worthy of trust.
6019-the-earth-as-modified-by-human-acti:
George P. Marsh, revising his Man and Nature, argues that no winds, storms, earthquakes, seas, or seasons have changed the earth so much as man has since he received dominion over it. His object is to show the character and extent of changes made by human action in the globe's physical conditions.

Marsh warns of imprudence and urges caution in large operations that disturb organic and inorganic arrangements. He also holds out the restoration of disturbed harmonies and the improvement of waste and exhausted regions. The book stands as an early work of environmental thought, sober and far-seeing.
6149-the-boy-aviators-treasure-quest-or-:
Captain Wilbur Lawton, pen name for John Henry Goldfrap, sends the Boy Aviators on a treasure quest for a golden galleon, the fourth of six cloth-bound titles at fifty cents. Earlier books took them to Nicaragua with insurgents, on secret service with wireless, and to Africa on an aerial ivory trail.

Contents promise the eagle and the buzzard, Billy's strange tale, a trial flight, Eben Joyce appearing, and a strange story. The golden galleon, a fire alarm by aeroplane, a race nearly lost, and fog follow. Lawton writes brisk air adventure, where young fliers chase treasure by engine and nerve.
6162-herbert-carter-s-legacy-or-the-inve:
Horatio Alger Jr. tells Herbert Carter's Legacy, or The Inventor's Son, in the same spirit as his tales of street boys. Alger, son of a clergyman, Harvard graduate, and former Unitarian pastor at Brewster, settled in New York in 1866 and drew public attention to the needs of street boys.

He mingled with them, gained their confidence, showed personal concern, and stimulated honest, useful living. With his first story he won boys everywhere, and over seventy stories sold more than a million copies in his lifetime. Herbert Carter inherits an inventor father's name and must turn legacy into honest effort.
6301-the-eve-of-the-french-revolution:
Edward J. Lowell looks at the French Revolution in two ways, first at great events that astonished Europe and America, and second at the slower causes beneath them. The Bastille, the march on Versailles, the September massacres, and the Terror all draw the eye. Napoleon's restoration of order does too, yet Lowell warns that historians, scenting battle, have sometimes hurried over the ground before it.

The book opens with king and administration, as Louis XVI takes the throne in 1774 with power nearly absolute in theory. Provincial estates still meet but with narrow functions, and the Paris parliament, once a check on law, has been dissolved. Lowell writes a clear, sober history of old France on the eve of upheaval, asking what made a despotic seeming order crack.
6310-the-pastor-s-son:
William W. Walter writes, in his preface, that his sole reason for this book is to point readers to another book, whose Christ truth will free them from trouble. If in sin, it shows the way out; if sick, it will heal; if grieving, it will mend a broken heart; if poor, it will give plenty. The novel that follows is built as a witness to that claim, plain and earnest.

On a beautiful Thanksgiving morning, the Reverend James A. Williams tells his son Walter that the sky is cloudless and the breeze almost June like, though it is November 30. He expects a large church crowd for an excellent sermon, yet his joy fades at his son's face, for Walter, nearly seventeen, has been sickly and feeble since birth. Physicians, climate changes, and every promised relief have failed, and father and son must talk faith through suffering.
6358-the-history-of-england-a-study-in-p:
A. F. Pollard traces England as a study in political evolution, from foundations in 55 B.C. to a century of empire ending in 1911. An American visitor at Hastings, musing that a little island has often been conquered, sets the theme: how a conquered island became an empire that conquered others. Pollard warns that mere incidents will not satisfy readers who see history as interpretation of human development, not a simple story.

Nine chapters carry the argument, from submergence after 1066 and emergence of the English people to nationalism, struggle for self government, expansion, industrial revolution, and democracy. Edward's peerage policy, Richard II as a new monarch born before his time, and noble factions fighting for the crown illustrate the method. Pollard writes a compact, argument driven history, with chronology, bibliography, and index to support it.
639-the-god-idea-of-the-ancients-or-sex-:
Eliza Burt Gamble traces how sex shaped early god ideas in this study, grown from her Evolution of Woman. She argues that gods reflect the inner life of peoples, and that sex is the root fact in nature and in worship alike. Tree, sun, and fire cults, dual gods, and the split of female and male elements fill the chapters.

Gamble writes with earnest, scholarly care, drawing on monuments, symbols, and sacred sites. Later chapters treat Israel, Phoenicia, and Christianity as continuations of older faiths. The book serves as a bold early feminist history of religion, where the divine bears the marks of human sex and society.
6402-the-romance-of-isabel-lady-burton:
Volume two of Isabel Lady Burton's romance, told in part by herself and in part by W. H. Wilkins, continues Book Two through Damascus and beyond. Chapters run from in and about Damascus and early days there, through the desert to Palmyra, Bludan in the Anti Lebanon, gathering clouds, and Jerusalem and the Holy Land. The recall follows, with true reasons for Burton's recall, the passing of a cloud, and early years at Trieste.

A journey to Bombay, India, Trieste again, and shadows lengthening lead to Gordon and the Burtons, a sword hanging and a sword falling. Book Three, widowed, opens with the truth about The Scented Garden, a return to England, and the tinkling of a camel's bell. At Safed, Jews flock to the travellers' tents with hospitality. Wilkins and Burton write a life of travel, faith, and loss, in her voice and his.
643-the-death-of-the-lion:
Henry James writes of fame and its costs in this short novel, first published in 1915 in Martin Secker's edition. A young journalist, taken on by a weekly paper, sets out to write on Neil Paraday, a writer once obscure and now celebrated. The narrator hopes the piece will lift his own career as much as his subject's.

James writes with dry, watchful irony, letting the press, friends, and admirers crowd a shy author till his work suffers. The tale turns on how praise can harm the praised. It endures as a sharp study of literary fame, where a lion dies not from neglect but from too much attention.
6456-public-opinion:
Walter Lippmann's Public Opinion, dated 1921 at Wading River, Long Island, opens with Plato's cave: beings chained in an underground den, seeing only shadows before them, firelight behind. Chapter one, The World Outside and the Pictures in Our Heads, tells of an island in 1914 where Englishmen, Frenchmen, and Germans lived without cable, mail steamer coming once in sixty days. In mid September they still talked of Madame Caillaux's trial, then learned they had been at war for six strange weeks.

For six weeks they acted as friends when in fact they were enemies, yet their plight, Lippmann argues, differs little from our own. A mid passage contrasts two business partners in war: one enlists for a dollar a day, sacrificing all, while the other takes a war contract for handsome profit over costs. Lippmann writes democracy's central problem: how opinion forms from pictures in heads, not the world outside.
6473-practical-argumentation:
George K. Pattee, assistant professor of English and rhetoric at Pennsylvania State College, writes Practical Argumentation to be practical from the student's standpoint and the teacher's. Argumentation is often criticised as purely academic, or a mere stepping stone to law, but Pattee defines it as the art of presenting truth so others accept it and act on it. Debate is its special oral form, carried on by opposing sides.

By argumentation, he argues, men overthrow error and discover truth, threshing a problem until chaff blows away and kernels of truth remain. Courts, assemblies, and all discussing bodies recognise this, and men of affairs hear advocates of different systems before great enterprises. A mid passage turns to government and armies, where discipline and subordination entrusted to leaders outweigh private convenience in war. Pattee writes a working rhetoric for students.
6485-hugh-wynne-free-quaker-sometime-bre:
S. Weir Mitchell's Hugh Wynne, Free Quaker, sometime brevet lieutenant colonel on General Washington's staff, first appeared in book form in 1896 and reached a nineteenth edition with corrections. Mitchell used the new edition to rectify mistakes in names, dates, and localities. Those errors passed unnoticed by ordinary readers, but troubled local archaeologists and readers who ask a novelist to combine scholarly accuracy with creative imagination. Howard Pyle's pictures include a frontispiece asking, is it yes or no, Darthea?

A mid passage shows a gay, winning creature telling her story freely, unlocking her heart for her listener, who laughs that she has a key called love. She kisses him and asks if he says such pretty things to other women. Mitchell writes Revolutionary Philadelphia through a Quaker turned soldier, where conscience, love, and war pull one man three ways.
6486-the-life-of-the-venerable-mother-ma:
A religious of the Ursuline community writes The Life of the Venerable Mother Mary of the Incarnation. Its materials come from her son's life of her, published in 1677, and the history of the Ursuline monastery at Quebec, published in 1863. Her infancy, childhood, and youth open it: early call to union with God, charity to the poor, purity of soul, and inclination for religious life. Married life follows, with rule of life, love of prayer, fulfilment of duty, and patience under trial.

Her husband's death brings a first year of widowhood, solitude in the world, and charity to the poor, then a call to divine union, austerities, and vows of poverty and obedience. A mid passage shows the obstacle removed by her husband's death, leaving her free when duty allows separation from her son, now twelve, who can dispense with care. She watches his infancy with tenderness before answering her call.
6663-country-life-in-canada-fifty-years-:
Canniff Haight, looking back as a man past sixty, recalls country life in Canada fifty years before his writing. Haight dedicates the book to the young men of Canada. Their honor and energy will shape their great heritage, he says. The book opens with a preface in which Haight steps to the footlights to state his aim. He writes as one who lived the days he paints.

Farm, town, and home life in old Ontario fill the pages, with the warmth of a man who would be a boy again. Haight quotes Childe Harold on happy years, and his tone stays fond throughout. Country Life in Canada Fifty Years Ago is a pleasant, personal memoir of a vanished rural world.
6668-annette-the-metis-spy-a-heroine-of-:
Edmund Collins tells of Annette, a Métis maiden who becomes a heroine of the North-West Rebellion. The chapters open as a chief falls in love with the half-breed maiden, then follow Annette's brave resolve, her lover in danger, and divers adventures on the prairie. A daring escape, a fight, a capture, and a guardian swan all lie ahead.

The tale opens at sunset, with two riders hurrying ponies along a blind trail toward purple hills. Collins writes in the bold, romantic style of his day, with the prairie itself as a stage. Annette, the Métis Spy, is a stirring, old-style adventure of love and courage in a troubled Canadian west.
6699-inns-and-taverns-of-old-london:
Henry Shelley sets forth the historical and literary ties of old London's inns, taverns, coffee-houses, clubs, and pleasure gardens. His preface notes a puzzle: Teutonic folk are said to love home above all, yet Londoners of the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth centuries poured zeal into substitutes for home. Those substitutes fill these pages.

From ancient hostelries to famed coffee-houses where writers, wits, and plotters met, Shelley traces who drank, talked, and schemed where. The book, dated 1909, reads as a walking tour through literary London. Inns and Taverns of Old London is a rich, anecdotal guide for lovers of the city and its books.
6734-drusilla-with-a-million:
Elizabeth Cooper opens with a call down a sunny line of old ladies: Drusilla Doane, O Drusilla Doane. A little old woman, birdlike in glance, brings word that two men wait in the parlor to see Drusilla, and the darning of a tablecloth stops as all stare. Drusilla, white-haired and expectant, answers that she is here.

From that homely start grows a tale of a plain old woman who comes into a million, and of the kin, suitors, and schemers who follow the money. Cooper writes with humor and warmth, in a voice close to small-town talk. Drusilla with a Million is a gentle, funny novel of wealth, worth, and a late chance at life.
6806-the-hallam-succession:
Amelia Barr's Hallam Succession moves from Americans in Yorkshire and Martha Craven's trouble to Richard and Elizabeth, Wesley and Methodism, and Antony's plans. Christmas, renewal of a covenant, separation, and a return home follow, with Texas and liberty, a squire's death, Antony's sin, and Elizabeth's trial ahead. The tale ends in Texas, at the sunset of life.

Barr, author of Jan Vedder's Wife, writes a long family saga across England and the American southwest, with faith and love as its threads. Her tone is earnest and romantic. The Hallam Succession is a rich, old-style saga of two families, two lands, and a lasting covenant.
6844-the-poetical-works-of-mrs-leprohon:
Mrs. Leprohon, born R. E. Mullins, sings in her poetical works as a brave pioneer of Canadian letters, giving her people her best in songs of duty, patriotism, and hope. Her introduction hopes that, when Canada's literature is written, room will be kept for pioneers who sang ere life in the young land ceased to be a struggle. Wealth and leisure, it says, will in time give writers an audience prepared by culture.

Leprohon's verse is earnest, patriotic, and domestic, with a love of home and country. The volume gathers her best lyrics in one place. The Poetical Works of Mrs. Leprohon is a warm, historic Canadian poetry book, worth a look for lovers of early Dominion verse.
6898-the-boys-of-columbia-high-on-the-gr:
Graham Forbes follows the Columbia High football boys in their struggle for the silver cup, opening with practice and a road to town. The chapters mix sport with school mystery, from the strange history of Ralph and treachery in camp to the abduction of Bones and a singing school night. Frank turns chauffeur, an unwilling pilot flies, and a great marsh hides dangers of its own.

Rivals from Clifford press hard, and the side faces a feared epidemic scare and a hard fought first half. The tale builds to a finish won by four inches, with a message from Tokio closing the book. Forbes writes for boys who love a game played hard and a team that holds together under strain.
6929-poemata-latin-greek-and-italian-poe:
John Milton's Latin, Greek, and Italian poems appear here in William Cowper's translation, with spelling modernized and notes set after each poem. The contents open with complimentary pieces addressed to the author, then elegies, including verses to Charles Diodati, on the death of the Cambridge beadle, and on the Gunpowder Plot. Poems in various metres follow, on the Fifth of November, on bishops, and on nature's decay.

Other pieces sing of Leonora in Rome, tell the fable of the peasant and his landlord, and mark the approach of spring. The collection shows Milton as a young scholar poet writing across tongues before Paradise Lost. Cowper's English keeps the verse clear for readers who lack the Latin, Greek, and Italian.
6946-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Charles Farrar Browne, known as Artemus Ward, speaks here in his complete works, opening with a biographical sketch by Melville Landon. Part one gathers essays, sketches, and letters, from his first business letter and a piece on forts to the Shakers, the Atlantic cable fete at Baldinsville, and a visit to Brigham Young. The showman, the lecturer, and the humorist all appear in these pages.

Part two turns to war, with the show confiscated, thrilling scenes in Dixie, and a Fourth of July oration. Later pieces include an interview with President Lincoln, a talk with Prince Napoleon, and notes on woman's rights and the press. The collection preserves a comic voice that charmed America and England alike.
6960-a-narrative-of-the-life-of-mrs-mary:
Mary Jemison, taken by Indians in 1755 when only about twelve, lived among them to old age, and James Seaver took this narrative from her own words on November 29, 1823. It tells of the murder of her father and his family, her sufferings, her marriages to two Indians, and her troubles with her children. It also records Indian barbarities in the French and Revolutionary wars and the life of her last husband.

An appendix adds the tragedy at the Devil's Hole in 1783, Sullivan's expedition, and the traditions, manners, and customs of the Indians as Jemison knew them. Seaver presents many historical facts never before published, in her voice as he heard it. The book remains a rare first hand account of captivity turned into a life.
7037-beric-the-briton-a-story-of-the-rom:
G A Henty tells of Beric the Briton at the Roman invasion, opening with a preface to his dear lads. His series on England's wars would be incomplete, he says, without the age when Romans ruled the island. Native valor, acknowledged even by Roman historians, yielded only to superior discipline, not to want of bravery or physical strength.

Roman rule, for a time, greatly benefited a people who had wasted strength in perpetual tribal wars, since it brought Roman civilization. In the end it proved disastrous, since Britons defended by Roman soldiers lost their military virtues. When the legions left, they could not resist the Saxons. Beric's tale follows that rise and fall through a young Briton's eyes.
704-the-mansion:
Henry van Dyke wrote this short tale about John Weightman, a rich New York man whose grand house stands as a sign of his success. Weightman prides himself on wealth well used, yet he has shut his heart to need. A dream-like journey after death tests what his mansion, and his life, were truly worth.

Van Dyke sets earthly splendour against a heavenly standard, where love and mercy count more than stone and bronze. The tale is brief and pointed, written for readers who enjoy a moral fable with a twist. Its fame rests on that closing reversal, which asks whether a life built for show can stand when judged by grace.
7061-a-march-on-london-being-a-story-of-:
G A Henty tells Wat Tyler's insurrection in A March on London, opening with an illustration of Edgar striking a foe a buffet that sends him reeling. His preface notes the later fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries are known better than ages before or after, thanks to Froissart, Monstrelet, and Holinshed, whose full detail leaves nothing to desire. The uprising of the Commons, chiefly folk still in serfdom under Richard the Second, was in itself justifiable.

English serfdom never reached continental harshness, yet serfs bore grievous disabilities, giving part of their time to a feudal lord's work. Henty follows Edgar from such a world to the march on London, where commons demand justice from a young king. The tale blends chronicle fact with a boy's adventure in revolt.
7116-vestiges-of-the-natural-history-of-:
Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation, published in London by John Churchill in 1844, traces the world from space to man in a single scheme. Contents run from the bodies of space, their arrangements and formation, through the constituent materials of earth and other bodies, to the earth formed in the era of primary rocks. Sea plants and corals mark the commencement of organic life.

Fishes abound in the old red sandstone, land plants begin with the carboniferous formation, and reptiles open terrestrial zoology in the new red sandstone. Mammals commence with the oolite, grow abundant in the tertiary, and present species begin with superficial formations. The book closes with general and particular thoughts on the origin of animated tribes, including man.
7171-linda-condon:
Linda Condon first appears as a grave girl of about ten, slim and still, with a straight black bang across a clear pale brow. Her eyes stay longest in the mind: blue, velvet-rich, and sharp with a colour that startles the heart. Joseph Hergesheimer draws her with care, letting one face carry the whole opening scene.

Her mother supplies the gaiety for the whole family, bright where Linda is sober, and the contrast shapes their home from the first page. The novel follows Linda from this quiet childhood portrait onward, watching how a watchful, uncommon girl meets the world around her. Hergesheimer's prose stays slow and exact, lingering on looks and moods.
719-the-plays-of-w-e-henley-and-r-l-stev:
W. E. Henley and Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these plays together, blending Stevenson's romance with Henley's stagecraft. Deacon Brodie, the best known, turns on an Edinburgh tradesman who is respectable by day and a burglar by night. Beau Austin, Admiral Guinea, and Robert Macaire round out the set, with rogues, sailors, and gallants.

The plays are brisk melodramas, built for strong acting and sharp scenes rather than for the closet. They show Stevenson trying his hand at the theatre, with Henley's help, before his novels made him famous. The volume is a treat for those who like Victorian stage romance and the roots of the Deacon Brodie legend.
7234-species-and-varieties-their-origin-:
Hugo De Vries delivered these lectures at the University of California on the origin of species and varieties by mutation, edited by Daniel Trembly MacDougal for the Carnegie Institution. De Vries sets his own claim beside Lamarck and Darwin in the opening pages. Where they saw origin as a natural fact or an object of inquiry, he makes it an object of experiment.

The lectures argue that new forms can arise by sudden mutation rather than by slow shading alone, and De Vries supports the claim with botanical work. His prose stays that of a lecturer, clear and stepwise, moving from old views to new tests. The book marks a bold early statement of mutation theory in the years after Darwin.
726-a-psychological-counter-current-in-r:
William Dean Howells wrote this essay on a shift he saw in recent fiction: against a strong tide in one direction, a counter-current was already forming. He notes how reform breeds reaction and reaction breeds reform, and how a new turn in taste often starts as a faint drift before it becomes a flood.

Howells applies this law to the novels of his day, praising the inward, psychological turn he saw rising against coarser fashion. His prose is reflective and urbane, the work of a critic watching his own age. The essay offers a short, shrewd guide to how literary fashions change, and why no single school holds the field for long.
7344-archibald-malmaison:
Julian Hawthorne's Archibald Malmaison opens with a child's wish that fairy stories were true, set against an adult's preference for acknowledged fiction. Hawthorne calls the inconsistency more apparent than real. Experience teaches that the greater the fairy story, the less the truth, and the greater the truth, the less the fairy story, since romance's graces clash with fact's crude straightforwardness.

Childhood idealism, he writes, believes the most beautiful must on that account be most true, and the novel tests that belief in a strange tale. Hawthorne, author of Garth, Sebastian Strome, and Dust, writes in his father's shadow yet with his own eerie touch. The book invites readers to weigh wonder against truth.
7350-how-to-prepare-and-serve-a-meal-and:
Lillian B. Lansdown joins two household arts in one volume: how to prepare and serve a meal, and interior decoration. The meal chapters run from before the meal is served and the waitress's entrance through breakfast, luncheons, and informal home dinner. Formal dinner, afternoon teas, and suppers follow, with carving hints, menu planning, and menus for Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Lent, including a chapter outside the Eighteenth Amendment.

Decoration follows, on lines and curves, form, colour, and proportion, then on single rooms: living room, drawing room, library, bedroom, nursery, play room, and hints on period furniture. Lansdown writes for a hostess who must feed guests well and house them beautifully. The book makes domestic craft orderly and gracious.
7377-five-lectures-on-reincarnation:
Swami Abhedananda, a disciple of Ramakrishna who taught Vedanta in the West, sets out the Hindu doctrine of rebirth in five plain lectures. He begins with the body itself: the gross physical body, he argues, expresses a subtle body, a minute germ of living substance carrying mind and vital force in potential form. Birth, growth, decay, and death follow the changes of that subtle body.

From that basis the lectures explain how the soul passes from life to life, carrying its tendencies forward like a seed carrying a plant. The talks draw on Vedanta philosophy while keeping the language direct, so readers new to the subject can follow the argument. The book serves as a clear, short introduction to reincarnation as taught in the Hindu tradition.
7404-john-james-audubon:
John Burroughs, himself a famous American naturalist, writes the life of the man who painted America's birds. The pioneer before Audubon was Alexander Wilson, a Scottish weaver turned poet. He emigrated in 1794 and described more than three hundred species before his death in 1813. Audubon did not simply continue Wilson's work; he began again, as a pioneer in his own right.

Burroughs stresses what the two men shared. Both were famous walkers, covering hundreds of miles on foot. Both loved nature at first hand rather than from books, and both kept journals of their wanderings. The book follows Audubon from his studies and drawings of birds to his place as chief of American ornithologists. It is a naturalist's tribute to a naturalist, warm and well informed.
7412-coningsby-or-the-new-generation:
Benjamin Disraeli wrote Coningsby in 1844, between his early novels and his later career as prime minister, and it is his great political novel. Its hero, Harry Coningsby, grows up in early nineteenth-century England. Educated among the young men of his class, he must find his way in a political world of parties, patronage, and reform. The title names the theme: a new generation coming to power.

Disraeli, himself a young politician turned novelist, writes from inside the world he describes. The novel mixes drawing-room comedy with serious argument about what England should become after the Reform era. Readers meet ambitious young men, powerful patrons, and the clash of old Toryism with new ideas. It remains the classic novel of English politics in the 1830s.
7441-the-writings-of-john-burroughs-volu:
John Burroughs named this volume for the stream of his boyhood. Pepacton is the Indian name of his native stream in the hills where he was born and where his kindred sleep. The name is said to mean marriage of the waters, and Burroughs likes the fit: the book is itself a union of many currents, essays gathered from years of walking and watching.

The chapters include footpaths, a bunch of herbs, and the ways of birds and beasts along the water. Burroughs writes as a neighbor of nature, not a distant scientist, finding lessons in common sights. Readers of his earlier volumes will recognize the voice at once: plain, observant, and rooted in one beloved countryside, the watershed that made him a naturalist.
7443-windy-mcpherson-s-son:
Sherwood Anderson dedicated this novel to the living men and women of his own Middle Western home town, and it begins there. Sam McPherson is thirteen, tall and big-boned, walking the board platform of Caxton, a little corn-shipping town in Iowa, on a long summer twilight evening. He walks with extreme deliberateness, lifting his bare feet with care, a boy already taking his own measure.

The novel follows Sam from that platform into manhood, as the son of Windy McPherson, the town talker, tries to make his own way in the world of business and ambition. Anderson writes about the price of success and the pull of home, in the plain Midwestern voice that would soon make Winesburg, Ohio famous. It is a novel of growing up in small-town America.
7472-the-duke-of-stockbridge-a-romance-o:
Edward Bellamy, later famous for Looking Backward, wrote this romance of Shays' Rebellion from his own Berkshire ground. It opens on August 17, 1777, as the first sunbeams glance down the long valley of Stockbridge, where the Housatonic creeps around the base of Fisher's Nest. The village, with its wide grassy streets, rail fences, and low houses, is drawn with loving local knowledge.

From the march of the minute men, the story moves through the Revolution toward the postwar years, when debt and taxes drove Massachusetts farmers to rebellion under Daniel Shays. Bellamy follows Stockbridge folk through those troubles, mixing romance with history. The novel gives a local, human view of a rising that shook the young republic and helped bring on the Constitution.
7523-the-lady-of-the-decoration:
Frances Little tells this novel in letters, and the first is dated San Francisco, July 30, 1901. Its writer calls herself a soldier on the eve of battle, whistling in a stuffy hotel room to keep her courage up. In the morning she sails for the Flowery Kingdom, Japan, after years in which roses never strewed her path at home. A crowd of loving, tearful faces fades as her train pulls out.

Behind her lies a sudden release: death put an end to a bondage, and a kindergarten course, taken to please a friend and keep her mind off things, pointed a new way. The letters that follow trace a young American woman making a life abroad, among strangers, schools, and ceremonies. Little dedicates the book to all good sisters, and to hers in particular.
7539-quotes-and-images-from-chesterfield:
Lord Chesterfield's letters to his son, written between 1766 and 1771, are the classic manual of eighteenth-century worldliness. This volume gathers their most quotable passages with images. The quotations run in alphabetical order, so a reader can browse advice the way one browses a dictionary of conduct. Each entry is short enough to carry away and use.

The advice is unmistakable Chesterfield. A little learning is a dangerous thing, and a joker is near akin to a buffoon. A favor may make an enemy while an injury may make a friend. Above all, keep absolute command of your temper, avoid speaking of yourself, and never be vehement about trifles. The collection distills a father's worldly wisdom into its sharpest sentences.
7779-of-captain-mission:
Daniel Defoe's Of Captain Mission, drawn from The History of the Pyrates, volume two, presents a pirate captain of unusual principle. Modern scholarship, the introduction notes, has traced the great pirate history to Defoe since John Robert Moore's 1932 case, despite its old mask as Captain Charles Johnson.

Editors from Michigan, California, and other universities frame the text with notes on its making. Mission's story, part of a larger gallery of sea robbers, raises a sharp question: can a man who lives by plunder also live by a code? The volume offers Defoe's answer in brisk, vivid prose.
7800-outlines-of-english-and-american-li:
William J. Long's Outlines of English and American Literature introduces the chief writers of both nations, the books they wrote, and the times they lived in. Dedicated to his sister Millie, it opens with Chaucer's line on the way to good adventure, and a portrait of Shakespeare after the Chandos picture.

That portrait's history runs from player John Taylor through Davenant, Betterton, and the Duke of Chandos, a chain the notes trace with care. Through short lives, summaries, and context, the book gives students and general readers a clear, friendly map of two literatures side by side.
7829-american-prisoners-of-the-revolutio:
Danske Dandridge's American Prisoners of the Revolution, dedicated to her grandfather Lieutenant Daniel Bedinger, gathers scattered accounts of patriot suffering in British hands. A boy in prison stands in the dedication for all that was bravest and most honorable in the patriots of 1776.

Dandridge admits little here is original. She reprints scarce, out-of-print narratives, above all Captain Dring's, in their own words, since retelling would weaken them. For students and general readers, the volume preserves firsthand testimony of prison ships, hunger, cold, and endurance under a foe. It keeps their voices alive.
7833-samantha-on-the-woman-question:
Marietta Holley's Samantha on the Woman Question, by Josiah Allen's Wife, follows Samantha to a family reunion near Washington, birthplace of the first known Allen. Chapters promise a woman wanting her rights, tender eyes, striving with an emissary, moth-millers and minny fish, and a women's parade.
