Suárez explains that charity counts as perfection substantially, principally, and entirely, since other virtues accompany it and serve it. Faith and hope prepare the way but do not themselves constitute perfection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-n:
An entry on Christopher Norton, martyr, executed at Tyburn in May 1570. His father Richard Norton of Norton Conyers, Yorkshire, known as Old Norton, had kept the Catholic faith through Henry the Eighth and Edward the Sixth. He governed Norham Castle under Mary and served as sheriff of Yorkshire in 1568. Pardoned once for the Pilgrimage of Grace, he joined the northern rising of 1569 with his brother Thomas, nine sons, and many kin.

Attainted, Old Norton fled to Flanders with four sons, two sons were pardoned, and one apostatised, leaving the faith. Christopher, the seventh son, and his great-uncle were captured and proved steadfast Catholics, then hanged, disembowelled, and quartered. The apostate Edmund and a sister live on in Wordsworth's White Doe of Rylstone, a poem that keeps the Norton name joined to loyalty, loss, and a ruined house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-circumcision:
Circumcision, the cutting away of the foreskin, is practised by peoples across the world. Egyptians, Colchians, and Ethiopians knew it in ancient times, as did tribes in Sumatra, New Guinea, Samoa, Australia, and the Americas. Herodotus traced it to Egypt, but its wide spread casts doubt on a single origin. Suggested reasons range from tribal marking and initiation at puberty to cleanliness, nobility, and religious offering.

For Jews it was the sign of the covenant given to Abraham, and the article weighs its relation to Gentile practice. Muslims keep it by tradition, not by Koranic command, usually between seven and twelve years. In Catholic teaching it was no mere ceremony but a sacramental rite. Augustine and Aquinas held it conferred remission of original and actual sin, though not full release from temporal punishment as baptism does.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-citation:
A citation is the legal act by which a judge calls a person before a tribunal for trial. A verbal citation has the judge send an apparitor to summon the accused to a fixed day. It is edictal when issued by public summons, and real when the person has been arrested by officers of the law. Citations are simple or peremptory. The simple form fixes a day without threats. The peremptory form binds strictly and warns that no later summons will follow.

Ordinarily a citation is so necessary that its omission voids every later act of the trial. Exceptions cover a person caught red-handed, an accused already before the tribunal, and danger in delay. A valid citation must name plaintiff and defendant, state the cause, and fix day and place, binding the case to the judge who issued it. Contumacy by a defendant raises a presumption of guilt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-dablon:
Claude Dablon, a Jesuit missionary born at Dieppe in February 1618 and dead at Quebec on 3 May 1697, entered the Society of Jesus at twenty-one and reached Canada in 1655. Sent at once with Chaumonot to the Iroquois at Onondaga, he kept a diary picturing the journey's terrors. In 1661 he went with Druillettes toward Hudson Bay, seeking missions and perhaps a passage to the China Sea, but the expedition failed.

In 1668 Dablon joined Allouez and Marquette on Lake Superior, the trio Bancroft calls illustrious, and he first told the world of the region's rich copper mines. He chose Marquette for the expedition that found the Upper Mississippi and published Marquette's letters and charts. He also proposed a half-league prairie canal from Lake Michigan to the Illinois River. After founding Sault Sainte Marie he led the Canadian missions from 1670 to 1680 and again from 1686 to 1693.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clifton:
Clifton, a diocese of England covering Gloucestershire, Somersetshire, and Wiltshire, was founded by Pius the Ninth when he restored the English hierarchy in 1850. Before that it belonged to the Western District, one of four vicariates set up by Innocent the Eleventh in 1688, covering Wales and six south-western counties. In 1840 Wales became a separate vicariate, leaving the district to the English counties alone.

As the vicars apostolic lived chiefly at Bath, Joseph William Hendren, the Western District's last vicar apostolic, became the first Bishop of Clifton. The diocese thus represents the old vicariate, and its bishop keeps the Western District archives, a prime source for English church history from 1780 to 1850. Earlier papers perished in the Gordon Riots of 1780. Hendren moved to Nottingham a year after the foundation, succeeded by Thomas Burgess. A cathedral chapter of a provost and ten canons rose on 28 June 1852.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-co-education:
Co-education now generally means educating the sexes together, but it carries several meanings. Mere juxtaposition uses the same buildings, equipment, and teaching staff for both sexes without the same methods or regimen. Co-ordinate education teaches both sexes by the same methods and teachers, but each sex keeps its own classes and, at a university, its separate college. Identical education teaches both sexes the same things together, in time and place, by the same faculty and methods, admitting age and proficiency but not sex.

It is this third and narrowest sense that has drawn widespread discussion, growing rapidly in the United States, slowly in Europe. Co-education is practically universal in American public elementary grades and common in private schools, including Catholic parochial schools. In secondary schools, the Commissioner's Report for 1905 to 1906 counted 7,962 public co-educational high schools with 283,264 boys and 394,181 girls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colophon:
Colophon, a titular see of Asia Minor and one of the twelve Ionian cities, fills Sophrone Pétridès's entry. It lay between Lebedos and Ephesus. Two sons of Codrus, King of Athens, founded its colony in Greek antiquity. It gave birth to the philosopher Xenophanes and the poet Mimnermus. Lysimachus, a successor of Alexander, later destroyed it. Notium served as its port, and nearby stood Clarus, with its famed temple and oracle of Apollo Clarius.

Colophon's cavalry won renown, and its pine trees yielded a rosin, colophony, prized for musical instrument strings. Under Rome the city lost weight, and its name moved to the site of Notium. The Notitiae still list Colophon as a suffragan of Ephesus into the twelfth or thirteenth century. Lequien names only four bishops, two of them legendary. Its ruins lie at Ghiaour-Keui, a small village near Smyrna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-ant:
Adrian Fortescue's entry traces the Communion antiphon, from Communio, once sung while the people received the Blessed Sacrament. It now follows that moment, displaced from its old place. In the Ambrosian Rite it is called the Transitorium, since the celebrant crosses to the Epistle side to read it. It is the fourth and last changeable choir part of the Mass, after Introit, Gradual, Offertory. It dates at least to the fourth century. Augustine, who died in 430, defended its use in Africa against Hilary.

Two changes mark its history: removal to a place after Communion, and shortening. Fortescue notes its present form and sources in the rubrics and in Duchesne and Benedict XIV. The entry gives singers and students a compact history of a short chant. It runs from early African controversy to a settled place in the Mass, sung by the choir as the faithful communicate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-compensation:
John Augustine Ryan's entry treats compensation as the price paid for human labor. Wherever free men could sell their labor, they saw its pay as a matter of right and wrong. Christian lands shared that conviction. Early in the fourth century, Diocletian's edict fixed maximum prices and set a wage schedule for nineteen classes of workers. Its preamble claimed justice for the people as its motive. Through the Middle Ages and nearly to the nineteenth century, most European lands regulated wages by law.

Church Fathers implied a laborer's right to life-sustaining pay, holding that God meant the earth for all. Today Catholic teaching is precise on the just minimum. It sets that ethical floor without declaring what full justice in pay would demand. The entry leans on Levasseur, Brants, Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum, and Ryan's own Living Wage of 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-de-forb:
Camillus Maes's entry follows the Comte de Forbin-Janson, Bishop of Nancy and Toul, founder of the Holy Childhood. Born at Paris on 3 November 1785, he was a Knight of Malta from childhood, a soldier at sixteen. Napoleon made him Auditor of the Council of State in 1805. His family hoped for a statesman, but in 1808 he entered Saint-Sulpice seminary. Ordained in Savoy in 1811, he became Vicar-General of Chambéry, then chose French missionary work with Abbé de Rauzan.

Refusal to sign the Gallican Declaration drew persecution, and exile forced him from France in 1830. Gregory XVI sent him touring the United States in 1839. Louisiana first felt his zeal, and he gave a third of Spring Hill College's price near Mobile. From New York to Quebec, his missions stirred Catholics, and French Canada kept his memory. Back in France he founded the Holy Childhood in 1843, dying near Marseilles in 1844.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concelebratio:
Adrian Fortescue's entry defines concelebration as the rite where several priests say Mass together, all consecrating the same bread and wine. Once common in East and West, it survived late into the ninth century, when priests stood around their bishop and consented to his sacrifice. Rome modified the rite, perhaps under Pope Zephyrinus from 202 to 218, so each priest consecrated a separate host, held by deacons in patens or corporals, while all shared one chalice.

By the sixth century the rite marked all station days. By the eighth it remained only for the greatest feasts: Easter, Christmas, Whitsunday, and Saint Peter. Other days saw priests assist without consecrating. In the Latin Church it survives only at ordinations of priests and bishops. There the new priests consecrate with the bishop and receive under one kind. At a bishop's consecration, the new bishop instead communicates with his consecrator under both kinds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concepcion:
F. M. Rudge's entry covers Concepción, a diocese in Chile suffragan to Santiago de Chile. It takes in the provinces of Arauco, Bío-Bío, Concepción, Ñuble, Maule, Linares, and Malleco, across 27,901 square miles. Pius IV issued its erection bull on 22 May 1563. Since then, except for a vacancy from 1818 to 1832, a bishop has always sat at Concepción. Its institutions include an orphan asylum and a Capuchin missionary college.

Ten congregations of men and seven of women work in the diocese, among them the Sisters of Providence, Mercy, Christian Charity, Good Shepherd, and Sacred Heart, numbering 393 in all. The Catholic population runs to 835,790, with 52 parishes, 190 priests, 91 secular and 99 regular, and 135 churches and chapels. College and seminary stand beside nine Catholic schools with 2,550 pupils. The entry points readers to Chile for the wider story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-condition:
Francis Aveling's entry defines condition, from Latin conditio, as what is needed, or at least helpful, for a cause to act, without itself causing the effect. Light suits my writing, yet I, not the light, cause the writing. A condition is a circumstance in which a cause acts readily, or alone can act. It differs from a real principle giving existence to an effect. Conditions split into the sine qua non, without which a cause lies inoperative and irreplaceable, and the merely helpful kind, where one of several conditions may serve.

Combustion of wood offers an irreplaceable case. Some modern philosophies treat condition as accidental modification. Writers professing theism yet defining God through conditions, removing imperfections toward plenitude, miss the strict sense, Aveling argues. The entry closes with Thomas's third way in the Summa, on knowing whether God exists, where conditions frame the proof without causing its conclusion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confirmation:
Thomas Scannell's vast entry treats Confirmation, the sacrament where the Holy Ghost comes to the baptized to make them strong Christians, soldiers of Jesus Christ. Names vary: bebaiosis, a making fast; teleiosis or consummatio, a perfecting tied to baptism; Sacrament of the Holy Ghost; Sacrament of the Seal; imposition of hands; chrism anointing. West says confirmatio, Greeks myron. The entry moves through practice, doctrine, rite, minister, matter, form, recipient, and effects.

In the West the bishop usually administers it, opening with hands imposed and prayer, then anointing. The East drops the opening imposition and prayer, anointing with words on the seal of the Spirit's gift. The bishop alone serves as ordinary minister. Only the baptized, unconfirmed, in grace, may receive. Confirmation stands to baptism as growth to generation, adding grace, not removing sin. The entry closes amid Anglican debate, noting some Catholics conceding no visible sign ordained by God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Blanche Mary Kelly's entry covers the Sisters of Notre-Dame de Sion, founded at Paris in May 1843 by Marie-Théodore and Marie-Alphonse Ratisbonne. Théodore, sub-director of the Archconfraternity of Our Lady of Victories, gained Gregory XVI's leave to work among Jews. With his brother he raised a congregation under Our Lady of Sion, mother-house at Paris. Affre, Sibour, and Cardinal Fornari encouraged it warmly, and Pius IX granted indulgences on 15 January 1847.

Holy Land foundations led the expansion, chiefly a convent, orphan asylum, and school near Jerusalem's Ecce Homo arch, with Saint John's founded from it. Saint Peter's orphanage added art and manual schools. At Ecce Homo 170 pupils, Jews, Mohammedans, and schismatics, studied beside 100 day scholars. Houses followed in London, Rome, Versailles, Trieste, Vienna, Prague, Galatz, Bucharest, Jassy, and Constantinople. Five hundred sisters served, guided by the Priests of Notre-Dame de Sion.

The entry surveys Immaculate Conception congregations, opening with the Conceptionists. Beatrix de Silva, sister of Blessed Amadeus, founded them at Toledo in 1484. Having fled a jealous queen's court to a Toledo Dominican convent, she lived forty years in holiness without joining. Devotion to the Virgin moved her to found a new congregation. With companions she took a castle Queen Isabella set apart. In 1489, by Innocent VIII's permission, the sisters adopted the Cistercian rule and daily Office.

Other bodies follow in turn. Lamennais founded the Missionaries of Rennes at Saint-Méen for seminary care. Georgian priest Peter Carisciarian founded Constantinople's Servites in 1864 for Georgian Christians, with sister Servites running two schools open without creed distinction. Canon Kinet founded the Sisters of Providence at Jodoigne in 1833, settled at Champion near Namur in 1836. Abbé Noailles founded Bordeaux's Sisters of the Immaculate Conception in 1820 as a Holy Family branch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-consecration:
Augustin Joseph Schulte's entry defines consecration as separating a thing from profane to sacred use, or dedicating it to God's service through prayers and rites. The custom reaches remotest times, with rites in Egyptian and pagan cults. Among Semitic tribes it formed a threefold act: separating, sanctifying, devoting to the Deity. Hebrew Law applied it to the whole people, Moses's People of God.

Exodus 24 describes altar and twelve stones, with twelve youths performing the holocaust. Aaron and his sons received consecration in Exodus 29; Levites represented the first-born. The Church distinguishes consecration from blessing. The Roman Pontifical holds one of persons, a bishop's, and four of things: altar, altar-stone, church. Eastern prayers carry the same import. Unqualified, consecration ordinarily means the Mass act changing bread and wine. A bishop's consecration marks priesthood's plenitude, its day a Sunday or Apostle's feast, its rite most splendid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-consubstantia:
Thomas Scannell's entry treats consubstantiation, a heretical doctrine attempting to hold Christ's Real Presence in the Holy Eucharist without Transubstantiation. Under it, Christ's Body's substance exists together with bread's substance, and His Blood's substance together with wine's. Hence the name. How two substances coexist finds various explanations. The subtlest theory holds that, just as God the Son took a human body without destroying its substance, so in the Blessed Sacrament He assumes bread's nature. Hence the theory also bears the name Impanation, founded on Incarnation's analogy.

Full treatment belongs with the general doctrine of the Holy Eucharist. Here the entry traces the heresy's history briefly. Earliest ages set the background, while Berengarius and his modern followers appealed chiefly to reason and the Fathers for their opinions. Cited works span Harper, Franzelin, Schwane, Vernet, Streber, Hedley, Waggett, and Gore, grounding the sketch in Eucharistic theology across Catholic and Anglican writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-contemplation:
Augustin Poulain's entry treats contemplation through mystical theology, since neither explains clearly without the other. Supernatural acts no effort of ours can produce, even slightly or for an instant, are called mystical. Seeing one's guardian angel, independent of effort, counts as mystical.

Mystical states bear names: supernatural or infused, and extraordinary. Ordinary prayer and acquired contemplation follow in four degrees: vocal prayer, meditation, affective prayer, and prayer of simplicity. The last two, prayers of the heart, border mystical states. Mental prayer rich in affective acts counts as affective. Feeling neither relish nor facility for certain acts, one should not force them. Higher contemplation, or mystical union, unfolds in four stages, from incomplete union, the prayer of quiet, to full, semi-ecstatic union. After Saint Teresa, Saint John of the Cross holds first place for observation, though his classifications confuse, and both tower over later repeaters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-contrition:
Edward Hanna's entry treats contrition, Latin contritio, a breaking of hardness. Holy Writ abounds in repentance calls: Ezekiel's call to turn and live, Luke's warning that without penance all perish. At times repentance includes exterior satisfaction, but always implies knowing wrong done to God, hating evil, and desiring to turn and do good. Psalm 50 voices this pattern, as does the Pharisee and publican parable.

Nature follows: inward repentance theologians call contrition. Need stands firm: until the Reformation no theologian denied contrition's need for pardon. Catholic teaching splits hatred of sin in two: perfect contrition, from love of God offended, and imperfect contrition, its lesser twin. Marks require contrition, perfect or imperfect, to be inward, from grace, whole, and supreme. Inward means real heart sorrow, not mere outward show. Supernatural means prompted by grace and faith's motives, not merely natural ones. Whole, per Trent, includes firm purpose against future sinning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conversion:
Benedict Guldner's entry traces conversion, from Latin converto and conversio, change. In the Vulgate, in patristic Latin, and in later ecclesiastical Latin, conversion means moral change. It means turning to God and the true religion, passing into modern languages. Conversion usually means an infidel's turn to the true religion, or a schismatic's or heretic's turn to the Catholic Church.

Every man must seek the true religion, embrace it when found, and live by its precepts. The normal process begins with examining the Church's credentials, often painful labour. Since the duty rests on Divine right, no civil law can forbid fulfilling it. Reception follows abjuration of heresy or profession of faith, conditional baptism, and sacramental confession with conditional absolution. Force, violence, or fraud may never bring an unbeliever's conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-core-dathan-a:
Florentine Bechtel's entry treats Core, Dathan, and Abiron, revolt leaders against Moses and Aaron in Numbers 16. Core, son of Isaar, came from the Caathite Levite family. Dathan and Abiron were sons of Eliab, son of Phallu, of Ruben's tribe. A fourth leader, Hon, son of Pheleth, also a Rubenite, never appears again, suggesting textual corruption. Core headed the rebellion, hence the sedition of Core, and the rebels, the congregation of Core.

Many people, unreconciled to the exclusive Sinai priesthood, wanted the old order restored, with priestly functions exercised by each family's oldest member. Yet all shared jealousy of Amram's house, where civil and religious authority concentrated, aiming at its overthrow. Core's sons did not perish, and later descendants appear among the singers. The critical school reads the story as a combination of three narratives, one telling a revolt under Dathan and Abiron against civil authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coronation:
Herbert Thurston's entry treats coronation under five headings: Constantinople's emperors; Visigothic and Celtic elements; English coronation orders; the Western Empire and the Roman Pontifical; and other ceremonials. A coronation rite, ideally, creates the monarch, though changing succession theory may make it rather the ratification of an accomplished fact.

Down to Constantine's reign, coronation properly speaking did not exist, for he first used the diadem. The next epoch-making change introduced the Patriarch to set the diadem on the elected sovereign's head. Phocas in 602 became the first emperor crowned in church. Records of procedure stay somewhat defective, yet church crowning certainly continued from that time. One passage suspects the adoration's timing, just after the emperor received the Host, was motived by some design. Western inauguration rites show first coronation-order traces in Spain and Great Britain, with close liturgical relations via Celtic channels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corporation:
John Willis's entry treats corporation, Latin corpus, a body. A corporation is an association recognized by civil law and regarded in law as an artificial person. Chief Justice Marshall of the United States Supreme Court defined it as an artificial being, invisible, intangible, existing only in contemplation of law. Being law's mere creature, it holds only those properties its creation charter confers, expressly or as incidental to its existence.

Chancellor Kent of New York defines a corporation as a franchise possessed by one or more individuals subsisting as a body politic. English law distinguishes corporations first as aggregate or sole, then as ecclesiastical or lay. Under English common law, corporations depended on a charter, Latin charta, a paper, granted by the king. Ecclesiastical corporations as such find no recognition in United States law, federal or state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ch:
The Council of Chalcedon, the Fourth Ecumenical Council, sat from 8 October to 1 November 451 in Bithynia, Asia Minor. Its chief task was to defend orthodox teaching against Eutyches and the Monophysites, who so stressed Christ's unity that his two natures blurred into one. Discipline and jurisdiction also claimed the fathers' attention.

Session by session, the council heard testimony and read the fathers, and on 22 October proclaimed Christ true God and true man, one person in two natures. Bishops signed amid acclamation, and later sessions settled jurisdiction, including Jerusalem's bounds. Monophysite refusal persisted in Palestine, Syria, Armenia, and Egypt, where followers remain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
This long reference entry surveys the councils held at Avignon across eight centuries, from a little-known meeting in 1060 to a synod in 1849. It treats each council in turn, noting who presided, what was decided, and how the decisions touched clergy, laity, and rulers in southern France.

Early meetings deposed a usurping bishop, excommunicated the people of Toulouse for sheltering Albigensian heretics, and defended church property and clerical rights. Later councils regulated confession, urged regular attendance at parish churches, and protected would-be crusaders who had failed to depart. The 1849 council closed the sequence with ten chapters on faith and discipline, and the entry cites its sources throughout for readers who want to dig deeper.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-covington:
A diocesan entry covers Covington, the Kentucky see east of the Kentucky River, established in 1853 by dividing the Diocese of Louisville. It spans 17,286 square miles, with a total population near 900,000, of whom about 54,000 were Catholics at the time of writing.

Early congregations were served by clergy in the tradition of Flaget, Badin, David, and Nerinckx. German Catholics predominated in Covington and Newport, while the Irish were the majority inland at Lexington, Frankfort, and Paris. The entry lists bishops, parishes, schools, and religious orders, and notes how a lack of industry south of the Mason-Dixon line handicapped the region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-creation:
A long doctrinal entry defines creation as God's act of bringing a thing's whole substance into being out of nothing. It distinguishes this from ordinary making, where material already exists, and explains that nothing here is not a stuff from which things are made. It means the absence of any prior material.

The entry then traces the idea through history: its scriptural roots, its statement by the Fathers against pagans and Gnostics, and its fuller development by the Scholastics with Aristotle's theory of causes. Arguments for creation follow, along with a discussion of creation and evolution. Readers get a systematic account of one of Catholic theology's central doctrines, with a full bibliography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cremation:
A long entry traces cremation, the burning of the dead, from ancient practice to modern Church law. Pre-Canaanites burned their dead until about 2500 BC, while Jews, Egyptians, and Persians largely did not. Greeks and Romans varied with their views of the afterlife, and by the fifth Christian century the practice had ceased in the West under Christian influence.

Church legislation then made burial in earth or tomb part of Christian burial, and later Roman decrees forbade cremation. The entry explains the motives: in modern times cremation was often tied to a public profession of irreligion and materialism, promoted first by Freemasons. It closes by asking whether cremation marks culture, and answers that the Church could conform if the custom ever became universal without offence to faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dagon:
A scriptural entry examines Dagon, a Philistine deity whose name most scholars derive from the Semitic root for fish, meaning little fish. The Bible's account at Azotus suggests a figure with face, hands, and a fish-like lower body. Coins of Philistine and Phoenician cities match it, showing a composite being, human above and fish below.

Dagon was the foremost god of maritime cities such as Azotus, Gaza, Ascalon, and Arvad, and was sometimes paired with the half-fish goddess Derceto or Atargatis. A minority view, resting on Philo Byblius, makes him a god of corn and agriculture instead. The entry also notes the Ark's sojourn in Dagon's temple and the Syrian peoples' religious abstinence from eating fish, naturally linked to a fish god's worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-beaton:
A biographical entry traces David Beaton, Cardinal Archbishop of Saint Andrews, born in 1494 and murdered on 29 May 1546. A younger son of John Beaton of Balfour, he studied at Saint Andrews, Glasgow, and Paris, and in 1519 became James V's resident at the French court. His uncle, Archbishop of Glasgow, gave him the rectories of Campsie and Cambuslang and the abbacy of Arbroath.

Returning in 1525, Beaton sat in Parliament and became Lord Privy Seal. He negotiated James's French marriages, attended the king's wedding at Notre-Dame in 1537, and rose to cardinal and primate. As Scotland's leading churchman he opposed English influence and Protestant reform, and his murder by Protestant lairds in Saint Andrews Castle opened a new phase of Scotland's Reformation struggle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-william:
A biographical entry follows David William Bacon, first Bishop of Portland, Maine, born in New York in 1813. He studied classics at Montreal's Sulpician College and theology at Mount Saint Mary's, Emmitsburg, and was ordained at Baltimore in 1838. After missions at Utica, Ogdensburg, New York City, and Belleville, he founded Brooklyn's third parish in 1841, completing a suspended priest's unfinished church.

Named first Bishop of Portland in 1855 and consecrated at Saint Patrick's Cathedral, he found only six priests and eight churches in all Maine. Know-Nothing bigotry, the Civil War, and Portland's great fire of 1866 all hindered him, yet his zeal, tact, and energy prevailed. At his death he left 63 churches, 52 priests, 23 parish schools, and about 80,000 Catholics to his successor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dedication:
A liturgical entry treats dedication, the setting aside of places for a sacred purpose, though the word is sometimes used of persons consecrated to God's service. Christians believe God fills all space, yet they reserve special spots for communion with the Creator and worship. Old Testament precedent runs from Jacob and Moses to Solomon's temple dedication.

The New Law surely kept the custom by apostolic usage, though persecutions make early references rare. A fragment ascribed to Jerome notes Rome's dedication of the first church built and consecrated by Peter. The first authentic accounts come from Eusebius and Sozomen, on Tyre's cathedral in 314 and Constantine's Jerusalem church. Etheria's pilgrim narrative fully describes Jerusalem's dedication festival as witnessed in the fourth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deduction:
A philosophy entry explains deduction, from Latin for leading out, in two parts: as an argument and as a method. As an argument it moves from known truths to other truths that must follow from them. As a method it is the chain of such moves by which we learn more.

The typical form is the syllogism, whose essential feature is necessary connection between premises and conclusion. Granted the premises, the conclusion must follow, with no greater certainty than the premises themselves. The entry shows this in hypothetical and categorical forms, treats demonstration as certain deduction, and contrasts deduction's descent from general to particular with induction's ascent. Both, it argues, rest on abstract necessary truths. In plain terms, if the start is true, the end must be true too. That must is the whole point of the move, and it is what makes the thought safe to trust.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-degradation:
A canon law entry defines degradation, a penalty by which a cleric is entirely and perpetually stripped of all office, benefice, dignity, and power from ordination. By a set rite he is made a layman, loses clerical rights, and passes to the civil power. Yet degradation cannot remove the character conferred in ordination, nor free him from celibacy or the Breviary.

Degradation is twofold: verbal, the mere sentence, and real, its execution, parts of one punishment, not two penalties. Unlike deposition, it strips him wholly of orders, rule, and church rights, and leaves him fully under civil rule. Any bishop may speak the sentence, but only a consecrated bishop can carry it out, and only Rome can lift it. Today dismissal with perpetual deprivation usually takes its place. In short, he keeps the mark of ordination for life, but loses post, pay, and place among clergy for good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-delegation:
A canon law entry defines delegation, from Latin delegare, as commissioning another to exercise jurisdiction in the delegator's name. Jurisdiction itself is the power of one holding public authority and pre-eminence to rule and govern others. Roman law used delegation for substituting one debtor for another, and modern civil law uses it for committees acting for parliament or courts.

Canon law distinguishes delegation by a person, ab homine, from delegation by law, a jure, which may come from a juridical or moral person. Thus bishops hold certain powers over exempt regulars as delegates of Trent. One acting as delegate of the Apostolic See faces appeal to the pope, since the jurisdiction is really his. Sections cover delegated powers for liceity and validity, the delegate's duties, and the end of delegation by death or completion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demonic-posse:
A doctrinal entry that separates two kinds of attack by evil spirits. Obsession strikes the body from outside, while possession takes control of it from within. The soul itself, the entry insists, can never be seized or robbed of freedom, though its command over the body may be blocked.

Cases range from frequent reports among ancient pagan peoples to a single case in the Old Testament, then to the fuller Gospel record. Later pages test whether the phenomenon is real, answering writers who deny evil spirits or their power over the body. Church practice for dealing with the possessed is left to companion entries on exorcism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denunciation:
A canon law entry on denunciation, the act of laying another's crime before a superior. Evangelical denunciation follows Matthew's steps: speak alone first, then bring witnesses, then tell the church, all aimed at reform rather than revenge. Judicial denunciation, by contrast, seeks punishment as well as correction once the Church built a criminal process.

A denouncer differs from an accuser by bearing no duty to prove the charge, and modern diocesan courts put a promotor fiscalis in the accuser's place. False accusers once faced the penalty they sought for others, though that reprisal rule has lapsed. Denunciation is strictly required only in set cases, such as marriage impediments, abuse of the confessional, and leaders of secret societies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deposition:
A canon law entry on deposition, a lasting penalty that strips a cleric of office, benefice, and the exercise of orders. Total deposition takes all powers, while partial deposition takes only some, and no penance alone earns release, though a superior may restore a truly amended man. It bars future offices too, which sets it apart from simple privation and from suspension.

Early centuries already expelled guilty clerics to lay communion while leaving their ordained character intact. Use of the word itself is traced to the Synod of Agde in 506, and down to the twelfth century the two penalties meant the same thing. Later law drew the lines that separate deposition from degradation, which alone takes away clerical privilege.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-derogation:
A canon law entry on derogation, the partial repeal of a law, set against abrogation, its total repeal. Roman jurist Modestinus first framed the distinction, and canon law took it up, though loose speech still uses derogation for either kind. Dispensation differs again, easing named persons rather than cutting the law itself.

Papal rescripts often carry derogatory clauses, and their absence can flaw the document's form. Rules for reading derogations demand strict and specific terms, with no need for fresh promulgation when nothing contrary is imposed. General laws do not sweep away special ones by accident, since superiors are presumed unaware of the particular law they never meant to touch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desecration:
An entry on desecration, the loss of the sacred character that consecration or blessing gives to places and things. Objects set aside for worship gain a stamp that bars profane use, and they lose it when they cease to be what they were. As a rule they keep their blessing while they stay morally the same and fit for their first purpose.

A broken chalice unfit for the altar loses its consecration on its own, with no ceremony needed. A sound vessel that only needs regilding cannot be stripped by rite at all, though the bishop's leave is sought before a craftsman handles it. Churches, altars, and altar stones each have their own listed triggers, from ruin to a cracked stone or a broken anointed corner.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desertion:
A canon law entry on desertion, the culpable abandonment of a state whose duties one freely accepted. Leaving the faith counts as apostasy, as does a cleric quitting his orders or a religious quitting solemn vows. Quitting a congregation under simple vows is mere desertion instead: no excommunication follows, though clerics face suspension and the path usually ends in dismissal.

Later cases cover a cleric who abandons his benefice, judged under rules from the Council of Trent, and desertion in marriage, where malice must be weighed by the proper judge. Sources point readers to the canonists on non-resident clerics, to appeals, and to Sanchez on marriage. Each strand turns on the same question: what duty was freely taken, and how was it left?
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-detraction:
A moral theology entry on detraction, the unjust harming of another's good name by telling a fault the person truly has, or is honestly believed to have. Calumny differs at once: the slanderer states what he knows is false, while the detractor tells what he takes to be true. As a breach of both charity and justice, detraction is generally a mortal sin.

Guilt shrinks to venial when the matter is slight or little heed was paid to the harm. Weighing a case means weighing the charge itself, the detractor's standing for truth, and the standing of the person attacked, since a small flaw can wound a high reputation deeply. A duty to pay for money loss follows the detractor, and that burden passes even to his heirs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devolution:
A canon law entry on devolution, the right of a higher church authority to fill a benefice when the rightful patron or collator fails. Failure may mean neglect or naming an unfit candidate, and the loss of right lasts only for that vacancy, never for good. When a chapter or private patron leaves a post empty six months, the diocesan bishop steps in.

Neglect by the bishop moves the right to the metropolitan, and where bishop and chapter share the power, the faithful partner keeps it alone. A vacant see needs a vicar capitular within eight days or the metropolitan names one, while chapters electing an archbishop, bishop, or abbot get three months before Rome takes over. Law aims both to cure neglect and to punish misuse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dibon:
Dibon was an ancient town east of the Jordan. The Bible names it as a camp of the Hebrews on the road to the Promised Land. Later the tribe of Gad rebuilt it, and in the age of the prophets it passed to the Moabites. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets its ruins at modern Diban, near the Arnon valley.

Black basalt rubble, an acropolis, cisterns, and burial caves still mark the site. Scraps of Roman and Christian building lie among them. The entry also notes the great find made there, the stone stele of Mesha, king of Moab. Now kept in the Louvre, it bears the proud title of the Dibonite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dijon:
Dijon is a French diocese covering the whole department of Cote-d'Or, answering to the archbishop of Lyons. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that the Concordat of 1801 first gave it Haute-Marne as well, until Langres was restored in 1821. Its story reaches back to the sixth century, when Saint Gregory of Langres raised a great basilica over the tomb of Saint Benignus.

Travelers from Italy brought the acts of the saint's martyrdom, and Burgundy counted Benignus, a disciple of Saint Polycarp, among its first preachers. The entry moves from these origins through abbeys such as Fontenay and Flavigny to the Dijon of 1907. Art, sculpture, and monastic history all find a place in its survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dispensation:
Dispensation is the act by which a lawful superior relaxes a law in a single case. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry stresses that it differs from repeal, since the law stays in force for all others. It also differs from a kindly reading of the lawgiver's intent, since dispensation lifts a case that truly falls under the law. Its reason lies in the needs of souls and the common good.

The entry treats dispensation in general and then at length in marriage, the field where most readers meet it. It separates dispensations from vows, fasting, and abstinence, which have their own articles. For students of canon law, it is the classic statement of how mercy and order meet in a single act of authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-distraction:
Distraction, from a Latin word for drawing away, is treated here as it strikes prayer and the giving of the sacraments. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes the plain truth that mental prayer and a wandering mind destroy each other. In spoken prayer, a want of inner heed, if willed, spoils its perfection and earns blame, yet stray thoughts do not rob prayer of its true character.

So long as the will to pray stood at the start, and nothing outward clashes with prayer, the act remains human and keeps its worth. Wilful distraction is sinful, though not mortal, unless it risks error in what is needful for a sacrament to hold. The entry thus steadies anxious pray-ers with a sane and merciful rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divination:
Divination is the seeking of knowledge about future or hidden things by means that cannot truly yield it. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry calls it the unlawful twin of prophecy, since prophecy gives lawful knowledge of what is to come. Magic seeks to act, while divination seeks to learn, and its supposed power is always traced to gods or evil spirits. It is nearly as old as the human race itself.

Egyptians, Chaldeans, Hindus, Romans, and Greeks all kept diviners, as did shamans of northern Asia, mgangas of Africa, druids of the Celts, and medicine-men of America. The entry finds fraud mixed with self-deception throughout, with vague forecasts that favored vice and harmed virtue. Modern fortune-telling, it suggests, is the same old trade in new dress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dolores-missi:
Dolores Mission, also known as Mission San Francisco de Asis, ranks sixth among the twenty-one missions of the California Indian chain. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry dates its formal opening to 9 October 1776, though the feast of Saint Francis on 4 October was the day meant for it. The absence of the presidio commander delayed the rite, and the first Mass near the site had been said in a tent by Father Palou in June.

Palou gives 1 August as the founding day in the mission records, yet the friars always kept 4 October as the patronal feast. The entry draws on Palou's own writings and on Bancroft and Engelhardt for the mission's early years. It offers a precise chronicle of a founding shaped by soldiers, friars, and feast days.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duc-de-saint-:
The Duc de Saint-Simon was born on 16 January 1675 and died at Paris on 2 March 1755. He left the army in 1702 and lived at court. There he grew close to the dukes of Chevreuse and Beauvilliers. With Fenelon, they guided the schooling of Burgundy's duke, a grandson of Louis the Fourteenth. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how, at the Sun King's death, he joined the regency council of the young Louis the Fifteenth and went as ambassador to Madrid in 1721.

When the Duke of Bourbon became minister in December 1723, Saint-Simon retired from public life. Between 1740 and 1746 he wrote his celebrated Memoirs, a precious record of the reign of Louis the Fourteenth. The Boislisle edition with commentary, already twenty-two volumes by 1911, stands as a monument of learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duchess-of-ai:
The Duchess of Aiguillon, Marie de Vignerot de Pontcourlay, was the niece of Cardinal Richelieu, born in 1604 and dead at Paris in 1675. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells of her 1620 marriage to the Marquis of Combalet, and of his death at the siege of Montpellier two years later. Widowed and childless, she joined the Carmelite convent in Paris, resolved to end her days there.

When Richelieu became premier she had to follow him, serving as lady of the bedchamber to Marie de Medicis and handing out his alms and liberality. Convinced of the vanity of honors, she sought no joy from wealth, only its giving. Flechier's funeral oration for her ranks among the masterpieces of French pulpit eloquence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eastern-monas:
Eastern monasticism before Chalcedon began in Egypt, the motherland of the monastic life. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how it sprang up at the start of the fourth century and spread across the Christian world within a few years. Its speed matched its staying power, and within Saint Anthony's lifetime the religious state had become a permanent mark of the Church, with its ideals and groundwork fixed.

The simple teaching of Egypt's first monks and hermits also set the broad outlines of ascetic theology, the science of the spiritual life. The entry follows the movement from desert cells to the monasteries of Constantinople, where fifty-four houses stood by 518. It argues that early monasticism holds far more than antiquarian interest for the Church today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eberhard-of-r:
Eberhard of Ratisbon, also called Eberhard of Salzburg, was a German chronicler who flourished near the start of the fourteenth century. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry admits that almost nothing is known of his life. Documents from 1294 to 1305 show him at work as a master, an Augustinian canon, and an archdeacon. His chronicle opens with Rudolf of Hapsburg's election and runs down to 1305.

He meant to write Bavarian history alone, but events outside Bavaria that seemed important drew him wider. The chronicle gains value from the fuller detail of its last five years, where important letters are added. The entry lists its editions, from Canisius through Bohmer to Jaffe in the Monumenta, a guide for students of medieval Bavaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Those who take up the church profession and the evangelical counsels with pure intent hold a special gift: an ecclesiastical or religious vocation. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry counts among its elements all the inner and outer helps and graces that lead to the resolve and to steadfast perseverance. Commonly the call shows itself through deliberation by reason and faith, though at times a flood of supernatural light makes deliberation needless.

Two signs mark a vocation, one negative, the absence of any bar, and one positive, a firm resolve with God's help to serve in the clerical or religious state. If God leaves a free choice, the soul must weigh the matter with care. The entry weighs the debates over vocation by attraction, citing Lahitton and his critics in the reviews.

Ecclesiastical jurisdiction means the right of guiding and ruling the Church of God. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry treats it under its general concept and classes, its growth in the strict sense, and its present scope. Like every society, the Church Christ founded for men's salvation needs a ruling power, and Christ bestowed it.

Just before ascending, he charged the apostles together to proclaim his teaching to all nations, baptize them, and teach them to keep all his commands. The entry notes that the decree Lamentabili of 1907 rejects denials of that commission. It cites Hergenrother, Laurentius, and Sagmuller, mapping a power that runs from the apostles to today's courts.

A cleric may hold the right to a yearly sum from a church or benefice income, for just reasons a church superior approves: an ecclesiastical pension. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry derives the word, by one account, from pendeo, to depend, and by another from pendo, to pay. The term sometimes names a kind of benefice, as when a cleric gains a perpetual vicarship and lives on its income.

In its usual sense, however, it means not a benefice but money paid for a time to a third person. That money comes from the fruits of a benefice held by another, under a superior's warrant. The oldest case in church history is said to be Domnus of Antioch, pensioned from the see he gave up at Chalcedon in 451. Ferraris and Wernz stand among the sources.

An ecclesiastical person, in the strict sense of the term, is one bound to the Church by a special tie. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes the wider sense first, anyone who belongs to the visible society of the Church and has not been cast out by canon law. Custom, however, reserves the phrase for those marked by tonsure or orders, with a share in jurisdiction, or by vows in an approved religious order or congregation.

That closer union brings particular duties not laid on the general faithful. The entry is short, citing Scherer alone, and it points readers to the article on clerics for the fuller account. For students of canon law, it draws a clean line between the baptized at large and those set apart for church service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-bolton:
Edmund Bolton was an English historian, antiquary, and poet who lived from about 1575 to about 1633. Born of Catholic parents in Leicestershire, he studied at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, and then law in London, moving among writers and scholars such as Cotton, Camden, and Ben Jonson. His verses appeared with Sidney, Spenser, and Raleigh in England's Helicon.

His faith kept closing doors: a life of Henry II was turned down because it spoke too well of Saint Thomas of Canterbury. Friends, among them Buckingham, tried to help his debts, and he won a small court post under James I. The entry paints a gifted, unlucky man whose learning outran the chances his religion allowed him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-education:
Education in its widest sense is the subject of this long, wide-ranging entry. It defines schooling as the growth of mind, knowledge, and character through all the events that shape a child. In a narrower sense, it is the planned work of home and school in training young minds. What a teacher aims at, it argues, rests on what he thinks a person is for, and on his ties to God, to others, and to the world.

History takes up much of the piece, from early peoples through the Middle Ages, when Church and State worked together under rulers such as Charlemagne, Alfred, and Theodoric. Later parts weigh the claims of Church and State, the choice of subjects, the training of teachers, and the order of schools from first lessons to higher study. It is a Catholic view of learning as both a human craft and a moral task.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-and-ha:
Edward and Harriet Thompson were an English husband and wife who both turned Catholic and spent their lives in religious writing. Edward Healy Thompson, born at Oakham and dead at Cheltenham in 1891, left Anglican orders for the Catholic Church in 1846. With James Spencer Northcote he edited the Clifton Tracts from 1851, and he wrote lives of saints and devotional books.

Harriet Diana Thompson, born in 1811 and dead in 1896, joined the Church when her husband did and wrote stories of Catholic life that won many readers. Her best-known work was a life of Charles Borromeo, alongside tales such as Mary, Star of the Sea and Mount St. Lawrence. The entry pairs two quiet workers whose pens served English Catholics for decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-anthon:
Edward Anthony Hatton was a Dominican apologist born in 1701 and dead at Stourton Lodge near Leeds in 1783. Probably the son of a Lancashire yeoman listed as a Catholic non-juror, he was schooled at the Dominican college at Bornhem and professed there in 1722 under the name Antoninus. Ordained priest, he left for mission work in England in 1730.

He served as chaplain to Yorkshire families, took charge of the Middleton mission, and moved it to Stourton Lodge, where a new chapel rose in 1776. Twice provincial of the English Dominicans, he began a mission at Hunslet in 1776. His Memoirs of the Reformation, signed Constantius Archaeophilus, came out after his death in 1826 and drew chiefly on acts of Parliament and Protestant historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-barron:
Edward Barron was an Irish missionary bishop who carried the faith from Philadelphia to West Africa, born at Waterford in 1801 and dead at Savannah in 1854. Trained at the Propaganda College in Rome, he served in Ireland, then joined the diocese of Philadelphia, where he became pastor of Saint Mary's, head of its seminary, and vicar-general.

In 1840 the Holy See asked American bishops to care for black Catholics in Liberia, and Barron sailed from Baltimore in December 1841 with Father John Kelly. Consecrated in Rome in 1842 as titular Bishop of Constantia and Vicar Apostolic of the Two Guineas, he worked in Africa until fever forced his return in 1845. He died of yellow fever at Savannah while helping its bishop in an epidemic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-diccon:
Edward Dicconson was titular Bishop of Malla and Vicar Apostolic of the Northern District of England, born in 1670 and dead in 1752. Son of Hugh Dicconson of Wrightington Hall, he was sent to Douai at thirteen or fourteen, finished philosophy in 1691, and was ordained in June 1701. He stayed on as procurator, teacher of theology, and vice-president from 1713.

A surviving diary shows his world. In 1704 he visited Paris to greet the exiled Stuart king and his mother Mary of Modena. In 1705 he spent a week at Cambrai with Fenelon, then archbishop there. After work on college funds in Paris he joined the English mission in 1720. He served as chaplain at Chillington. He went to Rome as envoy of the secular clergy before his consecration at Ghent in 1741.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-rishto:
Edward Rishton was a Lancashire priest and scholar born in 1550 and dead in Lorraine in 1585. He studied at Oxford from 1568 to 1572, turned Catholic, and went to Douai, where he was the first Englishman to matriculate. While still a student he drew up a chart of church history, and after ordination at Cambrai in 1576 he was sent to Rome.

Back in England in 1580, he was arrested. He was condemned to death with Edmund Campion and others in 1581. He was left in prison instead, first in the King's Bench and then in the Tower. Exiled in January, he reached Reims in March and, at Father Persons' urging, finished Sander's unfinished Origin and Growth of the Anglican Schism. Bound for a doctorate at Pont-a-Mousson, he fled plague to Sainte-Menehould and died of it there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-sheldo:
Edward Sheldon was an English translator of French devotional books, born at Beoley in 1599 and dead in London in 1687. Third son of Edward Sheldon of Beoley, he studied at Oxford and Gray's Inn and finished his schooling with a tour abroad. He married Mary Wake, with whom he had nine sons and four daughters, and lived quietly on his estate at Stratton in Gloucestershire.

In 1641, harassed for his religion, he moved to London and lived in retirement until his death. His four translations from French were The Holy Life of M. de Renty in 1658, The Rule of Catholic Faith by Dr. Veron in 1660, The Counsels of Wisdom by Fouquet in 1680, and Christian Thoughts for Every Day of the Month, also in 1680. The entry sketches a private man whose reading served English Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-election:
Election in canon law is the subject of this long, orderly entry. It is laid out under six heads. They cover the juridical concept, the electors, the persons eligible, the act of electing, what follows election, and the elections now in use. In its strict sense election means the choice, by lawful electors, of a fit person for a church office. That choice gives the person a real right to the post, even before later confirmation.

The entry carefully sets election apart from look-alike modes. Postulation names a person who is legally barred, and asks a superior to dispense him, so it confers no right. Presentation is the act of a patron, who may be a layman, while true electors must be clerics. Nomination, recommendation, request, and free collation each get the same close treatment, making the piece a handy reference for church lawyers and historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elizabeth-bar:
Elizabeth Barton, called the Nun of Kent, was a visionary put to death at Tyburn in 1534, probably born in 1506. At nineteen, a servant at Aldington in Kent, she fell ill, fell into trances, and spoke of things done elsewhere that she could not have known. Her parish priest reported her to the Archbishop of Canterbury, and a commission of Benedictines, Franciscans, and clergy examined her and judged in her favour.

Cured, so the tale ran, at a chapel of the Virgin before a crowd, she became a Benedictine nun near Canterbury and won wide fame for holiness. She protested against Henry VIII's divorce in God's name, wrote to the pope, and met Fisher, Wolsey, and the king. Cromwell moved against her in 1533, she confessed deception after examination, and a bill of attainder in January 1534 sealed her fate. The entry leaves open whether she was gifted or an impostor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ellakim-parke:
Ellakim Parker Scammon was an American soldier and educator, born at Whitefield, Maine, in 1816 and dead at New York in 1894. Appointed to West Point, he graduated in 1837 fifth in a class of fifty-two. He stayed on to teach mathematics. Future generals Grant, Rosecrans, and Newton were among his pupils. He served in the Seminole War and as an aide to General Scott in Mexico, winning promotion for bravery at Vera Cruz.

Just before sailing for Mexico in 1846 he became a Catholic convert. From 1847 to 1854 he surveyed the Upper Lakes with the topographical corps, and in 1856 he left the army. He taught mathematics at Saint Mary's College and at Cincinnati's Polytechnic College. He served as a volunteer brigadier-general in the Civil War from October 1862. He was consul at Prince Edward Island from 1866 to 1871. He taught at Seton Hall from 1875 to 1882.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emancipation:
Emancipation in Roman law was the act by which a slave freed from his master, or a son freed from his father's power, was declared legally independent. The entry first notes the Church's early use of the process in freeing slaves. Unable to end slavery at once, the Church softened it toward serfdom. It replaced the elaborate Roman forms with manumission in church. There a master's plain statement before bishop and congregation sufficed.

Freedom was often a first step to orders, since a slave needed manumission before ordination. In canon law a son who takes solemn vows in a religious order is likewise freed from his father's legal power. No positive law states it. Modern civil law does not recognise it. The entry also covers the release of a cathedral school pupil from his master, and of a cleric from his diocese on election as bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-encolpion:
An encolpion was a small reliquary worn on the breast, and this entry traces its forms and uses. The Greek name means that which is worn on the breast. Early Christians carried in such cases relics: cloth stained with a martyr's blood, parchments with Scripture texts, and fragments of the True Cross. The custom grew from the pagan habit of wearing bullae, or amulet cases, round the neck against enchantment.

The Church sought to cleanse the habit of superstition by swapping Christian objects for pagan charms. Jerome scolded women who treated little Gospel books and cross wood as magic. Encolpia came in oval, round, and four-cornered shapes, in materials from gold to glass. Two square gold examples were found in 1571 in tombs of the old Vatican cemetery. They were engraved with Christ's monogram between Alpha and Omega on one side and a dove on the other.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-england-befor:
England before the Reformation is a vast survey that limits England to the largest part of Great Britain south of the Solway, the Cheviots, and the Tweed, including Wales. Its area was 57,668 square miles, and its resident population in 1901 was over twenty-three million, nearly four-fifths of the United Kingdom. For history up to the Norman Conquest it points readers to the Anglo-Saxon Church article.

The account itself starts with William the Conqueror. It warns that pictures of a degraded English Church in the early eleventh century are much exaggerated. Edward the Confessor could not repair damage from Danish anarchy and long disorders at the centre of Christendom. Simony, neglect of clerical celibacy, and subjection of churchmen to secular power were real and widespread. Yet reform was already stirring, above all the monastic renewal begun at Cluny and taken up in Normandy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-england-since:
England since the Reformation takes the Protestant Reformation as the great dividing line in English history, as in Europe's. It quotes Macaulay's judgment that the Anglican Reformation sprang from no religious motive. Of its makers, Ridley alone did not treat it as a mere political job, though he played no very prominent part. The entry then traces the history of the change and marks its results.

Under Henry VIII the English schism was consummated in 1535 by the Act making the king Supreme Head of the Church of England, with power to reform errors, heresies, and abuses. That statute cut England from the unity of Christendom and handed the pope's jurisdiction to the Imperial Crown. The entry calls this the Anglican Reformation's unique mark: the bold taking of all papal authority by the sovereign, including the power to rule the Church and to define doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-enthronizatio:
Enthronization, from the Greek word for placing on a throne, has borne several meanings, and this entry sorts them out. In early use it meant placing relics on the altar of a church about to be consecrated. Such a church was called enthroned. In the Middle Ages the enthronization of marriage meant the blessing in the nuptial Mass. In the East the word was seldom used for induction to a parish benefice.

After consecration the new bishop was led to the episcopal throne and took possession of it. He received the kiss of peace, heard a passage of Scripture read, and gave an address. Letters announcing his communion in faith went to fellow bishops. Gifts went to those who had consecrated him. Today the rite keeps its form but has lost juridical weight. The pope's enthronization in the Chair of Saint Peter was once a ceremony of importance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-episcopal-int:
Episcopal intercession was the bishops' right to plead for criminals, granted by the secular power to the bishops of the early Church. It sprang less from any fixed law than from the great respect paid to the episcopal office in the early centuries. The seventh canon of Sardica, about 344, mentions it, as do Augustine, Jerome, and the historian Socrates.

Augustine pleaded repeatedly with Macedonius, governor of Africa, for condemned men. Martin of Tours pleaded with Emperor Maximus for the imprisoned Priscillianists in 384 and 385, and Flavian of Antioch pleaded with Theodosius I in 387 for citizens who had smashed imperial statues. Ambrose moved Theodosius to delay executions and confiscations for thirty days after sentence, to leave room for mercy and to shield the innocent. Bishops had free access to prisons and were urged to visit inmates twice a week and report cruel keepers to the emperor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ethelred-taun:
Ethelred Taunton was a writer, born at Rugeley, Staffordshire, England, on 17 October 1857, and dead in London on 9 May 1907. Educated at Downside, he desired to enter the Benedictine Order, but weak health prevented him. He entered the Institute of Saint Andrew at Barnet, founded by the convert George Bampfield, but health again prevented him from remaining. Finally he joined Manning's Oblates at Bayswater and was ordained priest in 1883.

Three years later he left the Oblates for the mission at Stoke Newington in North London. Here he built a new church, opened in 1888, but a fall of scaffolding injured him seriously, bringing partial paralysis and ending his active work. He continued, however, to be busy with his pen. He was widely read and wrote on many subjects. For a while he lived at Bruges, where he founded and edited Saint Luke's Magazine, which had only a brief existence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-miche:
Etienne-Michel Faillon, a historian, was born at Tarascon in France on 3 January 1800 and died at Paris on 25 October 1870. Avignon and Aix gave him his studies. He joined the Sulpicians in 1821 and was ordained priest in 1824. As director of La Solitude he wrote ascetic and biographical works and gathered material for later publications.

Montreal, during an official visitation in 1848, gave him the idea for his Histoire de la Colonie française au Canada. Twelve volumes were intended, covering the whole French domination from 1534 to 1759, but only three appeared, with the narrative ending in 1675. Two later voyages to Canada let him write biographies of Sister Marguerite Bourgeoys, Jeanne Mance, Mother d'Youville, and Jeanne Le Ber. Monuments inédits sur l'apostolat de Sainte Marie-Madeleine en Provence stands beside his life of Monsieur Olier among his chief works on Old France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-euchologion:
The Euchologion is one of the Service-books of the Byzantine Church, corresponding more or less to our Missal and Ritual. It contains directions for the deacon at Vespers, Lauds, and Liturgy. The priest's prayers and deacon's litanies for those hours follow. Then come the Liturgies, with rubrics for the holy Liturgy in general and a note on arranging the breads at the Proskomide.

The Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom is the frame into which the others are fitted. It gives the priest's and deacon's parts at full length, first for Chrysostom's liturgy, then for the differing parts of Saint Basil's, then for the Presanctified Liturgy. After the Liturgies come sacraments and sacramentals with rules, canons, and blessings. Comes the rite of churching the mother after child-birth, then canons about baptism, prayers over catechumens, the rite of baptism, and the washing of the child seven days later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evolution:
Evolution is the subject of a vast article. It sets out the scientific theory that today's species grew by descent from earlier forms, against the older theory of special creation of each species. It draws a sharp line between the bare fact of evolution and special systems that explain it, such as natural selection, the influence of surroundings, or Lamarck's use and disuse. The article is planned in seven parts, covering history, the meaning of species, variation and experiment, and the proofs from fossils, form, embryos, and geography.

Its history runs in three periods. Linnaeus built his system on the constancy of species, Buffon broke with him, and Lamarck founded the modern theory in his Philosophie zoologique of 1809. Darwin's Origin of Species of 1859 opened the second age, carrying natural selection into every branch of biology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-examination:
Examination is a process for testing fitness, an inquiry or investigation, used in schools, seminaries, and universities as a test of learning. Examinations also serve as tests for offices and posts and as means of reaching truth, and it is under these aspects that the question chiefly arises here. The bulk of the article is canon law, section by section.

Trent ordered a competitive examination, or concursus, for parochial benefices, so that parishes go to men of virtue and learning and the best candidate wins. Bishops may promote no one to orders until prudent and learned priests pass on his birth, baptism, morals, faith, and knowledge. Like rules govern bishops-elect, confessors, preachers, couples before marriage, and witnesses under oath in church courts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-excommunicati:
Excommunication is the Church's chief and severest censure. From Latin words for out of communion, it is a healing penalty, not a vindictive one. It strips a guilty Christian of all share in the common blessings of church society. It presumes grave guilt, and it aims to correct the offender and bring him back.

The excommunicated person stays a Christian, since baptism cannot be erased. Yet he stands as an exile, barred from public worship and from the sacraments. This vast article treats the subject under seven heads, from its history and kinds to absolution and current cases. It grounds the right in the Church as a society, citing Matthew 18 and Saint Paul's exclusion of offenders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exemption:
Exemption is the freeing of a church person, body, or house, wholly or partly, from the superior next above it. The body thus freed passes under a higher authority, or the pope himself. At first all in a diocese stood under the bishop. But bishops at times oppressed monasteries, which sought the shield of synods, princes, and popes.

That shield often grew into exemption, first given by Honorius I in 628 to Bobbio. From the eleventh century, papal reform work spread exemptions, until by the twelfth century they were the rule. Trent tried to curb abuses by restoring bishops' sway in many matters, but monasteries resisted. Exemption may come by grant, by immemorial use, or by origin, and it ends by withdrawal, contrary custom, or extinction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-extension:
Extension is the property by which the parts of material substance lie in order, one beyond another. That matter is not quite continuous to our senses, science shows. The microscope finds pores in the densest stuff, and gases seep through solids. Descartes held extension to be matter's very essence. Kant made it a subjective form stamped on sense by the mind.

Leibniz dissolved matter into unextended points, or monads, and Boscovich into simple forces, while atomists split bodies into minute particles. Catholic teaching, as summed here, calls extension successive, like a stream, or permanent. Permanent extension may be continuous, contiguous as a brick wall, or interrupted as a string of beads. Its marks are divisibility, measurability, and impenetrability. It is objective, not a mental mold, and distinct from substance, as the Eucharist shows, where bread's dimensions remain after its substance changes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-extreme-uncti:
Extreme Unction is a sacrament of the New Law for Christians who are gravely ill. It gives spiritual aid, comfort, and health, with remission of sins if need be, and bodily health on condition. A priest anoints the sick person, using set words. The article runs in ten sections, from the present rite and the name to effects, necessity, and repetition.

In the Western rite the priest anoints the organs of the five senses, eyes, ears, nostrils, lips, and hands, plus the feet, and for men the loins where custom allows. Each anointing says, through this holy unction and his tender mercy may the Lord pardon whatever sins thou hast committed by that sense. In urgent need one anointing on the forehead suffices. The East uses several priests, who bless the oil each time. Trent teaches Christ instituted it, hinted in Mark and proclaimed by James.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-lam:
The Lamoignon were a French robe family of judges and officials. Guillaume de Lamoignon took office as first president of the Parlement in 1658. He worked on codifying French law and defended Gallican liberties in 1663. His career ran through the Fronde and the rule of Louis XIV.

Earlier members included Chretien, a statesman, and Marie des Landes, called mother of the poor. Madeleine de Lamoignon aided foundlings and the Hotel-Dieu of Paris. Later came Nicolas, intendant of Languedoc during the Camisard rising. Malesherbes, the family's famous son, defended Louis XVI at his trial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fanon:
A fanon is a shoulder-cape the pope alone wears at solemn Mass. It has two pieces of white silk striped in red and gold. A small gold cross marks it, and a round opening fits the head. The pope wears it over the alb at pontifical Mass only.

The oldest Roman Ordinal, from the eighth century, calls it an anabolagium. Clergy in general wore it under the alb until the twelfth century. Innocent III then confirmed it as reserved to the pope alone. Square until the fifteenth century, it later took a collar form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Ascension is kept forty days after Easter, always falling on a Thursday. It recalls Christ rising into heaven from the Mount of Olives near Bethany. Eastern Christians called it the taking up and the salvation. By ascending, Christ completed the great work of human redemption.

Augustine held the feast apostolic in origin and universal long before his day. Its vigil and octave prepared the Church for the novena before Pentecost. Old customs included blessing beans, grapes, candles, and first fruits. Processions with torches and banners marked Christ's triumphant entry into heaven.

The Circumcision falls on 1 January, eight days after Christmas. Christ, though not bound by law, submitted to it as a true descendant of Abraham. At the rite he received the name Jesus, meaning Saviour. The ceremony took place in a private house of hospitality, not the Temple.

Early Christians struggled to keep the day amid the wild Saturnalia revels. Augustine urged fasting and prayer against pagan feasting and excess. The feast appears in the Gallican rite by the Council of Tours in 567. Later prayers also honour Mary, whose own feasts shape the day's office.

The Feast of the Dedication recalls the cleansing of the Jerusalem Temple. Judas Machabeus set it in 164 BC after Antiochus had polluted the shrine. Kept on 25 Kislew for eight days, it is also called the Feast of Lights. Unlike the great annual feasts, it could be kept in any synagogue.

Worshippers carried branches and palms and sang the joyful Hallel psalms daily. Mourning and fasting were barred during the joyful eight days. Lights burned in homes, recalling the temple lamps relit at the cleansing. Modern Jews keep the feast, now called Hanukkah, in December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flagellation:
Flagellation covers the whip, rod, and stick as punishment and as voluntary penance. Scripture mentions whips from Exodus onward, and Roman citizens were exempt from scourging. Christ scourged the money-changers, and Paul counted five scourgings of forty stripes save one. Pilate's scourging of Christ was a Roman punishment, meant as a substitute for crucifixion.

Monks adopted scourging as discipline from the fifth century, under rules like those of Columban. In Sparta youths prided themselves on enduring the lash, and in Russia the knout ruled longest. English soldiers were whipped within living memory, and Delaware still kept whipping for criminals. The article weighs whether Paul's chastising his body means scourging or mortification in general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-forty-hours-d:
The Forty Hours' Devotion, also called Quarant'Ore, is continuous prayer for forty hours before the Blessed Sacrament, the consecrated bread, set out for adoration. It commonly moves from church to church in succession. It opens with a solemn Mass of Exposition and closes two days later with a Mass of Deposition, each with a procession and litanies of the saints.

Its origin is obscure. A Milan chronicler describes the church-to-church round as a novelty beginning at Milan in May 1537. Pope Paul III soon granted indulgences, saying the prayers were meant to turn away God's anger and check the advancing Turks. St. Philip Neri and St. Ignatius Loyola helped spread the practice, which also took hold during carnival as an act of reparation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foundation:
An ecclesiastical foundation is the gift of temporal goods, land, money, or income, to a church body or cleric, by lifetime gift or by will. It is given on condition that some spiritual work be done in perpetuity or for a long time.

After Constantine gave the Church political standing and the right to accept legacies, bishops set such gifts aside for hospitals, orphan asylums, and homes for the aged. By the twelfth and thirteenth centuries pious generosity founded guilds and charities across Europe. Foundations are contracts: founder and administrator must agree, the bishop must consent, and the promised work, often Masses, must actually be performed, or the gift fails its purpose.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-mayro:
Francis Mayron, also called de Mayronis, born about 1280, probably at Mayronnes in the Basses-Alpes, and dead at Piacenza probably on 26 July 1327. He was a Franciscan theologian surnamed Doctor acutus, the sharp doctor, and Doctor illuminatus. He entered the Franciscan order at Digne or Sisteron and taught theology at Paris for a long time as bachelor. John XXII, at King Robert of Naples' request, ordered him made master of theology on 24 May 1323.

Mayron was a noted pupil of Duns Scotus, whose teaching he mostly followed. He is generally credited with introducing the Actus Sorbonicus at Paris. It was a disputation lasting from five in the morning to seven at night, in which one man defended his theses against all comers without help, food, or drink. His commentary on the Sentences appeared at Venice repeatedly from 1507, with treatises on formalities and first principles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-nicho:
Francis Nicholson, born at Manchester in 1650 and dead at Lisbon on 13 August 1731, was a controversial writer whose life crossed the religious divides of Stuart England. Son of a Manchester citizen, he entered University College, Oxford, as a servitor at sixteen. He took his bachelor's degree in 1669 and master's in 1673, and was ordained an Anglican clergyman. He served near Oxford and Canterbury with success in bringing Nonconformists back to the Church of England.

 Under James II he was a professed Catholic, writing on the Real Presence for Woodhead's discourse on the Eucharist. After the Revolution he joined the Carthusians at Nieuport, but his health failed. In 1699 he returned to England, entered the service of Queen Dowager Catherine of Braganza, and followed her to Portugal, where he lived at court and retired.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-thomp:
Francis Thompson, born at Preston in Lancashire on 18 December 1859 and dead in London on 13 November 1907. He was an English Catholic poet best known for The Hound of Heaven. His father was a provincial doctor, his mother died in his boyhood, and he was educated at Ushaw College. There he loved literature and neglected games, though he followed cricket with affection.

There he endured three years of destitution, working briefly as a bookselling agent and at a shoemaker's.
