His published account of the Neutrals, their land, and their customs, including a kind of oil like coal oil, was reused by Sagard and Leclercq.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-dixon:
Joseph Dixon was Archbishop of Armagh and Primate of Ireland in the mid-nineteenth century. Born at Coalisland in County Tyrone in 1806, he entered Maynooth at sixteen and was ordained in 1829. For eighteen years he held the chair of Sacred Scripture and Hebrew, teaching classes of about two hundred students.

His Introduction to the Sacred Scriptures, praised by Cardinal Wiseman, appeared in 1852. As primate, he held a synod in 1854, nearly finished Armagh's unfinished cathedral, and brought the Sisters of Charity, Marist Fathers, and Vincentians into the diocese. He also organized the Irish Brigade for papal service and fearlessly defended the Holy See.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-lambto:
Joseph Lambton was an English Catholic martyr of the Elizabethan persecution. Born in 1569, the second son of Thomas Lambton of Malton, he reached the English College at Reims in 1584 and at Rome in 1589. Ordained at only twenty-three, he was sent on the English mission on 22 April 1592.

Arrested at Newcastle on landing, with Edward Waterson, Lambton was condemned under the statute against priests. Cut down alive, he survived the first drop; the reprieved felon serving as hangman refused to finish, and a French surgeon at Kenton completed the sentence. The likely date of his death is 24 July 1592.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-le-car:
Joseph Le Caron was among the first four pioneer missionaries in Canada and the first to preach to the Hurons. Born near Paris in 1586, he served as chaplain to the Duke of Orléans, then joined the Recollects in 1611. He sailed from Honfleur in April 1615 and reached Canada in May.

Le Caron at once pushed into Huron country, the first missionary to visit their settlements, and stayed about a year. He returned to the Hurons in 1623 and evangelized the Montagnais of Tadoussac in the winters of 1618 and 1622. Sent home when the English took Quebec in 1629, he died of plague in France in 1632. He left the first Huron dictionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-steven:
Joseph Stevenson was an English archivist who edited medieval texts for half a century. Born at Berwick-on-Tweed in 1806 to Presbyterian parents, he studied under the historian James Raine at Durham and at Glasgow. He worked among government records and at the British Museum, then became a librarian at Durham Cathedral and rector of Leighton Buzzard.

Stevenson edited volumes for the Maitland, Surtees, and Roxburghe clubs and, from 1857, for the new Public Record Office, including Rolls Series volumes and calendars. Received into the Catholic Church in 1863 and ordained in 1872, he joined the Jesuits in 1877 at nearly seventy-two. His find of Claude Nau's Life of Mary Queen of Scots crowned his later years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-justification:
Justification is the theological term for the sinner being changed from unrighteousness to holiness and sonship of God. As an act, it is God's work alone, yet it presumes the adult's free cooperation with grace that comes first and helps throughout. As a lasting state, it means the soul's continued possession of sanctifying grace. Since the sixteenth century, Protestants and Catholics have differed sharply over what justification truly is.

The Reformers built on older ideas, including the Antinomian claim that faith alone suffices and the moral law need not be kept. Augustine already saw the apostles James, Peter, John, and Jude writing against such teaching. The entry then follows the historical debate, noting that Catholic scholars now doubt James wrote to correct Paul at all. The historical thread runs from the apostolic age through the Reformation, with the Epistle of James at its center.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kamerun-camer:
Kamerun lay in German West Africa, flanked by British Nigeria and French Congo, and reached northeast toward Lake Chad. It became an apostolic prefecture on 22 July 1890, entrusted to the Pallottini, with Father Henry Vieter as first prefect. The territory covered about 191,130 square miles, with some four million natives, Bantu near the coast and Sudanese inland, and about a thousand whites, mostly Germans. Palm kernels and oil, rubber, ivory, and cocoa were the chief exports.

The climate was hot, moist, and malarial, and the natives generally followed fetish worship, with a few Mohammedans. Stations rose at Marienberg on the Sanaga, at Kribi on the coast, and at Engelberg in the mountains, opened in 1894 as a sanatorium. Duala, the capital, followed in 1898, then Big-Batanga, Yaoundé twelve days inland, Irasa, and Einsiedeln, a seminary for schoolmasters. Raised to a vicariate in 1904, the mission counted eighteen priests, twenty-one brothers, and thirty sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kingston:
Kingston is the archdiocese of eastern Ontario, from Dundas County to Hastings County, taking in Addington, Frontenac, Grenville, Lanark, Leeds, Lennox, and Prince Edward counties. Its ground once belonged to the Diocese of Quebec.

In 1817 Upper Canada became a vicariate under Alexander Macdonell, consecrated at Quebec on 31 December 1820. He had brought Glengarry Fencibles, a disbanded Highland Catholic regiment, to Glengarry in 1803 and 1804, and St. Raphael became the province's first episcopal see. Two priests served the whole province in 1804, six by 1816. Leo XII made it a diocese in 1826 with Kingston as see, the first diocese in a British colony since the Reformation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kneeling-and-:
Genuflection, bending the knee, is a bodily sign of dependence and helplessness, taken up naturally for prayer and worship. Ambrose, Alcuin, and Rabanus Maurus all read it as humility, penitence, and a plea that softens God's anger.

Under the Old Law, Jews normally prayed standing, except in mourning: Anna stood before Eli, the Pharisee and the publican stood in the parable, and Christ speaks of standing to pray. Kneeling marked urgent, solemn, or fervent prayer instead. Solomon knelt to dedicate the Temple, Esdras fell on his knees, and Daniel knelt three times a day toward Jerusalem. Eastern art likewise shows prisoners and suppliants on their knees before a ruler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kyrie-eleison:
Kyrie Eleison, Greek for Lord have mercy, is an ancient cry used in every Christian liturgy. Arrian quotes it in the second century, and the Septuagint and New Testament already use the form as a near-liturgical plea, usually with an object: have mercy on me, or on us.

Its first certain liturgical use stands in the eighth book of the Apostolic Constitutions, where the people answer the deacon's litany clauses with it. That remains its Eastern role. Greek fathers of the fourth century mostly pass it over, though Chrysostom uses it often. Rome's Mass borrowed it from the East later, not as a leftover of Greek-language worship, and the pilgrim Etheria heard it at Jerusalem and glossed it as Miserere Domine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-labour-and-la:
Labour means work of mind or body done to produce useful things. The term is wide enough for actors, doctors, lawyers, clergy, servants, merchants, mechanics, factory hands, and farmers. In common speech it usually means hired labour, often hired manual labour, since wage earners outnumber the self-employed and hand workers outnumber brain workers.

The article uses labouring classes in that broad sense. Before the industrial revolution it takes in medieval master artisans and farm tenants. They worked partly for themselves and partly for a feudal lord, since both did work now done for hire. Skipping nomad and pastoral ages, which knew no distinct labouring class, it surveys labour's lot among the great peoples of antiquity. It starts with land tenure and the clan system.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lady-georgian:
Lady Georgiana Charlotte Fullerton (1812-1885) was a novelist, youngest daughter of Lord Granville Leveson Gower, English ambassador in Paris, where she was chiefly raised. In 1833 she married embassy attache Alexander George Fullerton in Paris.

Her first novel, Ellen Middleton, appeared in 1844 with strong High Anglican colour, so strong that Lord Brougham called it rank Popery, and Gladstone reviewed it. Her husband entered the Church in 1843, and she followed in 1846 under Father Brownhill. Grantley Manor of 1847, a study of character, is usually rated above her first book. After her only son's death in 1855 she gave herself to charity, joined the Third Order of St. Francis in 1856, and wrote novels, lives, poems, and translations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laicization:
Laicization, from Latin laicus, lay, strictly means reducing a person or thing of church character to lay condition. Laity simply names Christians outside the clergy, with no hostility implied toward clergy, Church, or religion.

In recent France, however, lay took on a sharply anti-clerical and even anti-religious sense, born of school struggles. Teaching orders were driven from public schools, religious teaching was banned there, and the school's new lay character was declared essential and inviolable. The word then spread to any institution stripped of church influence. It reached legislation that treats society as atheist, a state that bars God's name from its acts, and even a morality claimed independent of revealed religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lauda-sion:
Lauda Sion is the sequence St. Thomas Aquinas composed about 1264 for the Mass of Corpus Christi, taking its title from its opening words. Its sixth stanza proves its Mass purpose, recalling the solemn day when the Supper was first instituted.

Authorship was once given to St. Bonaventure, and a local Liege office of 1246 muddied the question, but Noel Alexandre's dissertation and a constitution of Sixtus IV settle it on Thomas beyond doubt. The poem calls everyone to unending praise of the Blessed Sacrament. It states the Catholic doctrine of the sacrament in detail. It shows ancient types fulfilled in the bread of angels. It closes asking the Good Shepherd for food and guarding here and a seat at the heavenly table hereafter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lay-communion:
Lay communion was the early Church's penalty that cut a cleric from the hierarchy and reduced him to the laity's standing, barring him from exercising his functions. Its exact nature is uncertain: some read it as excommunication with denial of the Eucharist, others as permission to receive communion only with the laity.

Apostolic Canon 15 lets an unauthorized priest outside his diocese receive with the faithful but not celebrate, and Canon 62 puts apostate clerics among the laity. Pope Cornelius in 251 received a bishop who had ordained for the heretic Novatian into communion as a layman, and Cyprian tells of Trophimus admitted the same way. Elvira about 300 gives the oldest canonical text on the practice, and Sardica, Hippo, Toledo, and Rome confirm it as settled discipline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lay-confessio:
Lay confession means confession made to a layman to win God's pardon, not confession by laymen, and the article treats it historically only, since it has no practical weight today. It takes two forms: confession apart from the sacrament, and confession meant to stand in for the sacrament when no priest can be had.

The first covers daily and venial faults, which need not pass under the power of the keys, and seeks the merit of humiliation in free avowal. The second covers even grave sins, declared to a layman only in urgent want of a priest. Bede's comment on James sets the pattern: slight faults mutually to equals, trusting their prayers, while grave leprosy goes to the priest for judgment and penance. Lanfranc later kept public sins for priests and allowed hidden faults to any churchman, failing that to an upright man, failing that to God alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lebanon:
Lebanon, Hebrew Lebanôn and modern Jebel Libnan, is the White Mountain. Its name comes from snow on its highest peaks nearly all year, or from limestone gleaming white at a distance. It forms the heart of central Syria's great range, running parallel to the sea for about 95 miles.

Two parallel chains of one formation compose it: western Lebanon proper and eastern Antilibanus. They split late in the Tertiary age as part of the Jordan fissure reaching to the Red Sea. Four strata show in deep ravines. First comes Araya limestone near 980 feet thick. Then fossil-rich sandstone and clay marl from 650 to 1,630 feet. Then Lebanon limestone near 3,580 feet with oyster beds. Last comes a thin Senonian flinty chalk. Western peaks top 9,800 feet, with Dahr el-Qodib and Qarn Sauda near 10,000 feet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-legitimation:
Legitimation, from Latin legitimatio, is the canonical act removing the irregularity contracted by birth outside lawful wedlock, and it therefore presupposes illegitimacy. All children born of marriage are presumed legitimate in canon law. That holds not only for valid marriages but for putative ones, reputed valid though truly invalid, if at least one party married in good faith.

That presumption favours children unless plain proof shows the husband's paternity physically impossible, through absence, impotence, or the like. Even a parent's sworn confession of wrongdoing does not otherwise touch it. Infants born at the seventh month's start after the wedding, or at the tenth month's end after the husband's death, still count legitimate. Children of doubtful marriages conceived before an invalidity sentence also keep legitimate standing, while offspring of affected ignorance, suspecting an impediment yet never inquiring, do not.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leon:
Leon is the diocese and civil province in Spain whose name comes from the Roman military colony Legio Septima Gemina, founded in the Asturias near ancient Lancia before Trajan's time. The name Leon, from Legio, matched the Spanish word for lion, which folk etymology made the city's heraldic badge and even that of the whole Spanish people. Civilians soon joined the soldiers. Christianity arrived early, with bishops known by the third century and martyrs under persecution.

Germanic invaders held off until Euric or Leovigild drove out the garrison. Mussulman invaders took the city but lost it to Alfonso I the Catholic. Destroyed again under Abderahman II in 846, it was rebuilt by Ordoño I, who raised a royal residence there that Ordoño II turned into a cathedral. Bishops of the period include St. Froilan (900-905), and the court stayed at Oviedo, so Leon grew slowly until 910.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lionel-albert:
Lionel Albert Anderson was an English Dominican friar, born about 1620, who spent his life as a Catholic priest when priesthood was a crime in England. He joined the Dominicans in Paris in 1638, was ordained in 1665, and worked in London under the false name Munson.

Titus Oates accused him of plotting against king and Parliament, and he was tried at the Old Bailey and condemned to death in 1679 or 1680. Charles II pardoned him after a year in Newgate prison, but sent him into exile for life. A later pardon from James II let him come home. He fled abroad with that king in 1688, then came back for good, and died in England in 1710 at about ninety-one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lionel-pigot-:
Lionel Pigot Johnson was an English poet and critic, born at Broadstairs in Kent in 1867 and dead by 1902, after a fall. Schooled at Winchester and at New College, Oxford, he became a Catholic in 1891 and spent his writing decade living alone in London's Inns of Court.

His family tree ran through soldiers, and his own loves ran wider than England: Wales, Ireland, and American ideals all drew him, and he called himself a Catholic nationalist. Only three books came out in his life: a study of Thomas Hardy in 1894, Poems in 1895, and Ireland and Other Poems in 1897. Friends recalled a small, frail man of grave courtesy, deep learning, and a fierce drive for perfect work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lisbon:
Lisbon, seat of a Catholic patriarchate, stands on the north bank of the Tagus, twelve miles from the sea, spread over seven hills. Legend ties its founding to Ulysses. Romans called it Felicitas Julia, and Moors held it from 716 until Alfonso Henriques retook it in 1145 with Crusader help. He then moved Portugal's capital there.

Quakes scarred the city, above all the great shock of 1755. It killed more than thirty thousand people and set fires that burned four days. Then the Marquis of Pombal rebuilt the centre around the Praca do Comercio. Old churches anchor the rest of the entry. There is the cathedral, once a mosque, the shrine of St. Vincent, the city's patron, and the castle of St. George, once a Moorish stronghold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-little-sister:
The Little Sisters of the Assumption are a congregation whose core work is nursing the sick poor free of charge, in their own homes, without regard to creed. Etienne Pernet and Marie Antoinette Tage, known as Mother Marie de Jesus, founded the group in Paris in 1865.

Nursing was only the doorway to wider care. Sisters pressed for conversions, sought to regularize irregular unions, and saw that children were baptized, schooled, and prepared for first Communion and Confirmation. Houses spread to Italy, Spain, Belgium, England, Ireland, and the United States, and a papal brief approved the congregation in 1897.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-loaves-of-pro:
The loaves of proposition, also called shewbread or presence-bread, were the sacred bread set before God in the Jewish sanctuary. Hebrew calls them bread of the faces, Greek calls them loaves of the setting forth, and Latin panes propositionis gave English its term.

Twelve loaves, made of fine flour sifted seven times and baked without leaven, were laid in two piles of six on the table of proposition, still hot. David ate such bread at Nob when fleeing Saul, after the priest saw his men were ritually clean. The entry weighs their size, their weekly baking by Kohathite priests, and their place among Mosaic offerings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-london:
London, England's capital and the British Empire's chief city, sits some fifty miles up the Thames. The name covers many Londons. There is the old City of one square mile. There is the County of London, with over four and a half million people in 1901. There is the police district, with nearly seven million across seven hundred square miles.

This huge survey treats the city under four heads: general history, the ancient Catholic diocese, London Catholics after the Reformation, and modern civil rule. Legend credits Brutus the Trojan with its founding. The entry prefers a humbler root, the lake-fort of Llyn-din. It then follows the city from Roman walls to Edwardian streets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lord-acton:
Lord Acton, Baron Acton, was a historian and Cambridge professor of modern history from 1895 to 1902, born at Naples in 1834 and dead at Tegernsee in 1902. His English Catholic family had settled in Naples, where his grandfather served as prime minister, and his mother came from the Bavarian Dalbergs.

Schooled at Oscott and then under Dollinger at Munich, he knew the chief tongues of Europe as well as his own. He sat in Parliament for an Irish seat, edited the Rambler and then the Home and Foreign Review, and broke with ultramontane counsels after the Syllabus of 1864. His fame rests on vast learning, liberal judgment, and the histories he planned more than finished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-siffren:
Louis Siffren Joseph Salamon was Bishop of Saint-Flour, born at Carpentras in 1759 and dead at Saint-Flour in 1829. After law and theology at Avignon, he became an auditor of the Rota under Pius VI, then joined the Paris Parlement and took part in the Diamond Necklace case.

Named papal internuncio at Louis XVI's court in 1790, he was jailed during the September massacres of 1792 and twice escaped death. Freed, he wandered in disguise as vicar apostolic, administered Normandy's dioceses in 1801, and became Bishop of Orthosia, then of Saint-Flour in 1820. His nine-year episcopate pressed clergy training, and his memoirs of the Terror later appeared in French and English.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucas-vasquez:
Lucas Vasquez de Ayllon was a Spanish explorer of Chesapeake Bay, who died on 18 October 1526. A member of the high council at Santo Domingo, he sent Gordillo to Florida in 1521, landing near Cape Fear in North Carolina.

Seeking a north-west passage to Asia, Ayllon himself sailed from Hispaniola in 1524 and tried the James River and Chesapeake Bay. Charles V granted him the land he found, and in 1526 he planted San Miguel de Guandape near the later Jamestown site, with 600 souls. Slave labour worked the venture, perhaps the first such use inside the present United States. Ship fever killed Ayllon, and only 150 survivors sailed home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucon:
Lucon is a diocese in La Vendee, suppressed by the Concordat of 1801, annexed to La Rochelle, and restored in 1821, joining the old see to most of Maillezais. Its monastery, founded in 682 by Bishop Ansoald of Poitiers under St. Philbert, became a bishopric in 1317.

Bishops of note include Nicolas Coeur, brother of financier Jacques Coeur, Cardinals Jean de Lorraine and Louis de Bourbon, and Armand Duplessis-Richelieu, the great cardinal, bishop from 1606 to 1623. Nicolas Colbert, De Mercy the exile, and Soyer, who served disguised through the Revolution, round out a line that mirrors France's own storms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-de-leon:
Luis de Leon was a Spanish poet and theologian, born at Belmonte in 1528 and dead at Madrigal in 1591. Son of the king's advocate at Madrid, he went to Salamanca for law at fourteen, then joined the Augustinians six months later.

Professor of theology by 1560, he used Hebrew texts and the Septuagint despite Trent's ruling on the Vulgate, and foes denounced him as a rabbinist. Arrested in 1572, he faced seventeen charges at Valladolid, not of heresy but of rashness toward the Vulgate. After nearly five years the tribunal sought the rack, yet Madrid's supreme council acquitted him in 1576, restored his chair, and warned him to teach with more care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luke-rivingto:
Luke Rivington was an English controversialist, born at London in 1838 and dead there in 1899. Fourth son of publisher Francis Rivington, he studied at Highgate and Magdalen College, Oxford, was ordained an Anglican in 1862, and preached at Oxford and All Saints, Margaret Street.

After a failed community at Stoke and a spell leading Cowley Fathers at Bombay, doubts took him to Rome, where he was received in 1888 and ordained priest in 1889. Back in Bayswater, he preached, heard confessions, and wrote a shelf of controversial works. They include Authority, Dependence, The Primitive Church and the See of Peter, Anglican Fallacies, and Rome and England, plus a new edition of Milner's End of Religious Controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mabinogion:
The Mabinogion is a body of medieval Welsh prose tales, the word deriving from mab, son, mabinog, bardic student, and mabinogi, a tale from his repertoire. They survive in the Red Book of Hergest, a bulky fourteenth-century manuscript held at Jesus College, Oxford.

Shaped near the end of the twelfth century from legends far older, some from Celtic paganism and Gaelo-Breton unity, only four tales are strictly Mabinogion. The Four Branches, Pwyll, Branwen, Manawyddan, and Math, keep much British Celtic myth in late, degraded form. The wider set adds Rhonabwy's Dream, Kulhwch and Olwen, Taliesin, and three Anglo-Norman tales on Celtic ground, once dismissed as children's stories, now prized as serious literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-madame-guyon:
Madame Guyon was a famed seventeenth-century French mystic, born at Montargis on 13 April 1648 and dead at Blois on 9 June 1717. Sickly, shuttled nine times in ten years between home, convent, and schools, she steeped herself in Francis de Sales and nearly became a nun.

At scarcely sixteen she married Jacques Guyon, twenty-two years older, and after twelve unhappy years lost two children and her husband, leaving her a widow at twenty-eight with three young children. Under the Barnabite Lacombe she passed through union of the powers for eight years. Then came seven years of mystical death, stripped of taste for spiritual things, before she reawakened transformed. Her teachings drew Fénelon, Bossuet, and the condemnation of quietism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-madura-missio:
The Madura Mission is the Jesuit movement that began at Madura and spread over India's eastern peninsula. Free of Portuguese political influence, it stands as an answer to the charge that the gospel spread by coercion. Ancient Jesuit India split into Goa province in the west and Malabar in the south, and Madura's field lay far from state machinery.

Its founder, Robert de Nobili, began in 1606 a method of living as the Brahmins lived, noble, learned, and ascetical. That won esteem and intercourse, and he moved by degrees from shared ground to distinctively Christian truth. He offered a purified faith without loss of native custom or rank. Fathers de Vico and Martini followed, and the mission grew where no Portuguese prestige could reach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malediction:
Malediction, or cursing, is traced here through four Hebrew words rendered maledictio in the Vulgate. The most general is 'rr, used of men more often than of God. Next comes qll, to treat lightly, often no more than reviling. Then 'lh, calling God to witness, shading into adjuration. Last is hrm, devoting a thing to God or dooming it to destruction, the familiar ban.

Among Semitic peoples, cursing was a religious act, calling a tribal god's vengeance on foes. Sinaitic law purified older usages rather than inventing them. At the conquest, Canaanite cities fell under the ban to guard Israel's set-apart faith. Hard texts remain, from the comminative psalms to Eliseus and the boys, and Augustine's readings are weighed. The New Testament ends the spirit of retaliation, while the ban idea runs deep into Paul on atonement and the promise that no curse shall remain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mamertine-pri:
Mamertine Prison, beneath the church of St Joseph of the Carpenters in Rome, is commonly matched with the prison Livy places mid-city above the forum. It has an upper chamber and a lower one. The lower, the Tullianum, began most likely as a cistern. 

The Tullianum is round, part rock-cut and part tufa, its layers stepping inward to a conical vault, later capped by a flat arch. Its upper chamber is uneven, with a restoration inscription dated A.D. 21. Sallust calls the lower dungeon repulsive for neglect, damp, and smell. Prisoners such as Jugurtha and the Catiline plotters were dropped through a floor hole to starve or be strangled. Legend puts St Peter here, with a well for baptising his jailers, but the well predates him and no sound evidence places Peter in the Tullianum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mammon:
Mammon is the New Testament word for riches, found only in Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16:9-13. Its spelling and root remain uncertain. Targums use the word often, yet never as a match for the Hebrew term for treasure. The margin of one Hebrew text even glosses a daughter as ill-gotten treasure to her father.

In Luke, Mammon is personified, and that figure fed the popular notion, stressed by Milton, that Mammon was a god. The Fathers give no firm support for a deity. Jerome glosses the word plainly as riches in the Syrian tongue. Yet the Middle Ages widely treated Mammon as a devil's name, as Peter Lombard and Piers Plowman show. The phrase Mammon of iniquity has drawn many readings. It can hardly mean ill-gotten gains, which must be restored. From a root meaning trust, it may mean riches in which men put their trust.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-edme-pa:
Patrice de MacMahon, Duc de Magenta and Marshal of France, was President of the French Republic, born at Sully in 1808 and dead at Montcresson in 1893. He joined the Algiers expedition in 1830 as aide to General Achard, served twenty years in Algeria, and won distinction storming Constantine. In Italy his decisive move won Magenta on 4 June 1859, and he was made marshal and duke on the field.

In the Franco-German War his vanguard lost at Wissembourg in August 1870, his corps was outnumbered at Reichshoffen, and wounded at Sedan he saw Napoleon III capitulate on 1 September. On 28 May 1871 he crushed the Paris Commune for Versailles. Elected president on 24 May 1873 by 390 votes to 2, he stood above parties. A seven-year term was fixed that November. He let the Republic's fundamental laws pass in 1875, and, a Legitimist at heart, slowed parties hostile to the Church as far as lawful prerogative allowed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mark-of-lisbo:
Mark of Lisbon, properly Marcos da Silva, was a Friar Minor, historian, and Bishop of Oporto, born at Lisbon and dead in 1591. At the minister general's instance he visited chief Franciscan convents in Spain, Italy, and France, gathering original documents on the order's history.

Earlier, in 1532, Minister General Paul Pisotti had ordered provincials to collect fifteenth-century documents to continue Bartholomew of Pisa's Conformities. Much of that haul reached Mark, and with Marianus of Florence's chronicle and his own gatherings he compiled in Portuguese his Chronicle of the Friars Minor. It was published at Lisbon from 1556 to 1568. It ran through several editions and translations into Italian, French, and Spanish, partly into English. The work is mostly lives of famed friars, so its title misleads a little, but it holds great value, since its original sources have since vanished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquess-of-r:
George Frederick Samuel Robinson, Marquess of Ripon, was a British Liberal statesman, born at 10 Downing Street in 1827 and dead in 1909. He married his cousin Henrietta Vyner in 1851, fathering Frederick Oliver, his heir, and Mary Sarah, who died in infancy.

He entered Commons for Hull in 1852, succeeding his father as Earl of Ripon in 1859 and his uncle as Earl de Grey the same year. He served in every Liberal administration for half a century. He was under-secretary for war and India, secretary for war, secretary for India, and lord president of the council. As chairman of the joint commission he drew the Treaty of Washington settling the Alabama claims, for which he became Marquess. Grand master of Freemasons from 1871 to 1874, he resigned to enter the Catholic Church at the London Oratory in September 1874. As Viceroy of India from 1880 to 1884 he won Indian love as no predecessor had.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquis-de-mo:
Louis-Joseph de Montcalm-Gozon was a French general, born at Candiac in 1712 and dead at Quebec in 1759. He claimed descent from Gozon, Grand Master of Rhodes of legendary fame, and his family's warlike spirit fed the saying that war is the tomb of the Montcalms. 

He served at Kehl and Philipsbourg, won the Cross of St Louis in 1741 after Bohemia, became colonel of Auxerrois in 1743, and took five wounds at Piacenza. He married Angelique-Louise Talon de Boulay in 1736 and fathered ten children. In 1755 he succeeded to Canadian command, and after halting invasion by land he faced Wolfe's naval attack on Quebec. On 13 September Wolfe's men scaled the Heights of Abraham at dawn, Montcalm rushed from Beauport, and his troops, equal in number but surprised, weary, and badly placed, lost. Wolfe died on the field, Montcalm the next morning, sealing New France's fate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquise-de-m:
Francoise d'Aubigne, Marquise de Maintenon, was born in Niort prison in 1635 and died at Saint-Cyr in 1719. Granddaughter of Protestant writer Agrippa d'Aubigne, she was baptised Catholic and spent childhood years in Martinique. Back in France she passed between Protestant and Catholic guardians.

Widowed at twenty-five by poet Scarron's death in 1660, she won a queen-mother's pension and entered court circles. In 1670 Mme de Montespan asked her to raise Louis XIV's children, and she grew close to the king. After the queen died in 1683, Louis married her secretly, and for thirty-one years ministers worked in her room while she received princes and ambassadors. She pushed court conversion, though Lavisse clears her of blame for revoking the Edict of Nantes. Her glory lay in schooling: she taught catechism at Avon, raised fifty girls at Rueil from 1682, and built Saint-Cyr, where she retired after Louis died in 1715.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-alonso:
Martin Alonso Pinzon was a Spanish navigator and Columbus's companion on the first New World voyage, born at Palos in 1441 and dead there in 1493. He backed Columbus through Fray Juan Perez of La Rabida, paid an eighth of Columbus's demanded share, built the three ships, and won their crews.

Pinzon commanded the Pinta, his brother Vicente Yanez the Nina. On 21 November 1492 he left Columbus off Cuba, chasing the fancied island of Osabeque, and first found Haiti, landing at a river long called after him. He seized four men and two girls for slaves, but Columbus made him return them when they met again on 6 January 1493. Off the Azores he deserted again, racing for Spain to break the news first. A hurricane drove him to Bayonne, where the king refused him audience, and he reached Palos the same day as Columbus, 15 March 1493.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-sherso:
Martin Sherson was an English priest and confessor, one of the Dilati among English martyrs, born in 1563 and dead in 1588. A Yorkshire native, he matriculated at Oxford's St John's College in 1575 at twelve, a poor scholar of rhetoric teacher George Mannering. He reached the English College at Reims on 1 April 1580 and was confirmed that June.

He left for Rome in March and entered the English College on 8 May 1581 at eighteen, where over-zealous study and prayer brought on spitting blood. Back at Reims in June 1585, he was ordained sub-deacon at Reims Cathedral in September, deacon at Laon in March, and priest at Laon on 5 April 1586. He sailed for England on 16 June and was jailed in the Marshalsea before 22 December 1586. Still there in March 1588, he died soon after, aged twenty-five.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-thomas:
Martin Thomas McMahon was a soldier and jurist, born at Laprairie, Canada, in 1838 and dead in New York in 1906. His parents brought him to the United States at three weeks old and settled in New York. 

When civil war broke out he raised the Pacific coast's first cavalry company, but quit its captaincy when it would not go to the front. Going east, he became aide-de-camp to General McClellan and served with the Army of the Potomac through the war, ending as brevet Major-General of Volunteers. For bravery at White Oak Swamp Congress gave him the Medal of Honor. After resigning in 1866 he served as New York corporation counsel, minister to Paraguay in 1868 to 1869, receiver of taxes, U.S. Marshal, assemblyman, and senator. In 1896 he won election as judge of the Court of General Session, holding it till death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mathias-chard:
Mathias Chardon, Charles in religion, was a learned French Benedictine of the Saint-Vannes Congregation, born at Yvoi-Varignan in Ardennes in 1695 and dead at St-Arnold monastery in Metz in 1771. He vowed at St-Vannes, St-Viton, in Verdun in 1712 and soon grew famous for learning.

At the congregation's 1730 general chapter at Toul, Chardon was forced to resign his professorship for opposing the Bull Unigenitus. He wrote Histoire des Sacraments at Paris in 1745 in six volumes. It was a historical treatise refuting Sacramentarian errors by showing how sacraments were administered in the Church and used from apostolic times to the present. An Italian translation followed at Verona in 1754, Brescia in 1758, and Capolago in 1835, and Migne reprinted it in his Cursus Theologiae, volume twenty, pages 1 to 1152. His work stands as a monument of Benedictine sacramental history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mathieu-richa:
Mathieu-Richard-Auguste Henrion, Baron, was a French magistrate, historian, and journalist, born at Metz in 1805 and dead at Aix in September 1862. After law studies he joined the Paris Bar as avocat a la cour royale. 

An untiring writer, he wrote most of his life for Catholic and royalist journals, first Drapeau Blanc, then Journal de l'Instruction Publique, and lesser journals. In 1840 he took over L'Ami de la Religion, which passed in 1848 to Abbe Dupanloup. Besides countless articles, he wrote many books breathing Catholic and royalist fervour, showing close observation and wide learning. Yet they lack sufficient criticism and sometimes fairness, since the baron belonged to the fiery mid-nineteenth-century French Ultramontanes and judged too often through religious and political bias. Chief works include Histoire des ordres religieux of 1831, Histoire de la papaute of 1832, and Histoire generale de l'Eglise of 1843 onward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-memberton:
Memberton, principal chief of the Micmac Indians of Nova Scotia when the French colony began in 1605, stands in mission annals as the tribe's first Christian. The French form corrupts the Micmac Maopeltu, short for Maoi-Napeltu, chief of all. On St. John's Day, 24 June 1610, he was baptized with twenty of his family by Father Jesse Fleche at Port Royal, now Annapolis.

Poutrincourt and his son stood as sponsors for King and Dauphin. He took the name Henry, for Henry IV, his wife Marie for the queen regent, and his kin took royal names. Though very old, he stayed vigorous and claimed to recall Cartier's first St. Lawrence visit in 1534. Long chief, war captain, medicine man, and master of tribal rites, he lived temperately amid paganism, keeping one wife where great men kept up to eight. He grew devoted to Jesuits Biard and Masse, who arrived in June 1611.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-menaion:
The Menaion, from the Greek word for month, names the twelve books, one for each month, that hold the offices for fixed feasts in the Byzantine rite. The Byzantine calendar runs two series: movable days turning around Easter, and fixed feasts of the Lord, the Virgin, and the saints on set days of the civil year. The menaia hold the second series, matching the Roman breviary's proprium sanctorum.

Their origin and first gathering are obscure, and the parts seem to have joined gradually. The Synaxarion, short lives of saints and histories of feasts akin to breviary lessons, appears to have come first, its lives ascribed to Symeon Metaphrastes. The menaia add the rest: canons with heirmoi, troparia, stichera, kontakia, and more, much of it ascribed to Romanos, the Byzantine Church's chief hymn writer of the fifth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mental-reserv:
Mental reservation names a doctrine grown from Catholic teaching on lying. That teaching holds that lying is never allowed, not even to save a life. A lie is evil in itself, and evil may not be done so good may follow. Yet we must keep secrets faithfully, and sometimes the easiest way is to say what is false. Writers of every creed and none have accepted the lie of necessity: when justice and truth clash, justice should win.

Catholic teaching frames mental reservation as a path that honours both justice and truth. Wide mental reservation was broached tentatively by St. Raymund of Pennafort. In his Summa of 1235 he quotes Augustine: a man must not kill his soul by lying to save another's life. It would be perilous to admit that a lesser evil may be done to stop a greater. Most doctors teach this, he says.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-methods-of-ab:
Methods of abbreviation grew from the stuff records were made on: stone, marble, bronze, or parchment. Lapidaries, engravers, and copyists all had to make the most of their space. Such shortenings are rare at the Christian era's start, when material was plentiful and none needed to scrimp. By the third or fourth century, however, material had grown scarce and dear, and artists aimed to fit long texts onto scant surfaces.

Ordinary writing is set aside here: the Romans owned an alphabet called Notae Tironienses, serving as modern shorthand does, needing special study, its signs still largely uncertain. Inscriptions cut in stone show abbreviations most often. At some late periods, as in medieval Spain, the habit was abused into undecipherable symbols. In epigraphy's best period, strict rules held. Common abbreviations fall under two heads: cutting the word to its first letter, and the second head the entry goes on to detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-migration:
Migration, the movement of peoples from place to place, is among the earliest events history records. The Bible's first recorded migration followed the confusion of tongues, when men scattered over the earth, and Exodus describes the Hebrew tribes' withdrawal from Egypt. Abraham's parting from Lot offers a typical early move, while Greek and Roman history likewise abounds in colonies abroad.

The article weighs why people move, for work, faith, or politics, then turns to immigration into the United States, a distinct story from 1789. It surveys treaties, notably the Burlingame Treaty of 1868 backing free movement, its reversal for the Chinese in 1880, and tighter laws. Over seventeen years about one in a hundred arrivals were turned back or sent home, though fear of refusal kept many more from sailing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miles-gerard-:
Miles Gerard Keon, journalist, novelist, colonial secretary, and lecturer, was born on 20 February 1821. He was the last descendant of the Keons of Keonbrooke, County Leitrim, and died at Bermuda on 3 June 1875. Only son of Myles Gerard Keon, barrister, he lost both parents in infancy. He was raised by his maternal grandmother and later his uncle, Francis Philip, Count Magawly.

At the Jesuit college of Stonyhurst he penned the prize poem marking Queen Victoria's accession. An adventurous walking tour across the Continent followed graduation, ending in a breakdown. Keon then turned to journalism and fiction, served as colonial secretary in Bermuda, and lectured widely. His novels and his colonial career made him a notable Irish Catholic man of letters in the Victorian age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-aspect-:
Vivisection, taken literally, means cutting into living creatures. In ordinary use it covers any scientific experiment on animals that employs the scalpel. By misuse it means any observation of animals under abnormal conditions. True dissection of living animals happens nowhere, since studying human structure is easier in the cadaver. Old tales of criminals dismembered at Alexandria under Ptolemy II and III rest on Celsus and Tertullian.

Animal experiment began when natural processes were learned by exact observation rather than by philosophy alone. It became indispensable to physiology and pathology, showing how living organs work. It lets researchers create diseases and track their stages. The entry weighs that scientific gain against the suffering imposed. It asks when pain may be inflicted for knowledge, what safeguards conscience demands, and how anaesthetics and care change the moral reckoning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mortification:
Mortification is one of the methods Christian asceticism uses to train the soul toward virtuous and holy living. Saint Paul coined the term from the image of dying to a mortal life and rising to an immortal one. If you live after the flesh you shall die, he wrote, but if through the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live.

Though it sounds like a law of death, it is more deeply a law of life. What it slays is the soul's disease, and by slaying that it restores true life. Sin first among diseases is met with penitence and the Church's means of forgiveness. Temptation is met by accepting hardship rather than yielding. The eager go further, subduing the rebellion of disordered appetite as far as this life allows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mosaic-legisl:
Mosaic legislation is the body of juridical, moral and ceremonial laws and decisions found in the last four books of the Pentateuch. Christian and Hebrew tradition ascribe it to Moses. The Hebrew name torah was already popular in David's era for this compilation, and after the captivity it became synonymous with the Pentateuch itself.

If torah springs from a root meaning to cast, the earliest divine decisions may have come through casting lots, with God regarded as their author. More developed are the rulings Moses gave at Rephidim in private disputes, guided by precedent and custom. The entry traces how priests and prophets used torah for moral, religious and ceremonial directions alike. Formal codification gathered these strands into the Law as later generations received it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-muratorian-ca:
The Muratorian Canon, also called the Muratorian Fragment after its discoverer and first editor Muratori, is the oldest known list of New Testament books. Its manuscript, once at Bobbio and now in Milan's Ambrosiana library, was written in the eighth century in uncultured Latin. The canon itself was composed at Rome or nearby about 180 to 200, probably translated from a Greek original.

The beginning is lost, and the surviving text opens near the end of the notice on the second Gospel. It then covers the third and fourth Gospels, Acts, and Paul's letters including Philemon, Titus and Timothy. It rejects spurious letters to Laodicea and Alexandria, and adds Jude and two letters of John. More than a bare list, it gives historical notes on each book, making it a prime witness to the early canon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nathaniel-bac:
Nathaniel Bacon, better known under the assumed name of Southwell, was a Jesuit priest and bibliographer, born in Norfolk, England, in 1598 and dead at Rome on 2 December 1676. He trained at Saint Omers, entered the English College at Rome in 1617, and after ordination in 1622 was sent to labour on the English missions. Two years later he entered the Jesuit novitiate, but soon passed to the Roman province, serving as procurator and minister of the English College.

Appointed in 1647 secretary to General Vincent Caraffa, he showed such business talent that four succeeding generals retained him. Retiring in 1668, he began the Bibliotheca Scriptorum Societatis Jesu, published in Rome in 1676. Based on Ribadineira's 1602 work, continued to 1641 by Alegambe, Southwell revised the originals with copious notes of his own. Oliver praised it for research, accuracy, elegance, piety and charity, and Southwell also wrote a Journal of Meditations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nerses-of-lam:
Nerses of Lambron, born 1153 at Lambron in Cilicia and dead in 1198, was son of Oschin II, prince of Lambron, and nephew of Patriarch Nerses IV. He mastered sacred and profane sciences, with excellent Greek, Latin, Syriac and probably Coptic. Ordained in 1169, he became Archbishop of Tarsus in 1176 and a zealous advocate of Greek-Armenian church union.

In 1179 he attended the Council of Hromcla, where union terms were discussed, and his address there counts as a masterpiece of eloquence and style. Union was decided but never completed, since Emperor Manuel Comnenus died in 1180 and his successors dropped the talks and persecuted Armenians. Leo II of Cilicia, seeking a royal crown, won Celestine III's favour on condition of union with Rome. Leo was crowned King of Armenia on 6 January 1198, with Nerses among the signing bishops, and Nerses died six months later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-atki: Nicholas Atkinson was a priest and martyr, probably to be identified with Venerable Thomas Atkinson. Dodd places Nicholas's death at York in 1610 but never mentions Thomas. Yet every fact Dodd relates of the one certainly fits the other, while no corroboration exists for Dodd's date of Nicholas's martyrdom. It seems probable, however, that an old Marian priest named Nicholas, or Ninny, Atkinson did exist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-de-br:
French Oratorian Nicolas de Bralion spent fifteen years in Rome gathering church history and liturgy before writing in Paris. Born around 1600, he entered the Paris Oratory in 1619 and worked at San Luigi dei Francesi, translating Bérulle and part of Ribadeneyra's lives of saints.

Back in Paris around 1640, he published a life of Saint Nicholas and the first serious French study of the archbishop's pallium. He also published a Christian history, a guide to Roman curiosities, and a practical manual for canons. He died in Paris in 1672. His fifteen Roman years were spent in research and literary work at San Luigi dei Francesi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-pavil:
Bishop Nicolas Pavillon of Alet, born at Paris in 1597, governed his southern French diocese for thirty-seven years with restless energy. Formed by Vincent de Paul's community at Saint-Lazare, he visited parishes, held synods, founded schools, and pressed moral reform on clergy and people alike.

An outsized sense of episcopal duty put him at odds with pope and king: he refused Alexander VII's formulary, resisted the royal droit de régale, and appealed to Rome against Louis XIV. Port-Royal admired him, and Alet became a Jansenist gathering place before his death in 1677.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-talon:
Jesuit writer Nicolas Talon, born at Moulins in 1605, joined preaching, prison visiting, and army chaplaincy to a lively pen. He entered the Society in 1621, taught literature with success, and served French troops in Flanders, winning the lifelong friendship of the Prince de Condé.

Talon stood beside the outlaw Aimé du Poncet through a long execution and saw him die penitent, a scene that stirred Paris. His books include lives of Francis de Sales and Francis Borgia, a Bible history for ordinary readers, and funeral orations for Louis XIII and Condé.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nikon:
Patriarch Nikon of Moscow, born Nikita in 1605 to peasant parents, tried to remake Russian worship and split his church in the attempt. A married parish priest turned monk after his children died, he rose through Novgorod to the patriarchate in 1652 on the favor of Tsar Alexis.

Nikon corrected Slavonic service books to match Greek usage, built monasteries, and ruled with an iron hand, but his reforms and pride alienated clergy, tsar, and people. Deposed by a council in 1666, he lived in exile until his death in 1681, while Old Believers kept his quarrel alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nomination:
Nomination, in strict canon law, means a civil ruler naming a person for a church benefice or office, leaving the church superior to confer the post itself. The right grew from royal and civic endowment of churches, and it follows the rules of patronal presentation.

Church and state thus split the act: the secular power freely chooses a fit candidate, while spiritual jurisdiction stays whole in the bishop or pope who institutes him. Modern appointments, the entry notes, usually rest on prior agreement between the two powers. In earlier days, the nominee himself sought canonical institution from his superior.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nomocanon:
A nomocanon, from Greek words for law and rule, binds imperial law and church canons side by side on the same subjects. Such collections belong to Eastern law alone, where emperors legislated heavily on church discipline in codes from Theodosius to Justinian and the Basilica.

The Greek church holds two main collections, the first from the late sixth century tied to John Scholasticus, whose fifty canonical titles gained matching imperial texts. The entry traces later forms of the work through Heraclius's reign and into Byzantine practice. Latin gave way to Greek as the official language of the empire under Heraclius, from 610 to 640.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-northampton:
Northampton, an English diocese covering seven eastern counties, serves a small Catholic flock amid farms and fens. Its 1910 tally lists 70 secular priests, 18 regulars, 73 chapels and stations, and 13,308 Catholics, with Benedictines, Franciscans, Carmelites, and Jesuits at work.

Norwich, Ipswich, and Cambridge anchor the diocese, and Cambridge holds a Decorated Gothic church to Our Lady and the English Martyrs, gift of Mrs. Lyne Stephens. Tradition also ties Cambridge to Simon Stock, who received the brown scapular there. The Duke of Norfolk built Norwich’s grand church in Transitional Norman style at his own expense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-obligation:
Obligation, a term borrowed from Roman law, names the legal bond that ties one person to act for another's benefit. Justinian's Institutes define it as a bond binding us by legal necessity to do something under the state's laws, a relation first seen as mutual and later as resting on one party.

Carried into ethics, obligation widens into duty itself, and its source becomes a central puzzle: why must we not murder, and what grounds that must? The entry sets out the Catholic answer, tracing moral obligation to reason, natural law, and God's authority over conscience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-obreption:
Obreption, from Latin words for creeping over, names a fraud that voids a church rescript by false statement. Dispensations and graces require a true motive, and petitioners must state the just causes behind their request; a supposititious or twisted fact taints the grant.

Silence about a fact that changes the case is its twin, subreption. A rescript fails when the falsehood touches its motive cause, but stands when only the impelling cause is touched or the error came from ignorance, and officials must verify causes before granting. Officials who forward rescripts must verify the causes alleged and see conditions fulfilled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occult-compen:
Occult compensation means secretly taking the value of one's own goods from a debtor who can pay but will not. Though it looks like theft, the entry argues it differs in root: the taker recovers only a certain due, aims solely to end a wrong, and acts from the right of self-defense.

Catholic moralists allow the practice only within strict bounds, warning that private justice without public sanction threatens social order and invites abuse. Denying the principle outright, they add, leaves the weak exposed to oppression by the strong, so the doctrine steers between two harms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-odo-of-cherit:
Odo of Cheriton, an English preacher and fabulist who died in 1247, stocked sermons with moralized animal tales. Probably a master trained at Paris and son of William of Cheriton, lord of Delce, he inherited family estates in Kent in 1233 and appears in London and Kent records from 1211.

His Parabolae, opening I will open my mouth in parables, gathers fables and anecdotes for preachers, many borrowed yet sharpened by pungent attacks on clergy and laity alike. The collection survives in many manuscripts and shaped later sermon books. A 1235 charter bears his seal: a monk at a desk beneath a star.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-omission:
Omission, in moral theology, means leaving undone something one can and ought to do, a breach that needs no positive act. Moralists stress that guilt lies not in doing nothing here and now, but in neglecting action under circumstances that demand it, freely and knowingly.

Its gravity follows the virtue slighted, the precept's weight, and the deliberation involved, and Aquinas generally rates omission less grave than commission, which embraces evil outright. Yet special matter can reverse that ranking, as when a morning duty fails through drunkenness one chose the night before.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-the-:
The Presentation Sisters, founded at Cork by Nano Nagle, teach poor children in Ireland and beyond. Nagle entered a novitiate with companions in 1775, took the habit as Mother Mary of Saint John of God in 1776. She made first vows in 1777 beside the Ursuline convent she had built.

First called Sisters of the Sacred Heart, they became Presentation Sisters in 1791, won Pius VI's approval for Moylan's Augustinian-based rules, and rose to an order under Pius VII in 1800. Cork, Killarney, Dublin, and Waterford houses grew to 62 convents and about 1,500 sisters, each community independent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oregon:
Oregon, a Pacific Coast state seventh in size in 1910, takes its name from the Oregon, now Columbia, River, whose origin stays obscure. Bounded by Washington, Idaho, Nevada, California, and the Pacific, it stretches 300 miles north to south and 396 east to west across 96,030 square miles.

Coast and Cascade ranges, dense with fir, spruce, and cedar, give way to a vast eastern plateau, and extinct volcanoes crown the Cascades near 9,000 feet. The entry surveys climate, lumber, farming, and mining, with missions, dioceses, and Catholic life from early explorers onward. Its coast range averages 3,500 feet and stands dense with fir, spruce, and cedar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orestes-augus:
American philosopher Orestes Augustus Brownson, born at Stockbridge, Vermont, in 1803, traveled from Presbyterianism through Universalism and Transcendentalism to Catholicism. Raised by upright Congregationalist farm folk on the catechism and Lord's Prayer, he read widely with few books and joined the Presbyterians in 1822.

Repelled by fixed election and reprobation, he became a Universalist minister in 1826, then a Transcendentalist essayist, before entering the Catholic Church in 1844. His Quarterly Review carried his later philosophy of church and state until his death at Detroit in 1876. At nineteen he could translate Virgil, with a fair knowledge of grammar and sums. He joined a church in 1822 and dreamed of going abroad as a missionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-a:
Our Lady of Arcachon is a wonder-working image honoured at Arcachon in France, seemingly carved in the thirteenth century. Cut from one block of alabaster about twenty inches high, it shows Our Lady in Eastern dress, holding the Divine Child on her right arm. Blessed Thomas Illyricus of Osimo, a Franciscan living as a hermit in the Arcachon woods, is said to have found the statue on the shore, battered by waves.

He built a wooden chapel at once, replaced a century later by a stone sanctuary. Drifting dune sands then forced a new church in 1723 on a hill above Arcachon Bay. The statue lived through both revolutions and won a coronation by brief of Pius IX on 15 July 1870. Pilgrims still stream to the shrine, and a town of villas grew round a church once ringed only by fishermen's huts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-arbitra:
Papal arbitration is an institution nearly as old as the papacy itself, resting on the shared bond that binds disputants. Law itself, the entry argues, grew from private revenge to public judgment as peoples felt social solidarity, learning that wrongs wound the whole body, not one victim alone. Compromise, pledges, trial by combat, ordeals, and courts all mark that growth, plainest in the jury's early history.

The same principle was bound to work between nations once Europe's groupings felt their own solidarity. Popes, as heads of a common Christendom, thus served as natural arbiters between princes and states. Later pages list famous cases, from medieval kings to modern disputes, and weigh when papal awards held, when they failed, and what limits bound the pope's power to judge between sovereigns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-ander:
Patrick Anderson was a Scottish Jesuit born at Elgin in Morayshire in 1575 and dead in London on 24 September 1624. Nephew of John Leslie, Bishop of Ross, he studied at Edinburgh University. Leslie had loyally backed Mary Queen of Scots and served as her ambassador in France. Anderson joined the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1597, and won repute as linguist, mathematician, philosopher, and divine.

Sent to the Scottish mission in 1609, his work thrived and his escapes from pursuivants were marvellous. In late 1611 he left for Paris to meet his superior, James Gordon, and undertook to gather nearly one hundred eager Scottish youths for the mission. First Jesuit rector of Rome's Scots College in 1615, he was later betrayed in Scotland. He was jailed in Edinburgh's Tolbooth, and freed, it is thought, at the French ambassador's plea for a confessor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-scarron:
Paul Scarron was a French poet and dramatist born at Paris on 4 July 1610 and dead on 7 October 1660. His father was a judge, an uncle Bishop of Grenoble. After the Sorbonne he took tonsure at nineteen and joined the household of Charles de Beaumanoir, Bishop of Le Mans, whom he followed to Rome in 1635. A year later he became canon of Saint Julian's Cathedral without holy orders, resigning the benefice in January 1652 on marrying Francoise d'Aubigne, later Madame de Maintenon.

By then a cripple confined to bed for life, nursed by his young wife with admirable devotion, piety, and patience, he kept a sharp mind and a busy pen. His comedies, from Jodelet in 1645 to The Ridiculous Marquis in 1656, offered scenes and odd figures Moliere borrowed. His burlesques Typhon and travestied Virgil won lasting fame, and his Comic Romance of 1649 to 1657, realistic in customs and manners, found copiers among later novelists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-antonio:
Pedro Antonio de Alarcon was a novelist and poet born at Guadix in 1833 and dead at Valdemoro in 1891. After early journalism at home, he went to Madrid and rose. When the July 1854 Revolution broke, he edited the journal El Latigo. In 1855 he published El final de Norma, written at seventeen. As a volunteer in the 1859 African war he wrote his lasting work, Diary of a Witness of the African War of 1860.

Parts like The Battle of Castillejos and The Taking of Tetuan are unsurpassed by any Spanish writer for description and narrative. His historical sketches, Historietas nacionales, may outlast his novels in fame. The Three-Cornered Hat of 1874 carried his name across Europe. Next year came El Escandalo, as sensational as Coloma's Pequencess. Better and worthier of knowledge is his novel The Child of the Ball of 1880. His poetic gifts show in Serious and Humorous Poems and Selected Comedies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perpetual-ado:
Perpetual adoration means the practically unbroken worship of the Blessed Sacrament outside Mass. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry sorts its senses. Adoration may run literally without pause, or break only briefly or by necessity. It may last a set span, such as the Forty Hours, or pass in relay across churches, dioceses, or the whole world. No trace of such a cult appears in the early Church.

It first shows itself in the later Middle Ages, around the start of the thirteenth century. The entry tests claims of earlier roots, from Ambrose and Augustine's neophytes to the reservation of the Host, and finds no firm proof. Later sections follow the devotion's growth through orders, confraternities, and diocesan relays into the widespread practice of the modern Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-persecution:
This long Catholic Encyclopedia study treats persecution as force or penalty imposed because of religion. The Church, it argues, has met it from cultured pagans, savage heathens, and modern agnostics, but worst of all from fellow Christians. The study faces a hard charge head-on: that the Church herself turned persecutor through the Inquisition and the religious wars of the Middle Ages and Reformation.

Its answer admits the fact and denies the conclusion. A church claiming a divine command, it says, cannot treat all faiths as equal, and the plea of self-defence cuts both ways, since pagan powers also claimed to defend themselves. Later sections survey persecutions country by country and age by age, testing where coercion crossed into injustice and where defence of a community stayed legitimate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-person:
Person is a word that travelled from the actor's mask to the heart of Christian doctrine. Latin persona first meant the mask, then the role, then any individual on life's stage. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry treats two questions: how person is defined, above all for the Incarnation, and how persona and its Greek counterparts were used in the quarrels over the Trinity.

The classic definition comes from Boethius: an individual substance of a rational nature. Each term gets a close reading, from substance set against accidents to the indivisible individual and the rational nature that limits personhood to intellectual beings. The entry then follows the word through the Trinitarian disputes, where saying three persons in one God demanded exact language. Psychology is left to the companion article on personality.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-hutton:
Peter Hutton was an English priest and schoolmaster of the Rosminian order, born at Holbeck near Leeds in 1811. Baptised at Lady Lane Chapel, then Leeds's only Catholic church, he was sent to Ampleforth in 1824 under his father's will. The Emancipation Act of 1829 barred his profession as a novice, so he taught classics at Prior Park instead, and studied at Louvain from 1836.

Recalled by Bishop Baines, he was ordained in 1839 and made president of St. Peter's College. In 1841 he entered the Institute of Charity despite the bishop's objections, finished his novitiate in Italy under Rosmini, and took vows in 1843. As rector and president at Ratcliffe College he ruled strictly, enlarged the buildings, grew the student body, and left manuscript translations of the Greek and Latin classics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petun-nation:
The Petun, or Tobacco Nation, were one of the three great divisions of the Huron Indians, beside the Hurons proper and the Neutrals. What the three shared in name, country, population, government, religion, and history before the Iroquois scattered them belongs to the article on the Huron Indians. That article also covers the Neutrals' fate and the Hurons proper's wanderings in full.

This short Catholic Encyclopedia entry exists to point readers onward. Once their scattered remnants drifted together again, the Petun became known to English colonists as the Dionondadies or Wyandots, the name they bear alone today. Their western migrations are therefore gathered under the article on the Wyandot Indians, to which this entry sends its readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philemon:
Philemon was a wealthy citizen of Colossae and the addressee of Paul's shortest, most personal letter. Converted probably by Paul at Ephesus, since Paul never visited Colossae, he was the apostle's dear friend and fellow worker, kind, charitable, and hospitable. His house served as a meeting place and church for Colossian converts, and tradition makes him bishop of the city, martyred with Appia, Archippus, and Onesimus under Nero.

The letter itself concerns Onesimus, a runaway slave Paul sends back, asking Philemon to receive him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother in Christ. Paul, an aged prisoner, will not command but begs, leaving the kindness voluntary rather than forced. The entry analyses the letter verse by verse and defends its Pauline authorship against doubt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-reping:
Philip Repington was Bishop of Lincoln and a cardinal who crossed from Wycliffite sympathy to high office, dying early in 1424. Educated at Broadgates Hall, Oxford, he became an Augustinian canon at Leicester, caught Wyclif's infection, and was suspended at Blackfriars in June 1382 and excommunicated at Canterbury that July. Recanting the same autumn, he returned to the Church's communion.

He became abbot of his house in 1394 and Chancellor of Oxford in 1397, 1400, 1401, and 1402. Henry IV made him confessor and chaplain, then Bishop of Lincoln in 1404. Gregory XII created him cardinal in 1408, but Pisa's deposition of Gregory voided the honour until Constance restored it. He resigned Lincoln in 1419, probably for court reasons. His Gospel sermons survive in Oxford, Cambridge, and London manuscripts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philipp-melan:
Philipp Melanchthon was Luther's collaborator and friend, born at Bretten in 1497 as Georg Schwarzerd's son. His grand-uncle Reuchlin, who knew him at Pforzheim, turned the family name into Greek Melanchthon. Entering Heidelberg before thirteen, he took his bachelor's degree in 1511, was refused a master's for youth, and moved to Tübingen. There his humanist learning and Greek scholarship made him famous before he joined Luther at Wittenberg.

His Loci Communes, completed in substance by 1535, systematized Reformation doctrine, and his Augsburg Confession of 1530 argued that Protestants still belonged within the Catholic Church. After Luther's death in 1546 he steered a middle course, rejecting the Augsburg Interim of 1548 yet accepting the Leipzig Interim, and drew bitter fire from stricter Lutherans. He died at Wittenberg in 1560, the gentle scholar beside Luther's storm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-pier:
Philippe Pierson was a Belgian Jesuit missionary in Canada, born at Ath in Hainaut in 1642. At eighteen he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Tournai and studied at Louvain, Lille, and Douai. He taught at Armentières and Béthune before sailing to Canada in 1666, where he taught grammar at Quebec College and staged a successful Latin play on the Passion.

Ordained in 1669 after two years of theology, he worked among Indians at Prairie de la Madeleine and Sillery. From 1673 to 1683 he spread Christianity among the Hurons of the Mackinac mission, writing from St. Ignace of a church growing in numbers and strong in faith. From 1683 he laboured among the Sioux west of Lake Superior until his death at Lorette, Quebec, in 1688.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-physical-effe:
The physical effects of abortion form a medical-moral study in this Catholic Encyclopedia entry, beginning with definitions. Loss in the first three months counts as abortion, months four to seven as miscarriage, and weeks twenty-eight to thirty-eight as early birth. Causes match those of miscarriage: sickness of womb or child, the mother's state, illness passed down or caught, infection, shock, or hurt.

Abortion may also be brought on by choice and crime, with drugs, tools, or both, by the woman herself or another. Harm follows the cause, the entry argues, but in every case abortion brings grave harm near and far, a sad break in nature's plan to be shunned with all one's strength. Abortion by crime it calls first-degree murder, answerable to a higher law when human law fails.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-physiological:
Physiological assimilation is the vital function by which an organism turns food into living protoplasm, and this Catholic Encyclopedia entry defends a philosophical reading of it. Modern scientists, it notes, define assimilation well enough, as Rosenthal does: cells bring forth from varied materials substances like those already in them. Yet they often deny again what they conceded, reducing the change to mere chemistry.

The entry objects that inorganic action merely passes from subject to subject, while assimilated matter gains the power to act on itself, develop, and perfect itself by its own motion. An animal seeks, selects, and proportions its food to its needs, anticipating an end. Such immanent action, proceeding from an inner principle and perfecting the agent rather than a foreign subject, marks life's difference from mechanism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-chaign:
Pierre Chaignon was a French Jesuit devoted to the spiritual direction of priests, born at Saint-Pierre-la-Cour in 1791. He entered the Society in 1819 and spent his whole life in ministry, chiefly guiding clergy. In thirty years he gave three hundred retreats to priests of France's principal dioceses, a labour that shaped his writing.

His chief work, Méditationes sacerdotales, appeared in several languages, including Bohemian, Polish, Italian, and English, Bishop de Goesbriand of Burlington translating it from the eleventh edition. He also wrote on easy salvation through devotion to Mary's immaculate heart, the six Sundays of St. Aloysius Gonzaga, the priest at the altar, and peace of soul, with brochures on a good death and the jubilees of 1869 and 1875. He founded a Union of Prayer for Deceased Priests, erected as a confraternity in 1861. He died at Angers in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-charro:
Pierre Charron was a French moralist, born at Paris in 1541. He studied law at Bourges, practised several years, then took orders and preached for thirty years with such success that bishops vied for his services. Queen Margaret of Navarre kept him as preacher in ordinary, and Henry IV delighted to hear him even before converting. At Bordeaux he formed a close, lasting friendship with Montaigne, who left him the right to bear his coat of arms.

Charron published Trois vérités in 1594, an opportune apology amid religious agitation, Discours chrétiens in 1600, and Sagesse in 1601. Sagesse, drawn chiefly from Montaigne, divides man's nature, man's duties, and the duties of each class. Its sceptical spirit, judging by natural light alone, drew fierce attack: Garasse called him atheist and patriarch of free-thinkers, and its second edition appeared only softened. He died suddenly of apoplexy in 1603 while preparing it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-coton:
Pierre Coton was a celebrated French Jesuit, born at Néronde in Forez on 7 March 1564. He studied law at Paris and Bourges, entered the Society at twenty-five, and met St. Charles Borromeo at Milan. Returning home, he preached with success at Roanne, Avignon, Nîmes, Grenoble, and Marseilles, and his acquaintance with Henry IV ripened into friendship.

He refused the vacant archbishopric of Arles, helped recall the exiled Jesuits, and survived an assassination attempt by their enemies. After Henry's murder, the satire Anti-Coton accused him of defending the regicide Ravaillac, a calumny he easily refuted, though its author, said to be the Protestant minister Pierre Dumoulin, could prove nothing. Coton had been confessor to the young Dauphin for two years before Henry's death and remained so after. His controversial works include Institution catholique and Genève plagiaire. He died at Paris in 1626, protesting his loyalty on his deathbed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-d-aubu:
Pierre d'Aubusson was Grand Master of the Hospitallers and saviour of Rhodes, born in 1423. He campaigned against the Turks, fought under the French Dauphin against the Swiss in 1444, then joined the Order of St. John. By 1460 he was castellan of Rhodes, soon captain-general of the city that had housed the order since 1309.

Raised to Grand Master in 1476, he foresaw Mehmed II's design and begged men and money from the order's houses, Sixtus IV, and Louis XI. He mustered only 450 knights and 2,000 auxiliaries against a Turkish fleet of overwhelming numbers and the best artillery of the day, appearing before Rhodes on 23 May 1480. Three months of almost ceaseless fighting cost the Turks 25,000 warriors, and the commander raised the siege. Christendom hailed him as the Shield of the Church and gave him a cardinal's hat. He died in 1503.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-lau:
Pierre de Lauzon was a noted Jesuit missionary of New France, born at Poitiers on 26 September 1687. Though sometimes called Jean, he always signed Pierre. He joined the Jesuits at Limoges in 1703, reached Canada in 1716, assisted at Lorette while learning Huron-Iroquois, and served Sault St. Louis, Caughnawaga, from 1718 to 1731, apart from a year teaching hydrography at Quebec College.

His Iroquois clamoured for his return and petitioned Governor Vaudreuil in May 1722, crediting him alone with stopping two-thirds of the village from moving within English reach. Named superior of Caughnawaga in 1723, he governed nine years so ably that General Retz placed him over the whole Canada mission in 1732. In 1733 he crossed to France for recruits, returning with Jean-Pierre Aulneau, massacred in 1736, after an eighty-day voyage of wind and disease in which he served as boatswain's mate. Failing strength recalled him to Quebec in 1741, and he died there in 1742.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-voy:
Pierre de Voyer, vicomte d'Argenson, was Canada's fifth governor-general, serving from 1657 to 1661, born in 1626. Fifth child of René, count d'Argenson, he took tonsure in 1636 for a church career, then chose arms, serving at Portolongone, La Bassée, Ypres, Lens, and Bordeaux, where he took many wounds. He became governor, reaching Quebec on 11 July 1658.

Canada then lay prey to Iroquois invasions. With only a hundred soldiers he inspired colonists by often rash bravery. Yet Dollard and his companions died averting blows from the little city, and the grand seneschal Jean de Lauzon fell in ambush. D'Argenson drew Iroquois children to him for instruction and as hostages and sent the Jesuit Le Moyne to negotiate. Wounded, unsupported by France, and weary of strife with the bishop, he sought recall and returned to France in September 1661. He died about 1710, buried at Mouzé at his request.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-talon:
Pierre Talon was a French-Canadian youth whose six years among the Cenis people of Texas left one of the earliest first-hand accounts of the region. He was born at Quebec in 1676 and sailed with his family in 1684 to join La Salle's ill-fated Louisiana colony. He was sent inland to learn the Cenis language.

After La Salle's murder and the massacre of the colonists, Talon and his siblings were taken by the Spanish to Mexico. They served as marines and were finally shipped toward Europe. His sworn evidence at Brest in 1698 describes the customs, rites, animals, and plants of the southern tribes he had lived among, and may record a sighting of the Mississippi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ponce-de-leon:
Ponce de León was the Spanish explorer who gave Florida its name and sought the fabled fountain of youth. He was born at San Servas in Campos in 1460 and served as a page to Pedro Núñez de Guzmán. He sailed to Hispaniola with Columbus on his second voyage in 1493.

After service against a native rising, he won leave to visit Boriquén, Puerto Rico, in 1508 and became its governor. In 1512 Charles V licensed him to find the island of Bimini, home of the fountain said to restore youth. Sailing in March 1513, he sighted the Florida coast on Easter Sunday, 27 March, and landed near present Saint Augustine on 2 April, claiming the land for Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-conon:
Pope Conon, birth date unknown, died 21 September 687 after a long sickness. He seems to have been the son of an officer among the Thracesian troops, was schooled in Sicily, and took priest's orders at Rome. His years, dignified looks, and plain ways moved Rome's quarrelling clergy and soldiers to drop their rival candidates and choose him.

Ravenna's exarch received notice before his consecration 21 October 686. He welcomed the Irish missionaries Kilian and his fellows, made Kilian bishop, and dispatched them to preach in Franconia. The fierce Emperor Justinian II held him in favour. Justinian told him the Sixth General Council's Acts had been recovered and that he meant to stand by them. He also forgave taxes and dues owed from several papal estates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-porphyreon:
