Porphyreon was a titular see under Tyre in Phoenicia Prima. Antioch's sixth-century list of bishoprics includes it, though the tenth-century list omits it. Lequien names five bishops: Thomas in 451, Alexander late in the fifth century, Theodore in 518, Christophorus in 536, and Paul, a contemporary of Justinian II, in 565 to 578.

Two towns bore the name. One north of Sidon is now El Djiyeh village between Saida and Beirut. The other, the Crusade historians' confusion with Caipha aside, lay near Castra by the Samaritans, six or seven miles north of Carmel by Pseudo-Antoninus's reckoning. Simeon Stylites the Younger confirms the site near Castra. Porphyreon's church of the Blessed Virgin was built by Justinian I, not Justinian II, as Procopius records. The entry fixes the see's identity against the Caipha confusion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-postcommunion:
The Communion act ends the core Eucharistic service. Justin Martyr adds nothing after telling of the Communion. Yet folk were not sent off with no last prayer of thanks and pleading, so each rite closes with a brief prayer or two and a blessing ere dismissal. The earliest full liturgy left to us, the Apostolic Constitutions, holds two such prayers, one of thanks and one of blessing. In the Leonine Sacramentary they bear no title, but their stamp is plain.

The Gelasian Sacramentary names the first postcommunio and the second ad populum. Both belong to the normal Mass through the year, though not each Mass has both. The ad populum prayers grow rare later, and their stamp shifts: the old terms tuere and protege fade, and many become plain collects. In the Gregorian book the second prayer, now Super populum, turns up almost only from Septuagesima to Easter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-postulation:
Postulation comes from the Latin postulare, to request. It is a plea to a fit church superior to raise to a dignity a man not strictly fit for it, owing to a church bar that can usually be lifted. Such bars are base birth, lack of due age, or the state of a bishop or regular needing his superior's leave. With an election, the votes must be twice those that would serve were the man fit.

The Holy See at times lifts the need by a grant of fitness. Postulation is solemn when laid ere the superior who can lift the bar. It is simple when that superior cannot lift the bar but his assent is still needed, as with regulars raised to a bishopric. Only bars that can be lifted allow postulation, and the plea must name each bar, on pain of nullity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pragmatic-san:
In the late Roman Empire a pragmatic sanction was an edict put out in due form by the emperor. The best known of later days is the sanctio pragmatica said to come from St Louis IX of France in 1269. It sought to curb Rome's growing power, its calls for tribute, and its growing hold on church posts. Papal taxes stood only in dire need, with leave of king and French Church. Yet Thomassy in 1844, Gérin in 1869, Viollet in 1870, and Scheffer-Boichorst in 1887 proved it a fake, put out between 1438 and 1452.

The Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges took up many useful acts of the Council of Basle of 1431 to 1437. By it the French king made law in purely church affairs, on his own secular say so. Rome strove to kill the law, and Pius II, pope from 1458 to 1464, called it a breach of papal rights.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-preconization:
Preconization, from Latin praeconizare, to publish, from praeco, herald, means in strict law a ratification in a public consistory. It ratifies a third person's choice of a holder for a consistorial benefice, such as a bishopric. The pope backs the election or postulation of a holder made by a chapter, or backs a candidate put forth by the civil power.

A fact finding process comes first. By present rule the Consistorial Congregation raises it, while the Secretary of State gives the facts for sees outside Italy. Some writers define preconization as the cardinals' report in that process at the consistory. Others take it as the notice to the pope that a cardinal will soon propose, in a head of state's name, the man that head has picked for a see. Still others take it as the pope's ratification, in consistory, of a nomination already made by decree.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-predestinatio:
Predestination, from Latin prae and destinare, in its widest sense is each Divine decree by which God has set and ordained from eternity all events in time. It rests on His sure foreknowledge of the future, above all for events shaped by man's free will. In that broad sense it matches Divine Providence and the rule of the world, which lie outside this entry.

Theology narrows the word to Divine decrees bearing on the supernatural end of rational beings, above all man. Since many are lost forever through their own fault, it must be twofold. One decree is to heaven for all who die in grace. The other is to hell's pains for all who die in sin or under God's displeasure. By present usage the latter decree is better called Divine reprobation. Later the entry weighs how many are saved, holding it likely that most Christians will be saved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prescription:
Prescription, from Latin prae, before, and scribere, to write, bears in later legal Latin the sense of limitation. It is a method made by law for gaining ownership or shedding burdens when fixed terms are met. It is thus acquisitive or liberating, the first oft called usucaption. It springs from civil law enactments confirmed by canon law, and moralists hold its ground valid in conscience. Public good calls for sure title to property and for as few suits as may be.

 A man who has duly gained land by prescription may keep it with a safe conscience, even if the old owner turns up to claim it.  Moralists agree that a thing whose ownership is to pass must stand open to prescription. It must be a thing that can pass in private barter and bear a title known to natural and positive law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presumption:
Presumption, from Latin praesumere, to take before, to take for granted, is here weighed as a vice against the theological virtue of hope. Pride may also breed it. It is the state of a soul which, from ill ruled trust in God's mercy and power, hopes for salvation with no deeds to earn it, or for pardon with no repentance. Presumption sins against hope by excess, as despair sins by defect, though the saying is but an analogy.

Suarez lists five ways to fall into presumption. One hopes by natural powers alone, unaided, for what is plainly supernatural: eternal bliss, or God's friendship regained after grave sin. One looks for pardon with no fit penance, which, if held in earnest, smacks of heresy. One expects God's special aid in working a crime, which is blasphemous as well as presumptuous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-promulgation:
Promulgation, from Latin promulgare, to make known, to post in public, is the act by which the lawmaking power makes laws known. It makes them known to the authorities who must execute them and to the subjects who must obey them.  A law's core is plainly the lawgiver's will, which he should make known somehow. That showing is promulgation, which need not stand apart from the law's making, if the making runs by outward acts.

Such is the use in England and most American states, but many lands, deeming it too harsh, require promulgation by a special formal act. Through it the law's text is made known to the community, such as printing it in an official journal or bulletin.  Promulgation must not be mixed with publication: the first makes the lawgiver's will known, the second spreads it among subjects bound to obey them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psalms-of-sol:
Eighteen apocryphal psalms, surviving in Greek and probably translated from a Hebrew or Aramaic original, form the first subject of this double entry. Commonly dated to the first century BC, they borrow heavily from the psalms of David and add little that is new. Their Messianic hope is dim, clouded by the gloom of Pompey's siege of Jerusalem. The entry sets them beside their better-known Davidic models.

A second apocryphal work follows: the forty-two Odes of Solomon, lyric poems recently discovered and published in 1909 by J. Randel Harris. Their existence had long been known from ancient lists, including a sixth-century synopsis and the ninth-century Stichometry of Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople. The entry traces that paper trail and closes with the new Syriac edition from Cambridge and Harnack's Leipzig volume, giving readers both works in one place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psychological:
Psychological assimilation borrows its image from the body: just as living tissue takes in food, so the growing mind takes in truth. This short encyclopedia entry notes that teachers often repeat the comparison without feeling its full force. The mind, like the cell, cannot hand its work to someone else. No trick of method lets a pupil dodge the final act of learning for himself. All a teacher can do is prepare the material and stir the pupil's mind.

The centre of the lesson should shift from the logical order of the subject to the present needs and capacities of the learner. Material must meet the pupil where he stands, rather than marching through a textbook's system. Sources in medical and physiological dictionaries back the analogy, and the entry leaves educators with a plain rule: present truth well, then let the mind do its own digesting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quilon:
The Diocese of Quilon, on the Malabar coast of India under Verapoly, takes the southern half of Travancore with the British lands of Tangacherry and Anjengo. This encyclopedia entry maps it from the northern branch of the River Ranee down to Cape Comorin, with the Ghauts to the east and the Indian Ocean to the west. One narrow coastal strip belongs instead to the Diocese of Cochin. Out of 1,600,000 people, Catholics number 116,090.

They worship in 161 churches and 29 chapels, served by 59 priests. Seventeen are Discalced Carmelite Fathers from European provinces, and the rest are native clergy. The bishop's residence, the cathedral and the preparatory seminary, with 32 students, all stand at Quilon, while nine more candidates study at Kandy Seminary in Ceylon. Foundling and widows' homes, a dispensary at Mulagamude, and hospital nursing departments under Sisters of the Holy Cross complete the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratisbon:
The Diocese of Ratisbon, also called Regensburg, answers to Munich-Freising. This encyclopedia entry covers the greater part of Oberpfalz with portions of Upper and Lower Bavaria and Upper Franconia, about 5,340 square miles. It divides into three episcopal commissariates, Ratisbon, Amberg and Straubing, and thirty deaneries. In 1910 it counted 473 parishes, 167 benefices, 80 expositorships, 371 curacies and 36 other pastoral offices, with 1,283 clergy and over 865,000 Catholics.

A coadjutor bishop, consecrated on 18 April 1911, served beside the ordinary, and the cathedral chapter held a provost, eight capitulars, six vicars and a preacher. History gives the diocese its great bishop Albertus Magnus. On his voluntary retirement, Leo Thundorfer, who began the cathedral, was elected for 1262 to 1277. Heinrich the Second of Rotteneck followed, leading a holy life as an excellent spiritual and secular prince. Albert of Stauf, an adherent of the Pisan popes, later pressed reform of monasteries and clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-breto:
Raymond Breton, noted French missionary among the Caribbean Indians, was born at Baune on 3 September 1609 and died at Caen on 8 January 1679. This encyclopedia entry tells that he entered the Dominican Order at seventeen. He was sent in 1627 to the priory of Saint Jacques at Paris, to finish his classical studies and take philosophy and theology. After gaining his theology degree, he sailed with three other Dominicans for the French West Indies in 1635.

Nearly twenty years went to the Antilles missions. Twelve of them he spent on San Domingo, practically alone among the Indians. The other eight he spent island-hopping, teaching and evangelizing the natives in their own tongue and mastering the various Carib languages. Back in France in 1654, he trained young priests for the West Indian missions. He wrote a history of the French mission among the Caribs from 1634 to 1643, a manuscript of great historical importance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-caron:
Raymond Caron was a Franciscan friar and author, born at Athlone, Ireland, in 1605 and dead at Dublin in 1666. This encyclopedia entry follows him from the Franciscan convent of his native town, where he made his preliminary studies. He then studied philosophy at Drogheda and theology at Salzburg and the Franciscan college at Louvain. Just after ordination he became professor of theology at Louvain, matching his reputation as a student.

In 1635 he published at Antwerp his Roma triumphans Septicollis, a defence of Catholic doctrine. Had he stayed at Louvain in the quiet life of author and professor, his peace of mind would have fared better. But in 1648 his order's superior in the Netherlands sent him to Ireland as visitator, with wide powers to correct and reform. Later writings from London in 1662 and 1665 earned him a loyalist name, but also his superiors' condemnation and a spell under ecclesiastical censure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reason:
Reason wears many senses, and this encyclopedia entry sorts them. Etymologically the word reaches us through French from the Latin ratio, the working noun of reor, I think. Donaldson traces res, the thing proposed to the mind, to a root meaning hand, so res is that which is handled, an object of thought. Ratio, set against res, names thinking's mode or act.

By extension ratio names the faculty of thinking, and also the formal side of thought, such as plan, account or ground. The entry then turns to concrete reasoning, where Newman observed that we are departmental, reasoning with unequal ease on different subjects. Even great inventors like Newton and Leibniz slipped on new ground. Aristotle had already stressed that we never think without an accompanying sense-process, and bees, the entry notes, remember only time and distance, leaving reason man's exclusive prerogative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-recollection:
Recollection, in the spiritual life, means attention to God's presence in the soul. This encyclopedia entry defines it as the mind withdrawing from outward, earthly affairs to attend to God and divine things. It matches interior solitude, the soul alone with God. Recollection takes two forms, active and passive, and the entry sets them side by side.

Active recollection can be won by our own efforts, helped by God's ordinary grace. Any devout soul can form the habit of thinking of God's presence and fixing attention on Him and His perfections. Passive recollection does not depend on our efforts. It is an extraordinary grace infused by God, who gathers the soul's faculties together and shows His presence and perfections. Mystical writers rank it as the first degree of infused contemplation, and recalling that our souls are God's temples aids its growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-redemption:
Redemption means man freed from sin's bondage into the liberty of God's children, through Christ's satisfactions and merits. This long encyclopedia entry notes that redemptio renders the Hebrew kopher and Greek lytron, which in the Old Testament generally mean a ransom-price. In the New Testament it becomes the term for the price, in First Corinthians, which the Redeemer paid for our liberation.

Redemption presupposes man's elevation to a supernatural state and his fall from it through sin. Sin draws God's wrath and enslaves man to evil and Satan. On God's side, redemption means accepting satisfactory amends, so that honour is repaired and wrath appeased. On man's side it means deliverance from sin's slavery and restoration to sonship. Saint Paul says where sin abounded, grace abounded more, with Chrysostom's drop against the ocean and Cyril's one for all closing the doctrinal picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regeneration:
Regeneration, from Latin regeneratio and Greek anagennesis and paliggenesia, is a biblical term tied to justification, divine sonship and deification through grace. This encyclopedia entry starts from the Bible: regeneration from God belongs inseparably to baptism, which Saint Paul calls the laver of regeneration. In His talk with Nicodemus, the Saviour declares that unless a man is born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter God's kingdom.

Christians read there proof that baptism may not be repeated, since a second regeneration from God contradicts itself no less than a second physical birth. The idea of birth from God enjoys favour in John's theology. Saint Augustine joins justification to faith working through charity, rooting it in the soul's renewal and sanctification, and thus becomes precursor and model of the Scholastics. Christ's word for the last day's resurrection as a regeneration closes the biblical survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religion:
Religion is treated here in seven parts: derivation and definition, subjective religion, objective religion, origin, universality, civilizing influence, and the modern scientific study of religion. The derivation of the word itself has been disputed since ancient times and remains open. Cicero derived it from relegere, to treat carefully, and Max Müller favoured that view. But the entry objects that religion predates the elaborate ritual such an origin assumes, and looks for a simpler root.

Later sections separate the prophet's office from the priest's, distinct in general though not always. Prophets held a lawful place under the Old Law, bringing warnings and moral awakening as well as foretelling, and in Christ the office was perfected for all time. In lower religions, by contrast, the prophet's role is marked by wild mental excitement, read by worshippers as the sign of a god's inspiring presence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-con:
Religious congregations of the Presentation gathers sisterhoods under one title. The Daughters of the Presentation were founded in 1627 by Nicolas Sanguin, Bishop of Senlis, a prelate atoning by a holy life for his youth. After serving the plague-stricken of Senlis, he founded a teaching order against the ignorance and vice of his diocese. Catherine Dreux and Marie de la Croix began teaching in 1626, forming a community the next year under the Rule of Saint Augustine. Urban the Eighth granted a bull of erection in 1628, and Louis the Thirteenth granted letters patent in 1630.

Municipal opposition melted before those approvals, and the community took root. The entry goes on to survey Presentation congregations, one of which counts two hundred members under a mother-house at Saint-Nicolas, with filial houses depending on it. Together they show a teaching tradition carried from seventeenth-century Senlis into the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-of-:
The Religious of Perpetual Adoration in Belgium are a congregation under simple vows, founded at Brussels in 1857 by Anna de Meeus. Her father, Count Ferdinand de Meeus, had a price set on his head in the Revolution of 1830. In 1843, aged twenty, Anna visited the sacristy near the chateau and other churches at the rector's request. The miserable vestments and altar furnishings struck her, and the sight shaped her work.

She pondered the poverty and neglect of Christ in the Blessed Sacrament and sought reparation by reviving faith in the Real Presence. Members promised a monthly hour of adoration, night and day, and a yearly offering for poor churches, working to dignify divine worship. The institute won the rank of prima primaria in July 1895. It reached England in August 1880 through Cardinal Herbert Vaughan, and opened its first American house at Washington in October 1900.

The Religious of the Perpetual Adoration at Einsiedeln are a cloistered congregation founded in 1526 by Sister Elizabeth Zwirer, who died in 1546, and following the Benedictine rule. Early in 1789 they began adoring the Blessed Sacrament by day before the closed tabernacle, and a lay group gave small sums for the sanctuary costs of perpetual adoration. Expelled in the French invasion of 2 May 1798, with their monastery ruined, they returned five years later after Napoleon's Concordat.

On Father Pierre Perrot's advice, they added adoration by night to adoration by day on 8 January 1846. A new church opened in 1882, adorned with three paintings of the adoration of Christ. Einsiedeln remains the only house of its kind, with its own novitiate, and in 1909 the community counted forty-six professed sisters and five novices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-pro:
Religious profession means either a declaration made or a state of life embraced. Its origins lie with Christians recognized as seekers of perfection: in the third century they appear as ascetics, asketai in Greek and confessores in Latin. Eusebius counts among them Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, and Polycarp. Hermits and monks followed in the fourth century, canons regular in the eleventh, mendicants in the thirteenth, clerks regular in the sixteenth, and lastly members of congregations.

Under law, solemn profession annuls a marriage contracted but not yet consummated, and bars any marriage as a diriment impediment. It leaves the professed religious unable, without the Holy See's permission, to acquire, possess, or dispose of property, though in Belgium and probably Holland that disability no longer applies. Simple profession may be perpetual or temporary: at the end of a temporary term, the religious is free to return to the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-tol:
Religious toleration begins from toleration in general: patient forbearance before an evil one cannot or will not prevent. Towards another faith it means a magnanimous indulgence, joined to a firm resolve to leave that faith and its adherents unmolested in private and in public. Inwardly, the tolerator still disapproves it as a false faith. This entry treats toleration from principle alone, leaving its history to a separate article, and works through four heads.

Those heads are the idea of toleration, the inadmissibility of theoretical and dogmatic toleration, the obligation of practical civil toleration, and the necessity of public political toleration. The discussion tests its principles against hard cases. It weighs severe punishments for grave crimes and American lynch law, where allowance is made for imperfect penal procedure without excusing the practice outright. Principle, not history, governs throughout.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-edouard-:
René-Edouard Caron, French Canadian statesman and magistrate, was born at Sainte Anne de Beaupré on 13 October 1800, son of farmer Augustin Caron and Elizabeth Lessard. He died on 13 December 1876. He studied at the Quebec seminary and entered the bar in 1826. Elected Mayor of Quebec in 1833, he held the office ten years, through the cholera of 1834 and the fire of 1845 that nearly destroyed the city.

Elected to the Legislative Assembly in 1834, he passed to the Legislative Council at the Union of the two provinces in 1841. He was Speaker of the Upper House in 1843, 1848, and 1851, sitting in the Cabinet on the two occasions. With Lafontaine and Morin he wrested equal rights for Lower Canada from an ultra-Tory oligarchy. He helped codify the laws in 1859, and in 1872 became Lieutenant-Governor of Quebec, holding it until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-renunciation:
Renunciation, from the Latin renuntiare, is the church-law term for resigning a church office or benefice. It means the abdication of a clerical dignity, made freely, for just reasons, and accepted by the proper superior. Any cleric may renounce his dignity, whether his office is lasting or short-term.

To count, the resignation must be free, never extorted by fear, threats, or fraud. It must go to the superior who conferred the office: the pope for bishops and holders of major benefices, the ordinary for parish priests and holders of minor benefices. The pope himself may abdicate, but having no earthly superior, he need only declare his resignation canonically. The entry names canonical irregularity, the people's ill-will, and scandalous behaviour among its cases.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reparation:
Reparation is a theological concept close to atonement and satisfaction, touching some of the deepest mysteries of the Christian faith. Man fell from the original justice in which he was created, and through the Son of God's Incarnation, Passion, and Death he was redeemed and partly restored. God might have pardoned offences freely, but in his providence he demanded satisfaction for the injuries done him, judging it better for man's education that wrongdoing carry the need to make amends.

That satisfaction was made fully to God by Christ's sufferings, Passion, and Death as man. The entry then turns to the devotional side. A pious widow of Paris conceived the Mass of Reparation in 1862. By Pope Leo the Thirteenth's authority, the Archconfraternity of the Mass of Reparation was sanctioned in 1886, its offering aimed at the propitiation of God's wrath.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reservation:
Reservation in canon law lets a superior hold back, in certain cases, power an inferior would else wield. It covers benefice appointments, release from vows, and absolution from sins and censures. The pope holds the power in full and may use it worldwide, while bishops, regular superiors, and others with quasi-episcopal power in the penitential forum may reserve their own subjects' absolution.

Parish priests and local superiors hold no such right. The chief reason for curbing confessors is to deter wrongdoers by making absolution hard to gain, and only graver mortal sins, external and done rather than merely tried, should be reserved. Nearly all papal reservations carry a censure and rest on it, while bishops' reservations mostly lack one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-restitution:
Restitution, in moral theology, is an act of commutative justice making exact reparation, as far as possible, for an injury done to another. Injury comes by detaining what is known to belong to another in strict justice, or by wilfully damaging his property or reputation. Since justice requires rendering to each what is his, keeping another's goods against his reasonable will, or damaging his goods or name, violates it, and restitution follows wherever the virtue is violated.

The obligation matches the Seventh Commandment, thou shalt not steal. If fruits or the property itself have perished, the possessor owes nothing for what no longer exists, and good-faith consumption excuses him, leaving the owner to bear the loss. But possession begun in bad faith binds the possessor to restore all that remains, fruits included, and to compensate the owner for every loss suffered through being deprived of his property.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-revelation:
Revelation means God telling some truth to a rational creature by means beyond nature's ordinary course. Revealed truths may be mysteries, otherwise closed to the mind and never fully penetrated even once revealed. But revelation is not confined to them: God may also use supernatural means to affirm truths reason could reach alone. Its essence is God's direct speech to man, even when the message comes mediately through a prophet.

The entry defends revelation's necessity for the bulk of mankind, from history and from the nature of the case. Human reason keeps its capacity, and here and there pagans may have freed themselves from prevalent errors and grasped enough natural law to reach beatitude. But such cases are few, the Church teaches, and for most people moral and religious truth remains out of reach without revelation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-revocation:
Revocation is the recalling or annulling of an act, the reversal of a deed, the recall of a grant, or the voiding of something previously existing. The term ranges widely in canon law: grants, laws, contracts, sentences, jurisdiction, and appointments may all be revoked by the grantor, his successor, or a superior, under the law's prescriptions. Revocation without just cause is illicit, though it often stands.

Laws and customs fall when changed circumstances leave them unjust or unreasonable, and concordats may be revoked when they seriously injure the Church. Minors and church institutions can have sentences in certain civil trials set aside, and contracts alienating church property are sometimes rescindable. A judge may revoke his own interlocutory sentence but never a definitive one. Many appointments end at will, others only after a trial or formalities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-angel:
Richard Angelus a Sancto Francisco Mason, Franciscan writer, was born in Wiltshire in 1599 and died at Douai on 30 December 1678. His nationality is disputed. All agree he was a Wiltshire native, but a Franciscan manuscript of 1721 calls him dean of a Catholic deanery in Ireland for some time, hinting his family may have been Irish. Gillow argues that any Irish deanery he held must have been under the Protestant Establishment, making Father Angelus, as contemporaries knew him, a seventeenth-century convert.

That manuscript note, however, was written forty-three years after Mason's death, and evidence shows his Douai ordination came four years after his profession. The entry leaves the Irish question open, resting on the Wiltshire birth, the Douai ordination, and the late manuscript claim. The entry weighs the late manuscript claim against the Douai evidence and leaves his Irish extraction unresolved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-archd:
Richard Archdeacon, also given as Archdekin or Arsdekin, was an Irish Jesuit born at Kilkenny on 30 March 1620 who died on 31 August 1693. He entered the Society of Jesus at Mechlin on 20 September 1642, teaching at Antwerp and Louvain: humanities, philosophy, theology, and Holy Scripture. His Theologia Quadripartita joined a miracles treatise in English and Irish and a Life of Saint Patrick. That Life carries a notice on Ireland, the so-called prophecy of Saint Malachy, and the principal controversies of the faith.

The book was meant for Ireland and sold fast, more than a thousand copies going in a few months. He republished it as the Theologia Tripartita, telling readers in the preface that he had more time for writing than for the earlier book. His miracles treatise is called the first book printed jointly in English and Irish.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-broug:
Richard Broughton, alias Rouse, Catholic priest and antiquary, was born about 1558 at Great Stukeley in Huntingdonshire and died on 18 January 1634. Claiming descent from the Broughtons of Lancashire, he was ordained at Reims on 4 May 1593 and soon returned to England. His contemporary John Pitts praised his harvest of souls and his learning, calling him as familiar with literature as he was learned in Greek and Hebrew.

Broughton served as assistant to the archpriest, canon of the chapter, and vicar-general to Bishop Smith of Chalcedon. By solid work and by controversy he earned a place in the study of antiquity beside Spelman, Reyner, Dugdale, and other noted antiquarians. Pitts's praise and his chapter offices mark a priest who doubled as a scholar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-malco:
A Georgia schoolmaster who became a popular storyteller late in life is the subject of this entry. Richard Malcolm Johnston, born at Powellton in 1822, was the son of a Baptist minister. He studied law, was admitted to the bar in 1843, and later held a university chair in belles-lettres. During the Civil War he ran a boys' school on his farm near Sparta while also serving on a general's staff.

After the war he started a boys' school, Penn Lucy, outside Baltimore. There the poet Sidney Lanier, one of his teachers, urged him to write for print, though he was already past fifty. His tales of old Middle Georgia, collected in Dukesborough Tales and later volumes, won him a wide readership for their humour and faithful local colour. He became a Catholic in 1875 and spent his last years writing and lecturing on literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-samps:
Richard Sampson was a Tudor churchman and diplomat who rose by serving Henry VIII, above all in the king's divorce proceedings. Educated at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, and at Paris and Sens, he became a doctor of canon law. Cardinal Wolsey made him chancellor and vicar-general in the diocese of Tournai, where he lived until 1517. He also gathered English preferments and served as ambassador to Emperor Charles V from 1522 to 1525.

Sampson became one of Henry's chief agents in the divorce case, and rewards followed: deaneries, rectories, and church treasuries. In 1536 he was elected Bishop of Chichester without papal approval, and in 1543 he was moved to Coventry and Lichfield on royal authority alone. He kept his see through Edward VI's reign, despite reports that he retracted his disloyalty to the pope. He also wrote in defence of royal prerogative and published explanations of the Psalms and Romans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-simps:
Richard Simpson was a Victorian scholar who left the Anglican ministry to become a Catholic writer and editor. Born in 1820 and educated at Oriel College, Oxford, he was ordained an Anglican clergyman and served as vicar of Mitcham. In 1845 he resigned that living and entered the Catholic Church. Years on the continent made him a skilled linguist, and on his return he edited the Rambler.

When the Rambler ceased in 1862, he joined Sir John Acton in founding the Home and Foreign Review. Church authorities judged it unsound, and it closed in 1864. Simpson then gave himself to Shakespeare studies and music. His books include a life of Edmund Campion, judged his finest work, an introduction to the philosophy of Shakespeare's sonnets, and The School of Shakespeare. Though he stayed a practising Catholic, his liberal views led him to help Gladstone write on Vaticanism. He died near Rome in 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-uller:
Richard Ullerston was an Oxford scholar and reform-minded churchman of the early fifteenth century. Born in the Duchy of Lancaster, he was ordained priest in December 1383 and became a fellow of Queen's College, Oxford, in 1391. He took his doctorate in divinity in 1394 and served as chancellor of the university in 1408.

That same year, at the request of the Bishop of Salisbury, he drafted a sketch of proposed church reforms, the Petitiones pro ecclesiae militantis reformatione. His other writings include commentaries on the Creed, the Psalms, and the Song of Songs. He also defended the Donation of Constantine and wrote a treatise on the military office for Henry, Prince of Wales. From 1403 he held a Salisbury prebend, and from 1407 the rectory of Beeford in Yorkshire. He died in August or September 1423.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-wilto:
Richard Wilton was a medieval scholar known only through a late and unreliable source, and this entry carefully sifts fact from fable. He died on 21 December 1239. Beyond that, all that is told is that he was an Englishman who joined the Trinitarians. He wrote commentaries on the Sentences, Genesis, and Jeremiah, plus treatises against heresies, on the soul's immortality, and on divine grace.

Every detail comes from Oldoinus and his Athenaeum Romanum of 1676, and the entry shows that the details will not bear scrutiny. Wilton never became Archbishop of Armagh, despite a claim that Innocent III nominated him. His name appears in no reliable list of cardinals, despite a claim that Gregory IX created him one. The further claim that he held doctorates at Oxford, Cambridge, and Paris is dismissed as impossible, at least for Cambridge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right-honoura:
Sir John Sparrow David Thompson was a Canadian jurist who became his country's first Catholic prime minister. Born at Halifax, Nova Scotia, in 1844 to rigidly Protestant parents, he left school early. He studied law and shorthand from the age of fifteen, and was admitted to the bar in 1865. He married in 1870 and became a Catholic shortly after.

His rise was swift and unbroken. Alderman of Halifax in 1871, he entered the provincial assembly in 1877, became attorney-general in 1878, premier of Nova Scotia in 1882, and a Supreme Court judge that same year. As Canada's Minister of Justice from 1885, his speech on the Riel question in 1886 fixed his standing among the country's great parliamentarians. He served as legal adviser at the Washington Fisheries Commission, was knighted, became premier of Canada in 1892, and sat as a British arbitrator at Paris in 1893. He died suddenly at Windsor Castle in 1894.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right-of-excl:
The right of exclusion, in Latin Jus Exclusivae, was the claimed power of Catholic monarchs to veto a candidate for pope. Under it, Austria, France, and Spain could have their cardinal protector declare, before the decisive ballot, a given cardinal unacceptable to his government. The veto was first spoken, later written, and could be used only once in a conclave, so governments saved it for the last moment. A veto declared after the election had no standing.

Its history is traced from the ballot of exclusion, by which states blocked a candidate by holding back a third of the votes. Spain raised the formal claim in the conclaves of 1605. The term Jus Exclusivae appears in the conclaves of 1644 and 1655, when Cardinal Sacchetti was excluded in both. Treatises by Cardinals Albizzi and Lugo debated the claim. Later conclaves used it again, notably against Cardinal Rampolla in 1903, before Pius X abolished it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right-of-opti: In canon law, the right of option lets a cleric obtain a benefice, or church office with income, by his own choice rather than by appointment. A canon of long standing in a chapter could give up the prebend he held and take another that had fallen vacant, following the chapter's rules. A second form existed in France before 1789, where a prebendary holding two incompatible benefices could choose which to keep. The right still survives for cardinalitial titles, the titular churches assigned to cardinals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right-of-pres:
The right of presentation is the chief privilege of church patronage, the right to name a cleric for a vacant benefice. In gratitude for founding or endowing churches, the Church grants founders who wish it the right of patronage. Presentation means putting forward a suitable cleric to the church authorities. That gives the cleric a real claim to the post. The superior who must institute him cannot simply give it to someone else.

Forms of patronage differ between bodies and individuals. Ecclesiastical patronage belongs to chapters and similar bodies. Lay patronage belongs to laymen or clerics acting privately. The entry explains how presentation is exercised: no special form is required, but in practice it is written, often after a vote or agreement among co-patrons. A patron past the age of puberty acts personally or through an attorney, while a younger patron acts through a mother, guardian, or protector.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right-of-volu:
The legal right of voluntary association is traced here from ancient Greece to the modern world. A voluntary association means any group freely united for a common end, unlike a necessary association such as a conscript army or the state itself. The term covers bodies as different as a manufacturing company and a religious sodality. How civil authority treats such bodies has varied by age and country.

Under Solon, Athenians could form societies freely so long as they broke no public law, and Greek festivals and games nourished countless groups. Rome was stricter, requiring a senate or imperial decree, yet collegia for worship, amusements, politics, burials, and trades flourished from early republican days. After the union of Church and State in 325, religious orders prospered, and in the chaos after Rome's fall, small private societies grew into the feudal order. The entry follows this shifting balance into later centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-henrys:
Robert Henryson was a Scottish poet of the fifteenth century, counted among the most original of Chaucer's northern followers. Born probably between 1420 and 1430, he died about 1500. His birthplace, parentage, and schooling are unknown, though he may have studied abroad at Paris or Louvain. The earliest edition of his Fables, from 1570, calls him schoolmaster of Dunfermline.

He probably taught at the Benedictine abbey school there, held minor orders, and worked as a notary. In 1462 he joined the new University of Glasgow. His poems include the Testament of Cresseid, a tragic sequel to Chaucer's Troilus, Orpheus and Eurydice, thirteen Morall Fabillis of Esope in rhyme-royal, and shorter pieces. The pastoral dialogue Robene and Makyne is often ranked his finest work. A true lover of nature, he described it with care and vividness. His Fables were re-edited by Gregory Smith in 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-of-cou:
Robert of Courcon was an English cardinal and Paris chancellor who policed the university's teaching on Aristotle. Born at Kedleston, he studied at Oxford, Paris, and Rome. In 1211 he became Chancellor of the University of Paris, in 1212 Cardinal of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, and in 1213 legate to preach the crusade. In 1215 he headed a commission on errors at Paris.

He also fought heresy in France and followed the crusaders to Egypt as legate of Honorius III, dying at Damietta in 1218. His Summa on canon law and ethics treats usury at length. His intervention at Paris, amid confusion over Arabic translations of Aristotle, proscribed the philosopher's metaphysical and physical treatises with their summaries. At the same time his rescript again condemned David of Dinant and Amaury of Bene as pantheists, while permitting Aristotle's Ethics and logical works as texts. It also set rules for academic discipline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rockhampton:
Rockhampton is a diocese in Queensland, Australia, born from a vast missionary territory. In 1862 Father Duhig visited the infant settlement on the Fitzroy River and said its first Mass. In 1863 Dean Murlay became first resident pastor, his parish running north to Cooktown and south to Maryborough. He put up the first Catholic church, a wooden building still standing.

Sisters of Mercy from Brisbane founded a house in 1873. Rockhampton stayed part of Brisbane diocese until 1882, when it became a see of some 350,000 square miles. Its first bishop, Dr Cani, a native of the Papal States and former pro-vicar of North Queensland, was consecrated at Sydney in May 1882. He added priests, bought church sites, set aside 3,000 acres for a Mercy orphanage, and began St Joseph's Cathedral, which he did not live to see dedicated. He died in 1898 after sixteen years, famed for humility, simplicity, and love of the poor and orphans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roger-anderto:
Roger Anderton was a Catholic layman of Lancashire whose family kept a secret press alive. His father was Christopher Anderton of Lostock; James was his brother and Lawrence Anderton his nephew. His name recurs on the Lancaster Recusant Roll, and four of his large family became nuns. For a long time he was credited with writing works by his nephew Lawrence, issued under the name John Brereley, priest, and by other hands.

The entry corrects that view: Anderton seems merely to have edited the works and printed them at a secret press maintained and protected by various Andertons. A list of these publications survives among the Blundell of Crosby manuscripts. He is thought to have revived the press at Birchley after the inquisition that followed James Anderton's death and the confiscation of his books. His death is placed in 1640.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roger-bacon:
Roger Bacon, surnamed Doctor Mirabilis, was a thirteenth-century philosopher who championed positive science, languages, and physics. Born at Ilchester about 1214 to wealthy parents who backed Henry III and lost nearly all their property, he studied at Oxford and Paris. He taught at the Oxford Franciscan school. His masters included Richard Fitzacre, Edmund Rich, and above all Robert Grosseteste and Adam Marsh, with Petrus Peregrinus at Paris.

Drawn by physics, he entered the Franciscans about 1240, though dates of 1251 and 1257 are also given. Illness halted his work for two years. When he resumed, superiors gave him other duties and barred him from publishing outside the order without leave, on pain of losing the book and fasting on bread and water. The ban was general, not personal. It aimed at Gerard of Borgo San Donnino, whose unauthorized heretical work of 1254 prompted the Narbonne decree of 1260. Bacon died at Oxford, perhaps on 11 June 1294.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roscommon:
Roscommon, capital of County Roscommon, takes its origin and name from a monastery St Coman founded in the eighth century. It stood on a wooded point, a ros, amidst marshes. Ware and his copiers made Coman author of a rule observed through three-fourths of Connaught. This is wrongly deduced from records of dues collected by his successors as Lex Comani. With the King of Connaught's support, Coman's foundation held some pre-eminence.

Roscommon became a seat of learning and authority, with scholars and scribes celebrated in the national annals. Maol-Iosa, son of Toirdhealbhach O'Conchubhair, was abbot, and his father gave the monastery a piece of the true cross brought from Rome in 1123. When Irish monasteries took the great orders' rules, Roscommon's monks became Augustinian canons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-francis:
Saint Francis, properly Saint François de Sales in Quebec, was a Jesuit-run mission village near Pierreville that sheltered Native peoples driven from New England by colonial wars. Founded in 1683 at the falls of the Chaudière, it first took in Abnaki and Pennacook refugees, then moved to its later site in 1700. After Norridgewock was destroyed and Father Sebastian Rasle killed in 1724, most Abnaki settled there, and the village became a centre of Native hostility toward New England.

In 1759 a New England force under Major Rogers surprised and burned the settlement, killing 200 people, but it was soon rebuilt and remains one of Canada's oldest mission settlements. Its men later fought for Britain in the Revolutionary War and again in 1812. Father Joseph Aubéry, in charge from 1709 to 1755, mastered Abnaki and left a manuscript French-Abnaki dictionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-pierre-:
Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, the only French possession left in North America, form a small island group south of Newfoundland with an area of 177 square miles. Known to Breton and Basque fishermen and named by the time Jacques Cartier identified the islands in 1535, the group was first settled in 1604. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia covers a prefecture apostolic tossed between empires.

Ceded to England at Utrecht in 1712 and restored to France in 1763, the islands were seized three times by the English and handed back three times by treaty. They also sheltered Acadians fleeing Grand Pré and Louisbourg. Bishops from Quebec and missionaries from Placentia served the scattered fishing folk. The entry gives the islands' stormy political story alongside the patient work of building a Catholic community there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salmeron:
Alfonso Salmerón, Jesuit Bible scholar, was born at Toledo on 8 September 1515 and died at Naples on 13 February 1585. After studies at Alcalá and Paris he met Ignatius of Loyola through James Lainez, and with Lainez, Faber, and Francis Xavier he joined the first companions of Loyola in 1536. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a founder of the Society of Jesus.

The little company left Paris in November 1536, reached Venice that January, and went on to Rome, where Salmerón preached before the pope and won leave to take orders early. He served the poor and children at Siena, took solemn vows on 22 April 1541 at St Paul's Outside the Walls, and was then sent by Paul III on missions across Europe. His scriptural commentaries made him one of the order's first great scholars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salvation:
Salvation, from the Greek soteria and the Hebrew yeshuah, means in Scripture first of all rescue from tight straits and other evils into freedom and safety. At times it names God's help against Israel's enemies, at times blessing on the harvest. But since sin counts as the greatest evil, Scripture uses the word mainly for rescue from sin and what follows from it. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia treats the doctrine in two parts.

First comes the salvation of the human race, which God might have worked by simple pardon without the Incarnation of the Second Person of the Trinity, yet chose to work through Christ. Then comes salvation in each person: grace, faith, works, and final perseverance. The entry sets out the Catholic teaching step by step, answering objections and grounding each claim in Bible texts and the Fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samson:
Samson, whose Hebrew name means sun, was the last and most famous of the Judges of Israel, his story filling chapters thirteen to sixteen of Judges. After Jephthah's deliverance the Israelites fell back into evil and were handed to the Philistines for forty years. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia retells the biblical narrative with its customs explained.

An angel appeared to the barren wife of Manoah of Dan, promising a son who would free Israel. Mother and child were to avoid strong drink and unclean things, and no razor was to touch the boy's head, for he would be a Nazirite, one set apart for God. A second visit, ending in flame from a burnt offering, revealed the visitor's heavenly nature. Born as foretold, Samson grew under the spirit of the Lord, and the entry follows his exploits to his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samuel-eccles:
Samuel Eccleston, fifth archbishop of Baltimore, was born near Chestertown, Maryland, on 27 June 1801 and died at Georgetown on 22 April 1851. Son of an Episcopalian father, he came under Catholic influence when his widowed mother married a Catholic named Stenson, and at St Mary's College, Baltimore, he converted. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a convert who rose to lead American Catholicism.

Entering St Mary's Seminary in 1819 and ordained priest in 1825, he studied further at Issy in France, then returned to become vice-president and, two years later, president of St Mary's College. Consecrated coadjutor in 1834, he succeeded Archbishop Whitfield that same October and also administered Richmond until 1841. Many new churches rose in his term, and he gave freely from his own funds to build them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanction:
Sanction, from the Latin sancire, kin to sanctus, holy, means first the authoritative act by which a lawmaker gives a law its binding force. In that sense the law itself is called a sanction, and church laws are often called canonical sanctions, imposed on conscience and obedience. Its short entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia untangles a word used in several senses.

In modern speech any measure that pushes people to obey counts as a sanction, whether reward for keeping the law or penalty threatened for breaking it. Such measures cover laws that command action and laws that forbid it. Some sanctions spring from the law's own nature, like those of natural law, and are called internal. Others are added by the lawmaker's act, and are called external, moral, psychological, legal, or penal by origin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sarah-atkinso:
Sarah Atkinson, philanthropist and biographer, was born at Athlone in Ireland on 13 October 1823 and died at Dublin on 8 July 1893. Eldest daughter of John and Anne Gaynor, she grew up on the Shannon's western bank in the Roscommon part of Athlone. She moved with her family to Dublin at fifteen and finished her schooling there. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows grief turned to good works.

At twenty-five she married Dr George Atkinson, part owner of the Freeman's Journal. The death of her only child in his fourth year moved her to spend her life in charity. With her friend Ellen Woodlock she took up the women paupers of the South Dublin Union and opened a home where many became useful members of society. Her Drumcondra house became a haven for the charitable and a literary salon, where she wrote her praised life of Mary Aikenhead and many essays.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sarah-m-brown:
Sarah M. Brownson, daughter of Orestes A. Brownson, was born at Chelsea, Massachusetts, on 7 June 1839. She married William J. Tenney of Elizabeth, New Jersey, in 1873 and died at Elizabeth on 30 October 1876, aged only thirty-seven. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia praises a short writing life of unusual independence.

She wrote literary criticism for her father's Review and many articles, stories, and poems for Catholic magazines. Her books include Marian Elwood of 1863, At Anchor, a Civil War story of 1865, and Heremore Brandon of 1869. Her chief work, a life of Demetrius Gallitzin, prince turned priest, appeared in 1873. Her novels are called interesting, genuine, and original, free-spoken yet kindly, above all toward the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sarayacu-miss:
Sarayacú, the chief Franciscan mission of the Ucayali river country in Loreto department, north-east Peru, stood on a small western arm of the river, about 275 miles above its Amazon junction. Its name means River of the Wasp. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia explains how two orders divided the evangelisation of Peru's eastern forests.

Jesuits from Quito worked the Marañón and its northern tributaries, while Franciscans from Ocopa college, founded in 1712 near Jauja, took the middle and upper Huallaga and Ucayali. Father Narciso Girbal founded Sarayacú in 1791 with wild Setebo Indians as first colonists. Bands from other tribes soon joined, and the settlement grew fast into the region's mission centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scranton:
Scranton, a suffragan see of Philadelphia established on 3 March 1868, covers eleven counties in north-eastern Pennsylvania across 8,487 square miles. Its cathedral city, in the heart of anthracite country, counted 130,000 people in 1910, with Wilkes-Barre, Williamsport, Hazleton, Carbondale, and Pittston behind it. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows coal and immigration.

Pioneer Catholic settlers were chiefly Irish and German, but coal work later drew many Slav and Italian labourers, until they formed almost half the Catholic population. The first recorded priestly visit came in 1787, when James Pellentz travelled up the Susquehanna to Elmira, ministering to scattered Catholics. The entry follows parishes, schools, and bishops as a mining diocese grew from scattered settlers into a settled church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-secularizatio:
When a man or woman under solemn religious vows is allowed to live outside the cloister, canon law calls it secularization. The leave may last for a time or for good. The person still holds the core of religious profession. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry on church law draws the line carefully. It is a kindly permission, not a punishment like expulsion. It does not cancel the vows the way a full dispensation does.

Temporary leave and permanent leave work differently. Permanent secularization cuts the person off from the order's support. Yet the vows stay binding, with obedience now owed to a bishop. Much of the piece covers the rules that grew up around finding a receiving diocese, holding property, and barring quick returns to office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seduction:
Moral theology treats seduction as persuading a previously virtuous woman into unlawful sexual relations without force. This entry weighs what the seducer then owes in conscience. Two cases frame the discussion. In one, marriage was promised. In the other, it was not. Bodily harm itself cannot be repaid in kind, since its performance is impossible. A civil court may still impose a money penalty.

Where marriage was promised, the received teaching binds the man to marry her. This holds whether or not she is pregnant. She has kept her side of a bargain whose remaining side is not itself sinful. The rule holds even for a feigned promise. The entry notes cases it does not cover, such as a woman who could plainly see the promise was hollow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-septuagint-ve:
The Septuagint is the first translation of the Hebrew Old Testament into popular Greek, made before the Christian era. This long entry treats its importance, its origin, its later history and manuscripts, and its critical value. Its importance stands on three legs. It is the oldest translation of the Old Testament, priceless for correcting the Hebrew text. It spread messianic hope among Gentiles. It gave Greek the theological words that later carried the Gospel.

Tradition told of seventy-two translators sent by Jerusalem to Alexandria for Ptolemy Philadelphus, working in separate cells to one identical text. The entry tests that legend against the evidence. It finds a likely core. The Pentateuch was translated at Alexandria in the mid-third century BC. Later books were rendered at different times by different hands, in styles ranging from free to fiercely literal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sexton:
A sexton guards the church building, its treasures, vestments, and vessels, and, as an inferior minister, attends to burials, bell ringing, and similar offices. This entry traces the office back to the clerical order of ostiarii, or doorkeepers. They held the church keys, guarded the sacred building and its holy vessels, books, and vestments, opened the church, and summoned the faithful to the mysteries. Some were set to guard the bodies and shrines of martyrs.

The Council of Trent said the sexton or sacristan should be a cleric, though it allowed a married man who took the tonsure and wore clerical dress. By custom those conditions have lapsed, and the office is usually held by a layman today. In many cathedral churches of Austria and Germany, however, a priest still holds the title of sacristan or custos, supervising the fabric and the canons' residences.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sidon:
Sidon, a titular metropolis of Pamphylia Prima on the coast of Pamphylia, was a colony of Cumae in Aeolia. From the tenth century BC its coinage bore Athena, the city's patroness, with a Pamphylian legend. For paying tribute to Alexander they gained a Macedonian garrison. Commercial and warlike, with a strong navy, Sidon stood in constant rivalry with Aspendus.

In its waters the Rhodians beat the fleet of Antiochus the Great, commanded by Hannibal with Sidonian ships on the right wing. From then on Sidon served as a haunt of pirates and a notorious slave market, and Constantine Porphyrogenitus still called it a nest of pirates in the tenth century. Turkish invasions and failing water emptied it by degrees, and its deserted ruins, now Eski Adalia, show a temple, basilica, gymnasium, aqueduct, baths, theatre, and ramparts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simeon:
Simeon, second son of Jacob by Leah, stands as patronymic ancestor of the Jewish tribe of his name. The name's original sense is unknown, but Genesis offers an explanation from the verb to hear. Leah is quoted as saying, because the Lord heard that I was despised, he has given this also to me, and she called his name Simeon. Matching explanations for Levi and Judah follow in the next verses.

In Genesis 34, Simeon and his full brother Levi avenge their sister Dinah, humiliated by a Sichemite prince. By a strange ruse they render the town's men helpless, slaughter them, and plunder the city. Jacob blames the deed, at first for selfish reasons. Then, in his blessing of Genesis 49, he curses their stubborn fury and vows to divide and scatter them in Israel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sion:
Sion, a Swiss bishopric directly dependent on the Holy See, is the oldest diocese in Switzerland and among the oldest north of the Alps. Its see first stood at Octodurum, now Martigny. Tradition names a Bishop Oggerius as early as 300, but the first authenticated bishop is Theodore, dead in 391. Where Saint Maurice's abbey now stands, he built a church honoring Maurice and drew nearby hermits into common life.

Theodore also rebuilt Sion's church. The diocese moved its see to Sion in 589 under Saint Heliodorus, since floods often threatened Octodurum. Frequent disputes with Saint Maurice's monks over jurisdiction followed. Bishops later doubled as secular lords of Valais, until the Revolution ended those rights. The 1907 constitution names Catholicism the canton's religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-richard-s:
Richard Sutton, co-founder of Brasenose College, Oxford, of unknown birth date, died in September or October 1524. Younger son of Sir William Sutton of Sutton, Leicestershire, he gave himself to law, joined the Inner Temple, and prospered. By 1498 he was a privy councillor and steward of Sion monastery near London, to which he gave land. His life's chief work was building and endowing Brasenose College with Bishop Smyth of Lincoln.

Their plans were laid in 1508, and over the following years Sutton bought endowment estates in Middlesex, Leicestershire, Oxfordshire, and Essex, formally handing them to Brasenose in 1519. In May 1523 Brasenose Hall and Little University Hall, leased from the university, passed to the new college. His other gifts included a chantry at Macclesfield and donations to Corpus Christi College and Sion monastery. Henry VIII knighted him between May 1522 and March 1524.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-william-h:
William Hales Hingston, Canadian physician and surgeon born at Hinchinbrook near Huntingdon, Quebec, on 29 June 1829, died at Montreal on 19 February 1907. His father, an Irish lieutenant-colonel in the Royal 100th Regiment, died when his son was eighteen months old, leaving the family in debt on a military-service estate. Raised in poverty, Hingston won through his mother's efforts a place at Montreal's Sulpician College. 

He then studied medicine while still clerking and graduated from McGill in 1851. With nearly one hundred pounds saved, he sailed to Edinburgh, then famed for surgery teaching. He became a favorite of Simpson and Syme. In two years he visited every important medical center in Europe on very little money. Back in Montreal he built a large practice, aided by self-sacrifice in the cholera epidemic. He became surgeon to the Hôtel-Dieu in 1860, and first performed in America an operation the entry singles out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sister-irene-:
Catherine FitzGibbon, in religion Sister Irene, was born in London on 12 May 1823 and died in New York on 14 August 1896. At nine she emigrated to Brooklyn with her parents, and in 1850 she joined the Sisters of Charity at Mount Saint Vincent, New York, taking the name Irene. 

Many infants were left at the sisters' school and house doors, evidently hoping for special consideration. Noting their constant increase, Sister Irene proposed a foundling asylum of the European kind. Archbishop McCloskey approved, and in 1869 she was charged with carrying it out. She organized a women's society to raise funds. A house at 17 East Twelfth Street opened on 11 October 1869 with a crèche at its door, took its first infant that evening, and forty-four more within the month. Before her death she added Seton Hospital for incurable consumptives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
The Sisters of the Assumption, a congregation of French nuns devoted to teaching young girls, began in 1839. Eugénie Milleret de Bron, in religion Mother Marie-Eugénie de Jesus, founded it under the direction of Abbé Combalot, an orator inspired to establish the institute during a pilgrimage. Their aim joined thorough secular education with moral and religious training meant to bear fruit for generations.

The sisters wear a violet habit with a white cross on the breast and a violet cincture, with a white veil. On certain chapel occasions they add a white mantle with a violet cross on the shoulder. From France the congregation spread to England, Italy, Spain, and Nicaragua, and several communities devote themselves to Perpetual Adoration and teaching poor children. The mother-house stands at Auteuil near Paris, where daughters of distinguished European families studied alongside English and American pupils.

Founded at Quimper, Brittany, by Abbé François-Marie Langrez, the Sisters of the Perpetual Adoration join adoration of the Blessed Sacrament with educating orphan children. Langrez, once an apprentice rope-maker, conceived the work in December 1821 after two homeless little girls crossed his path. He placed them with Marguerite Le Maître, a domestic servant, and other orphans soon found shelter.

By 1826 Marguerite's home held an oratory and a dormitory of thirty beds, and the first chapel opened on 21 November 1829. Olympe de Moelien entered in 1832 and became superior in 1833, and the first sisters took the habit in January 1835 and vows in March 1836. Adoration begun in March 1836 became perpetual day and night in 1843. By 1882 the institute housed 400 orphan girls with 128 religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-snorri-sturlu:
Snorri Sturluson, historian born at Hvammr in 1178 and dead in 1241, was the foremost Icelandic historian of the Middle Ages, joining statesman and scholar. As a child he studied at Oddi under Saemund the Wise's grandson Ján Loptsson, learning the old northern gods, the saga of Odin, and Scandinavian history. A rich alliance gave him the money to take a leading part in politics, but it won him dangerous enemies, and King Haakon of Norway finally had him murdered.

Snorri's importance rests on his writings, above all Heimskringla, the chief authority for early Iceland and Scandinavia. Its primitive sections are largely vague saga narrative, and only its later history, to 1177, is reliable. The Sturlunga Saga was probably only partly his work. He probably also wrote the Younger Edda, a poetry textbook whose first part, Gylfaginning, retells northern mythology from early songs, sagas, and his own poetic ideas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-solicitation:
Solicitation, in canon law, is the crime of a priest using the sacrament of penance to draw another person into sins of lust. This entry sets out how the Church defined and punished that abuse. The offence covers soliciting before, during, or just after confession. It also covers soliciting on the occasion of confession, in the confessional itself, or in any place used for hearing confessions.

Papal legislation on the point was severe. The entry traces the key documents, from Gregory XV's Universi Gregis of 1622 to Benedict XIV's Sacramentum poenitentiae of 1721. Later decrees of the Holy Office carried the same condemnation forward. Readers get a clear, sober account of a grave abuse of a sacred rite, and of the legal machinery built to condemn it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-solomon:
Solomon, the second son of David by Bathsheba, inherited the throne of Israel over his older brothers and ruled for forty years. This long entry weighs his reign from the biblical books of Kings and Chronicles. Chosen as his father's favourite, though not the logical heir, he came to power at about eighteen. His reign stayed almost free of the turmoil that marked David's years.

The entry follows his wisdom, his building, his trade, and his later failings. It sets the splendour of his court beside the strains it placed on the kingdom. Readers looking for a full portrait of the king behind the Temple will find it here. So will readers seeking the proverbs and the visit of the Queen of Sheba, with the biblical narrative laid out and judged with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-speculation:
Speculation, in business language, means putting money at unusual risk for the chance of unusual gain, and this entry draws the line between enterprise and gambling. A coal merchant who stocks up before a hard winter and a miners' strike shows enterprise, taking only ordinary business risks. While a man who buys prairie land on faint hints of a boom is speculating.

More strictly, the word covers dealings in futures and options on the exchanges, especially when the parties trade on price movements rather than goods. The entry weighs the practice from a moral and economic view, giving readers a clear vocabulary for judging where bold business ends and mere wagering begins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spiritual-dir:
Spiritual direction, in the technical sense, is the Church's work of guiding the faithful toward eternal happiness. And this entry treats it as part of the commission to teach all nations. The Church exercises it in public teaching, by word and writing, and in private guidance fitted to each soul, though the term usually means the private kind.

Every adult member meets such direction in the sacrament of penance. Where the priest acts not only as judge, absolving or retaining sins confessed, but as director of conscience, bound to instruct penitents. The entry goes on to set out the qualities and duties of a good director, making it a practical guide for priests and for lay people seeking counsel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-abbon:
St. Abbon, or Abbo, was a Benedictine monk of Fleury-sur-Loire, born near Orleans about 945 and dead at Fleury on 13 November 1004. He was famed for learning and holiness in the stormy age of Hugh Capet and the three Ottos. This entry follows a scholar devoted to philosophy, mathematics and astronomy, called early to England to run the school of the new monastery at Ramsey in Huntingdonshire before returning to Fleury.

Chosen abbot after Oilbold's death, he faced a rival backed by king and bishop, a dispute of national weight settled by the famous Gerbert, later Pope Sylvester II, in Abbon's favour. He attended the Synod of St. Basolus near Reims, and the entry presents a monk whose books and backbone steadied a turbulent church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ammon:
St. Ammon, sometimes called Amun or Amus, was an Egyptian ascetic born about 350, and this entry tells a marriage that became a double vocation. Forced into marriage at twenty-two, he persuaded his wife on their wedding night to take a vow of chastity. They kept it faithfully while living together for eighteen years, until he became a hermit in the desert of Nitria and she founded a congregation of religious women in her own house.

Nitria, a mountain above a desolate region seventy miles south of Alexandria beyond Lake Mareotis, held fifty monasteries and five thousand monks by the end of the fourth century. Jerome called the place the City of God. Whether Ammon built the first monastery there is disputed, but his fame drew anchorites who raised cells on mountain and desert alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-benignus-o:
St. Benignus of Dijon was a martyr honoured as the patron saint and first herald of Christianity in Dijon, an old city in the territory of the Gallic tribe of the Lingones. This entry follows a man whose martyrdom in a third-century persecution is historical fact, and who was publicly honoured as a martyr. His feast falls on 1 November, and his name stands under that date in the so-called Martyrology of St. Jerome.

Early in the sixth century no particulars about Benignus's person and life were known at Dijon. The common people reverenced his grave, Gregory of Tours says, but Bishop Gregory of Langres wished to end that veneration, because he believed the grave belonged to a heathen. A night vision taught him the burial spot was the holy martyr Benignus's, and he had the tomb holding the sarcophagus restored and honoured.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bernard-of:
St. Bernard of Menthon was born in 923, probably in the castle of Menthon near Annecy in Savoy. He died at Novara in 1008. This entry follows a man descended from a rich, noble family who received a thorough education. He refused the honourable marriage his father proposed, choosing instead to devote himself to the Church's service. Under Peter, archdeacon of Aosta, he rapidly progressed and was ordained priest.

His learning and virtue made him archdeacon of Aosta in 966, with charge of the diocese's government under the bishop. The ignorance and idolatry still prevailing among the Alpine people moved him to devote himself to their conversion. For forty-two years he preached the Gospel to those people, carrying the light of faith even into many Lombard cantons, with numerous conversions and many miracles worked.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-caedmon:
St. Caedmon was author of biblical poems in Anglo-Saxon, date of birth unknown. He died between 670 and 680. This entry follows a poet whose share in the so-called Caedmonian poems modern scholarship has steadily narrowed. The events of his life, however, are definitively established by the painstaking Bede, who lived in nearby Wearmouth in the following generation.

Bede tells us that Caedmon, whose name is perhaps Celtic, or a Hebrew or Chaldaic pseudonym, was at first a labourer at the double monastery of Whitby. That monastery was founded in 657 by St. Hilda, a friend of St. Aidan. One night, when the monastery's servants were gathered for good fellowship, the harp went round from hand to hand. Caedmon, knowing nothing of poetry, left the company in shame, as he often had. He retired to the stable, where the entry's famous story of his inspiration begins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-edmund-cam:
Edmund Campion, English Jesuit and martyr, was Oxford's brightest star before he gave his gifts to a forbidden mission. Born in London on 25 January 1540, son of a Catholic bookseller, he shone as scholar, orator, and tutor, becoming junior proctor by 1568. Yet conscience pulled him from preferment toward Douai, Rome, and the Jesuits, with novitiate years at Prague and Brunn. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 follows him to execution at Tyburn on 1 December 1581.

Sent back with Robert Parsons as one of the first Jesuit helpers of the English mission, Campion preached, disputed, and rallied wavering Catholics under fierce government pressure. A vision at Brunn had already foretold his martyrdom to him. The entry captures both the scholar's brilliance and the soldierly courage of his short, hunted ministry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-elizabeth-:
Elizabeth Ann Seton founded the Sisters of Charity in the United States, turning personal loss into a new American institution. Born in New York City on 28 August 1774 to a prominent non-Catholic family, she lost her mother at three and was raised by a brilliant, virtuous father. Widowed young after her husband's death, she wrestled through spiritual perplexity toward Rome. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 follows her to her death at Emmitsburg on 4 January 1821.

Received into the Church on Ash Wednesday 1805, she moved to Emmitsburg to lead a school and community. Against her will, and while raising her own children, she was elected superior. The rule, adapted from the Sisters of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul, won approval in 1812, and she and eighteen sisters made vows on 19 July 1813. Her daughters Anna and others died young, yet the community endured.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-erhard-of-:
Erhard of Ratisbon, a seventh-century Irish bishop on the continent, is a figure where legend outweighs certain fact, and this entry says so. Born in Ireland, then called Scotia, he travelled as a missionary bishop and met the hermit Hildulf in the Vosges, called his brother, likely in a spiritual sense. Each is said to have founded seven monasteries. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 probably identifies him with an Abbot Erhard named in a Merovingian diploma of 684.

At Ratisbon he founded the nunnery of Niedermunster. Divine inspiration then recalled him to the Rhineland to baptize Odilia, blind from birth, who gained sight at the font. He reconciled her with her father, Duke Attich, who had disowned her. The entry keeps the reliable core small: an Irishman, a Ratisbon see, and a famous baptism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hilarion:
Hilarion, founder of anchoritic life in Palestine, carried Anthony's desert example to a new land. Born at Tabatha, south of Gaza, about 291 to pagan parents, he was sent as a boy to Alexandria's schools, where he became Christian. At fifteen, drawn by Anthony's renown, he retired to the desert and spent two months with the great father of anchorites. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death in Cyprus to about 371.

Jerome's biography is the chief source, with a lost letter from Epiphanius of Salamis, who knew Hilarion late in life, and a newer life edited by Papadopulos-Kerameus. Sozomen adds oral traditions from disciples, including the conversion of his own grandfather and a relative by Hilarion. Jerome fixes his age from Anthony's death in 356, when Hilarion was sixty-five. The entry follows a desert founder through biography and memory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-martin-of-:
A Spanish priest and Augustinian canon regular, Martin of Leon spent his life in the city of his birth. Born at Leon before 1150, he was schooled in the monastery of St Marcellus, travelled to Rome and Constantinople, and then took the religious habit on his return. When bishops secularised St Marcellus, he moved to the collegiate church of St Isidore in that city, where he died on 12 January 1203.

Commentaries on several Epistles and on the Apocalypse form the core of his surviving work, beside many discourses on varied subjects. The religious of St Isidore honoured him early with a chapel and a yearly feast, yet the Church never placed him officially on the roll of saints. Readers get a compact life of a learned Leonese churchman whose books outlived his modest local cult.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-olaf-haral:
Olaf Haraldson, king of Norway from 1015 to 1030, forced Christianity on his kingdom and died a martyr. Born in 995 to King Harald Grenske, he sailed as a viking to England in youth and there grew earnest in the Christian faith. Baptised about 1010 at Rouen, he won election as king and set out to root out heathenism.

He tore down temples, raised churches, and brought bishops and priests from England to organise the Norwegian Church on Anglo-Saxon lines. His harsh methods stirred the great clans, who called in Cnut of Denmark and drove Olaf out. Returning to reclaim his throne, he fell at Stiklestad on 29 July 1030. The entry presents a legislator king whose severity made him both saint and exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-pantaleon:
Pantaleon, a physician martyr who died about 305, is famed as a healer and protector of doctors. Legend makes him son of the rich pagan Eustorgius of Nicomedia, taught Christianity by his mother Eubula, then estranged from the faith. He studied medicine and became physician to Emperor Maximian, until the priest Hermolaus won him back.
