Envious colleagues denounced him during the Diocletian persecution. The emperor tried to save him by pressing apostasy, but Pantaleon confessed openly and healed a paralytic as proof of Christ. Condemned as a magician, he survived torches, boiling lead, the sea, and wild beasts in legend before beheading. His cult spread widely in East and West, and physicians still claim him as patron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-pascal-bay:
Pascal Baylon, a Spanish Franciscan lay brother, is remembered for ardent devotion to the Eucharist. Born at Torre-Hermosa in Aragon on 24 May 1540, the feast of Pentecost called in Spain the Pasch of the Holy Ghost, he took his name from that day. His parents were virtuous peasants, and from seven to twenty-four he worked as a shepherd.

Received among the Alcantarine Franciscans, he lived in contemplation and self-sacrifice, famed for charity to the poor and unfailing courtesy. Travelling through France, he defended the Real Presence against a Calvinist preacher and narrowly escaped a Huguenot mob. Though poorly educated, people of every station sought his counsel. He died at Villa Reale on 15 May 1592, also a Whitsunday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-samson:
Samson, a Welsh bishop and confessor, wandered from Llantwit to Ireland and on to Brittany as a miracle-working abbot. Born in South Wales to Amon of Dyfed and Anna of Gwynedd, he was dedicated to God as an infant and raised by Illtyd at Llantwit Major. Ordained deacon and priest by Dubricius, he sought greater austerity in another monastery and became its abbot.

Irish monks returning from Rome impressed him so deeply that he sailed with them to Ireland, received an Irish monastery's submission, and later sent an uncle to rule it. Returning to Wales, he founded a lonely cell on the banks of the Severn, far from the haunts of men. He died on 28 July 565, famed as a worker of miracles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-serapion:
Serapion, bishop of Antioch from 190 to 211, is known chiefly through theological writings cited by Eusebius. Eusebius names a private letter to Caricus and Pontius against the Montanist heresy. He names a treatise to Domninus, who in persecution had left Christianity for Jewish will-worship. He also names a work on the Docetic Gospel ascribed to Peter.

In that last work Serapion warned the Christian community of Rhossus in Syria against the Gospel's erroneous character, after first allowing its reading. Eusebius quotes short extracts from the first and third works and thinks others may have existed. Jerome and Socrates add notices. Serapion is commemorated on 30 October. The entry gathers a bishop known by his pen rather than his deeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-state-of-wash:
Washington, the Evergreen State, sixteenth in size and twenty-ninth admitted to the Union, is named for the first president. Its total area holds 69,127 square miles. The old territory was formed by Congress on 2 March 1853 from Oregon Territory. It lay south of the 49th parallel. It stretched north of the Columbia's main channel to the 46th parallel and the Rockies.

Since Idaho's formation in 1863 the state lies between 45 degrees 32 minutes and 49 degrees north. It spans 117 to 124 degrees west. Its constitution was adopted at Olympia on 22 August 1889. The article traces exploration, settlement, government, resources, and education, then turns to Catholic history: missions, dioceses of Seattle and Spokane, parishes, and schools. It serves as a compact reference for a young Pacific state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-of-bo:
Stephen of Bourbon, a Dominican preacher and inquisitor, preserved medieval heresies and folklore in a preacher's handbook. Born at Belleville in the Lyons archdiocese toward the twelfth century's end, he was schooled by Mâcon's cathedral clergy, studied at Paris about 1220, and shortly after entered the Order of Preachers.

From 1230 he worked for many years as preacher and inquisitor across Lyonnais, Burgundy, Franche-Comté, Savoy, Champagne, Lorraine, Auvergne, Languedoc, and Roussillon. In his De septem donis Spiritus Sancti, or Tractatus de diversis Materiis Praedicabilibus, he gathered much useful matter from practical experience. Its most valuable parts were published at Paris in 1877 by Lecoy de la Marche as Anecdotes historiques. Taken whole, his work gives a clear view of the age's sects and superstitions. He died in 1261.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-studion:
Studion was the most important monastery of Constantinople, standing near the Propontis in the Psamathia quarter. Founded in 462 or 463 by the consul Studios, it was dedicated to John the Baptist. Its monks came from the Acoemetae, and its laws and customs later served as models for Mount Athos and many Byzantine houses.

Its monks stood loyal in the Acacian schism of 484 to 519 and through the iconoclast storms of the eighth and ninth centuries, though emperors drove them out more than once. Abbot Sabbas defended images at Nicaea in 787, Theodore of Studion brought the house its greatest fame and fostered study, and Naucratius restored discipline after the dispute ended. Only its church survives today, now a mosque.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-subdeacon:
The subdiaconate is the lowest of the major orders in the Latin Church. This entry defines it as the power to carry the chalice with wine to the altar, prepare what is needed for the Eucharist, and read the Epistles to the people. Theologians generally deny that Christ instituted it, and Scripture and the Apostolic Fathers mention only bishops, priests, and deacons.

Urban II at Benevento in 1091 called only diaconate and priesthood sacred orders, and Gratian states that the Church herself instituted subdeacons and acolytes over time. Trent's words about apostolic functions mean the duties were once part of the diaconate, later handed to lesser ministers as deacons grew overloaded. After ordination the subdeacon owed celibacy and the daily Office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-subreption: Subreption, in canon law, is the hiding of facts that law or custom requires an applicant to state when seeking a rescript, a written papal grant. Its effect matches obreption, the opposite fault of alleging what is false. It may be deliberate and malicious, or it may come only from ignorance or oversight. It may strike at the main reason for the grant, or merely at a secondary motive. For its effect on the grant's validity, the entry points readers to Rescripts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-supernatural-:
Supernatural adoption means God's gratuitous taking of a human being as his own child and heir. This entry asks whether the phrase is mere figure, what authority backs its reality, and what its nature and parts may be. Scripture, tradition, and theologians are weighed in turn to answer.

The Old Testament, compared by Paul to childhood and bondage, holds no text that conclusively points to adoption of the individual soul. Texts calling Israel God's son speak of the chosen people as a whole. Only the New Testament, with the fullness of time and the Redeemer's coming, reveals the privilege plainly, and the entry traces that revelation through the Gospels and Paul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-superstition:
Superstition, from roots meaning to stand in terror of deity or to pray that children survive, is defined by Thomas Aquinas as a vice against religion by excess. This entry unpacks that definition: superstition does not outdo true religion in worship, but gives divine worship to beings other than God, or gives it to God in an improper manner. Religion stands midway between excess and the defect of irreligion.

Four species follow: improper worship of the true God, idolatry, divination, and vain observances including magic and occult arts. Worship turns improper when incongruous elements are added to approved rites, idolatrous when creatures are treated as divinities, and divination when rites are used to pry future events from creatures. Closing pages weigh the forces that keep superstition alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sydney-hodgso:
Sydney Hodgson was a lawyer and martyr of unknown birth, executed at Tyburn on 10 December 1591. A convert to the Church, he was present in 1591 when Father Edmund Jennings said Mass at the London house of Swithin Wells. Topcliffe the pursuivant and his men burst in at the very moment of consecration.

Hodgson and other gentlemen of the congregation blocked the intruders until Mass ended, then gave themselves up. Tried on 4 December, his only charge was receiving and relieving priests and being reconciled to Rome. Offered life for a promise of occasional conformity to the Established Church, he chose death for his religion instead, and was condemned and executed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synaxarion:
The Synaxarion is a liturgical book of the Byzantine Church whose meaning changed over time. At first it was an index to the biblical and other lessons read in church, matching the Latin Capitulare. Then it grew to hold the full texts of those lessons, though for the Liturgy itself the Gospel and Apostle books took its place.

Since Byzantine Office lessons are always saints' lives, the Synaxarion became a collection of short lives and feast accounts, much like the Roman Martyrology's second nocturn lessons gathered in one book. Many medieval copies survive, valuable for church history, with Symeon Metaphrastes as chief collector. Basil II ordered a revision, and today the book lives inside the Menaia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-temptation:
Temptation, from Latin tentare, to try or test, is taken here as an incitement to sin. It may come by persuasion or by some offered good. It may be merely external, as in Christ's desert encounter after forty days of fasting. It may also be internal, a real assault on a person's will power. It sometimes springs from the propensity to evil left by original sin. Sometimes the Devil supplies it, stirring the soul's lower powers.

Temptation is not itself sin. However vivid the image or strong the inclination, without consent of the will there is no sin. Sin in any grade is a deliberate act of the will. Attack is not surrender, a comfort for souls mistaking fierce assaults for falls. Temptations are fought by avoiding occasions, by prayer, and by humble distrust of self with confidence in God. Sometimes the best resistance is indirect, turning attention elsewhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-abbey-of-:
The Abbey of Abingdon, in Berkshire, England, dates to 675. Cyssa, viceroy of Kinwine, King of the West Saxons, or his nephew Heane founded it. It honoured the Virgin Mary, for twelve Benedictine monks. Endowed by West Saxon kings, it grew in importance and wealth until Danes destroyed it in Alfred's reign. Alfred sequestered its estates because the monks had not requited him for beating their enemies. A collection of 136 charters from Saxon kings survives.

Among its abbots were St Ethelwold, later Bishop of Winchester in 954, and Richard de Hendred, appointed with the king's consent in 1262. Hendred wore mitre and pontificals on Trinity feast in 1268, and Willis supposes him the first so privileged. He attended the Council of Lyons in 1272. The last abbot, Thomas Pentecost, alias Rowland, was among the first to acknowledge Royal Supremacy. He surrendered the monastery in 1538, receiving Cumnor manor for life, with revenues valued at £1,876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-abominati:
The abomination of desolation matters chiefly because Matthew and Mark give its appearance in the Holy Place, or where it ought not, as Christ's signal for flight from Judea. The phrase itself is obscure. Interpreters turn to Daniel's Hebrew, since Matthew cites Daniel on the abomination, and the Greek phrase renders literally the Hebrew shíqqûç shômem. Scholars still disagree on the terms' sense.

Most read shíqqûç, usually rendered abomination, as anything pertaining to idolatrous worship. Others take it as a god's name. Most render shômem as desolation, others as a ravager, or as a participle meaning that maketh desolate. A suggestion reads the phrase as standing for bá'ál shámáyîm, Baal of heaven, a title in Phoenician and Aramaic inscriptions. It is the equivalent of Zeus or Jupiter, altered in Daniel through Jewish aversion to a pagan god's name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-american-:
A secret American society that stirred trouble across the northern states between 1891 and 1897 is the subject here. Known as the A.P.A., it spread anti-Catholic lectures and literature and worked against the election of Catholics to public office. Its oaths, printed in 1893 and 1894 after leaks and admissions by former members, bound men to put political power in Protestant hands alone.

Henry Bowers, a lawyer from Clinton, Iowa, founded the first council there on 13 March 1887. From that small start the movement swelled, won allies in politics and the press, and then faded as its claims were exposed and its influence broke. The entry charts that rise and fall with dates, names, and the society's own published rituals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-authorize:
King James's Bible, formally the Authorized Version, is the English translation at the centre of this entry. Produced by a commission appointed by James I, it remains in general use among English-speaking non-Catholics. To explain its birth, the entry first surveys earlier English Scriptures, from Bede's deathbed work on John's Gospel to the Wyclif Version of about 1380, made from the Vulgate before later revisions.

Gasquet's claim that the Wyclif text was Catholic in origin rather than Wyclif's own receives attention, along with Tyndale, Coverdale, and the Geneva Bible. Then come the translators of 1611, their rules, their sources, and their revision history. It is a clear road through four centuries of English Bible-making.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-biblical-:
A Roman committee charged with guarding the sound reading and defence of Scripture is described here, formally the Pontifical Commission on the Bible. Leo XIII created it by the letter Vigilantiae on 30 October 1902, to carry out the programme of his encyclical Providentissimus Deus on biblical study. Cardinals lead it, aided by consultors drawn from across the world.

First appointed in August 1901 with three cardinals and twelve consultors, it grew after formal establishment to five cardinals, including Rampolla, Satolli, and Merry del Val, with forty-three consultors by June 1907. Its task, its decrees, and its place among Roman congregations fill the entry, a concise guide to the body that set the rules for Catholic biblical scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-catholic-:
Catholic school leaders across the United States joined forces in the group described here. It covers seminaries, colleges, and schools, plus all friends of Catholic schooling. Bishop Conaty of the Catholic University first called seminary heads and teachers to meet at Saint Joseph’s Seminary, New York, in May 1898.

Philadelphia followed in 1899, then a fresh start at Saint Louis in 1904 at Bishop O’Connell’s urging. A like group of Catholic colleges and universities, called by Conaty at Chicago in April 1899, joined the fold. Yearly meets, sections, and printed reports made the group a hub for courses, books, and teacher training.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-counter-r:
Catholic revival from Pius IV's pontificate in 1560 to the Thirty Years' War's close in 1648 is the movement surveyed here under the name Counter-Reformation. Protestant historians coined the term, only lately taken up by Catholic handbooks. It misleads in one way: reform began inside the Catholic Church, and Luther himself was a Catholic reformer before turning Protestant.

Nine heads organise the account. They cover meaning of the term, Catholic fortunes at low ebb, Ignatius and Jesuits as pioneers, Trent's council, three great reforming popes, missions, progress in European states, church literature, and retrospect. Saints, schools, and seminaries rebuilt a shaken Church, and the entry weighs gains and limits with sober balance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-elevation:
Lifting of the Host for adoration, the Elevation of the Mass, is the rite whose late birth this entry traces. Eastern liturgies, notably Byzantine, show the consecrated Host with words Holy things to the holy, but that matches our Ecce Agnus Dei as prelude to communion, not Elevation proper. Western lifting at omnis honor et gloria, just before the Pater Noster, dates from the ninth century or earlier.

That earlier lifting likely invited adoration when the great consecratory prayer from Preface to Pater Noster closed. Showing of Host, and still more Chalice, to the people after Hoc est corpus meum appears no earlier than the twelfth century's close. Eudes de Sully, Bishop of Paris from 1196 to 1208, seems to have ordered it, and bells, lights, and genuflections grew around the moment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-feast-of-:
March 25 brings the feast examined here, the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, also known in old calendars as the Feast of the Incarnation and the Beginning of Redemption. In the East, where Mary's share in redemption earns its own feast on December 26, the Annunciation ranks as a feast of Christ. In the Latin Church it honours Mary.

Its birth likely falls shortly before or after the Council of Ephesus in about 431. Unknown at the Synod of Laodicea in 372, it appears in Proclus of Constantinople, who died in 446, and in the Gelasian Sacramentary of the seventh century. Spread, liturgy, and art follow, tracing a feast that joined Christmas in the Church's year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-incarnati:
Word made Flesh, the mystery at Christianity's centre, receives systematic treatment here in three parts: fact, nature, and effects. Old and New Testament proofs open the case, with tradition's witness behind them, before the human nature of Christ and the hypostatic union, one Person in two natures, take focus. Latin incarnatio, from caro or flesh, matches Greek sarkosis, rooted in John chapter 1, verse 14.

Heresies that split the Person or blurred the natures, Nestorianism, Monophysitism, and Monothelitism, are refuted in turn. Effects follow: on Christ's body and soul, on adoration of his humanity, and on the whole order of grace. It is dogmatic theology at its most thorough and most lucid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-orders-of:
Orders honouring the Annunciation, chiefly the Annunciades, are described here. Jeanne de Valois, daughter of Louis XI and wife of the Duke of Orléans, later Louis XII, founded the penitential order after her marriage was annulled. Retiring to Bourges against her confessor's opposition and papal counsellors' doubts, she pursued her design with steady resolve.

Her Rule, the Ten Virtues of the Blessed Virgin, set imitation of Mary as the order's aim. Alexander VI confirmed it in 1501, five members took the veil on 8 October 1502, and Jeanne herself professed on 4 June 1503. Gabriel Nicolai, renamed Gabriele Maria, revised the constitutions for Leo X, who placed the order under Franciscan jurisdiction in 1517.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-reformati:
Western Europe's sixteenth-century religious revolt is surveyed here from causes to consequences. Ostensibly aiming at internal renewal, the movement in fact broke from the Church and dropped principal Christian beliefs, in the entry's Catholic judgment. Causes reach back to the fourteenth century, though doctrine stayed pure, saintly lives remained frequent, and medieval institutions ran their course.

Civil and profane pressures, not doctrine, explain most unhappy conditions, the entry argues. Reformers' original ideas, methods of spread, national histories, varied forms, and results follow in turn. Luther, Calvin, and their heirs each receive treatment, closing with an assessment of what the revolt cost and changed across Christendom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-royal-dec:
A solemn denial of Catholic faith, forced on each British king or queen, is the theme here. Under the Bill of Rights of 1689 and the Act of Succession of 1700, each new monarch, until quite late, spoke it before Lords and Commons met. It also went by the names King’s Protestant Declaration and Declaration against Transubstantiation.

Coronation Oath, a name often misused for it, means something else: vows to rule justly and uphold the Protestant Reformed Religion set up by law. Catholics raised no grave qualm over that form. The Royal Declaration, by contrast, long stood as a sore grievance and a slur on millions of loyal subjects. Its past and final reform close the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-seal-of-c:
Secrecy of confession, guarded by deposition and worse, is the law expounded here from Gratian to Lateran IV. Gratian's Decretum, compiled about 1151, declares that a priest who dares publish a penitent's sins be deposed, adding lifelong ignominious wandering for the violator. Canon 21 of the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 bound the whole Church in sterner terms.

Priests must beware, by word, sign, or any manner whatever, of betraying the sinner. Wiser counsel may be sought only cautiously, with no mention of person. Violators face deposition from priestly office and confinement in a monastery for perpetual penance. Cases, exceptions, and moral reasoning fill a long and rigorous entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theobald-stap:
Kilkenny priest Theobald Stapleton, English by descent yet Irish-born, earns this brief entry for one pioneering book. Nothing survives of his career beyond priesthood in Flanders and a Brussels publication of 1639: Catechismus seu doctrina christiana latino-hibernica, the first book printing Irish in Roman type.

His purpose was to promote Irish in religious literature, and an appendix of nineteen sections taught readers how to read Irish. Sources Meehan on Irish Franciscan monasteries and Moore in the Dictionary of National Biography preserve the record. For historians of Irish print, Stapleton marks the moment the language stepped from Gaelic script into Roman letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-bals:
Greek canonist Theodore Balsamon, guardian of the laws at Constantinople, is the jurist examined here. Born in the twelfth century's second half at Constantinople, dying there after 1195, he served as deacon nomophylax and, from 1178 to 1183 under Patriarch Theodosius, ran all ecclesiastical trials. In 1193 he became Greek Patriarch of Antioch.

His Scholia, commentary on Photius's Nomocanon, first printed in Latin at Paris in 1561 and Basle in 1562, then Greek and Latin at Paris in 1615, remains his best work. Rhalli and Potli's Athens collection of 1852 to 1860 reprinted it. Balsamon insists on existing laws, gives canons precedence over civil constitutions, and shows animosity toward Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theological-d:
What counts as a binding definition of faith is the question at the heart of this entry. Vatican Council's fourth session, chapter four, taught papal infallibility in solemn terms. When the Roman Pontiff speaks ex cathedra, as pastor and teacher of all Christians, he defines a doctrine of faith or morals. He does so by supreme apostolic authority, for the whole Church to hold, with God's aid as promised to Peter.

From that teaching comes the notion of definition in theology, distinct from philosophy or canon law. It is a final decision by the supreme teaching voice, settling a faith or morals question and binding the whole Church. Four marks must meet: supreme authority, ex cathedra intent, faith or morals matter, and a will to bind all the faithful. History and cases illustrate each mark.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-abingt:
Thomas Abington, also called Habington, was an English antiquarian who lived from 1560 to 1647. His father served as treasurer to Queen Elizabeth, and Thomas studied at Oxford, Reims and Paris. He spent six years in the Tower of London after being accused, with his brother Edward, of joining the Babington plot to free Mary Queen of Scots.

After release he retired to Hinlip Castle, where he sheltered the Jesuits Henry Garnett and Oldcorne, men accused over the Gunpowder Plot. Condemned to death for that shelter, he saw the sentence changed to exile through his son-in-law Lord Monteagle. His History of Edward IV appeared after his death, alongside a translation of Gildas and manuscript histories of Worcester.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-andert:
Thomas Anderton was an English Benedictine monk born in Lancashire in 1611, the sixth son of a family that stayed Catholic through persecution. He made his profession at St. Edmund's monastery in Paris in 1630 and was ordained priest six years later. Offices followed in quick order: novice-master, sub-prior, prior of St. Edmund's, definitor, and secretary to the chapter.

From 1661 to 1666 he served as prior of St. Benedict's at Saint Malo, then returned to lead St. Edmund's again. Sent on the English mission, he died at Saxton Hall in Yorkshire in 1671. His one surviving book, a history of the iconoclasts under the Byzantine emperors, appeared in the year of his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-bouqui:
Thomas Bouquillon, a Belgian theologian born at Warneton in 1840, became one of the leading moral theologians of his day. He studied philosophy at Roulers and theology at Bruges, was ordained in Rome in 1865, and took a doctorate two years later. After teaching at Bruges and Lille, he retired to Maredsous to prepare a new edition of his treatise on fundamental moral theology.

In 1889 he accepted the chair of moral theology at the Catholic University of America in Washington, where he taught until his death in 1902. Colleagues praised his vast learning in theology, church history, canon law and bibliography, and his quiet, simple habits. His work helped lift moral theology from a set of compiled conclusions to a serious science.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-codrin:
Thomas Codrington, a Catholic priest who died about 1691, is chiefly remembered for trying to bring a new institute for secular priests into England. Educated and ordained at Douai, he taught humanities there before serving Cardinal Howard in Rome as chaplain and secretary. He joined Holzhauser's Bavarian institute for secular priests living in community.

Back in England in 1684, he became a royal chaplain under James II and worked, with John Morgan, to plant the institute among English priests living together under their bishop. Cardinal Howard urged the clergy to join, and some progress followed. The Revolution of 1688 cut the effort short, and Bishop Giffard later suppressed the institute in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-of-bec:
Thomas of Beckington, Bishop of Bath and Wells, was born at Beckington, Somerset, about 1390 and died at Wells in 1465. Educated at Winchester from 1404 and New College, Oxford, from 1406, he became a skilled canon lawyer and dean of the Arches in 1423. He also served often as an English ambassador abroad.

His influence with the young Henry VI won him the post of lord privy seal in 1442, and the next year the pope named him Bishop of Bath and Wells. Consecrated at the new foundation of Eton College in October 1442, he rebuilt the episcopal palace at Wells, improved the city, and gave generously to Winchester School and Lincoln College, Oxford.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-of-ecc:
Thomas of Eccleston, thirteenth-century Franciscan chronicler, entered the order about 1232 and studied at Oxford in the 1230s. His dates of birth and death are unknown, and he calls himself simply Brother Thomas; the name of Eccleston comes from Bale. After 1240 he was stationed at the London convent, apparently holding no office in the order.

His fame rests on De Adventu Fratrum Minorum in Angliam, a chronicle of the friars' coming to England under Agnellus of Pisa in 1224, running to about 1258. He spent twenty-six years gathering material, mostly from personal knowledge and spoken reports. Rough notes rather than a finished history, the chronicle still gives a vivid and reliable picture of the heroic early years of the English Franciscans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-presto:
Thomas Preston, a Benedictine also known as Roger Widdrington, died in the Clink prison on 5 April 1640. He studied at the English College in Rome under the Jesuit Vasquez, was professed at Monte Cassino in 1590, and was sent on the English mission in 1603, landing at Yarmouth. He lived with Dom Sigebert Buckley, last survivor of the Westminster monks, until Buckley's death in 1610.

Preston was indicted for being a priest and spent years in prison, at the Clink and at the Archbishop of Canterbury's palace at Croydon. Under the name Widdrington he wrote in defence of King James's oath of allegiance, against the Jesuits, a position many Benedictines and secular priests shared. Late in life he seems to have changed his views on the oath.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-scott-:
Thomas Scott Preston, Vicar-General of New York, was born at Hartford, Connecticut, in 1824 and died at New York in 1891. A serious and zealous youth, he trained at the Episcopal seminary in New York, led its High Church party, and was ordained deacon in 1846 and presbyter in 1847. He served at Trinity, the Annunciation and Holy Innocents, hearing confessions and urging frequent Communion.

Deep study of the Fathers convinced him that the branch theory, which treated Anglicanism as a branch of the one Church, could not stand. He was received into the Catholic Church in November 1849 without ever having read a Catholic book or spoken to a priest. Ordained in 1850, he became pastor at Yonkers, then secretary to the archbishop, and rose to vicar-general, chancellor and prothonotary apostolic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-staple:
Thomas Stapleton, a controversialist born at Henfield, Sussex, in 1535, became one of the ablest Catholic defenders of his generation. Educated at Canterbury, Winchester and New College, Oxford, where he became a fellow in 1553, he left England at Elizabeth's accession rather than conform. He studied theology at Louvain and Paris, and in 1563 refused Bishop Barlow's summons to deny the pope, losing his Chichester prebend.

In 1568 he joined Allen at Douai and helped found the English college there, lecturing in theology and giving his salary to its support. He took a doctorate with Allen in 1571, briefly entered the Jesuits in 1584, and in 1590 Philip II made him professor of Scripture at Louvain. He spent his incomes relieving needy English Catholics and died at Louvain in October 1598.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-stephe:
Thomas Stephen Buston, a Jesuit missionary and author born in the Diocese of Salisbury in 1549, worked in India until his death at Goa in 1619. He entered the Jesuit novitiate in October 1576 and sailed for India the next year, landing at Goa in October 1578. Settling on the island of Salsette, he became superior of the Jesuits there in 1584 and held the post for thirty-five years.

Buston wrote to teach and convert the local people, and his books are the earliest known to have been printed in Hindustan. They include a grammar of the Canara language and a Christian doctrine in the Brahman language. He also wrote a discourse on the life of Christ and the Purana, poems in an Indian tongue on the mysteries of Christianity. At his death he was widely honoured as an apostle and a saint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-worthi:
Thomas Worthington, third president of Douai College, was born at Blainscough Hall, Lancashire, in 1549 and died at Biddulph Hall in 1627. From a wealthy Catholic family, he studied at Brasenose College, Oxford, then went to Douai in 1573 to study theology. Ordained in 1577, he taught the Roman catechism at Douai and later laboured in England, teaching the ignorant poor with zeal.

Seized at Islington in 1584 after betrayal, he spent over two months in the Tower's pit, then was banished with twenty other priests in 1585. He later became president of Douai, but a visitation in 1612 found studies disordered, discipline slack and finances crippled. Summoned to Rome in 1613, he was replaced by Dr. Kellison, given a pension, and returned to the English mission in 1616.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thundering-le:
The Thundering Legion is the name given to the Twelfth Legion after a storm saved Marcus Aurelius's army in 174. Marching against the Quadi, the Romans were parched with thirst and near defeat when the legion's Christian soldiers prayed for help. A heavy thunderstorm broke, refreshing the Romans and scattering the barbarians, and the emperor gave the legion the surname Fulminata, meaning thundering.

Christian writers from Tertullian onward told the tale as a miracle, and Eusebius cites Apollinaris, a contemporary, in its favour. Pagan writers also record the storm but credit the emperor's prayers or the Egyptian magician Arnuphis. The entry weighs both traditions, the decree said to have ended persecution, and the legion's true history, separating legend from what the sources actually prove.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-transfigurati:
The Transfiguration of Christ is the high point of his public life, as his Baptism opens it and his Ascension closes it. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell it in full, while Peter and John, two of its witnesses, allude to it. About a week after Caesarea Philippi, Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain apart, where he was transfigured before their eyes.

Matthew and Mark use the word metemorphothe, rendered transfiguratus est in the Vulgate. The Synoptics explain it: his face shone as the sun, and his garments turned white as snow, or as light in the Greek text. That brightness flowed from his divinity shining within. Moses and Elias, Law and Prophets, stood beside him, and the Father proclaimed him his beloved Son, strengthening the three friends for the Passion he had just foretold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trenton:
A diocese created on 15 July 1881, suffragan of New York, covering fourteen counties of New Jersey across about 5,756 square miles. Its territory lay under New York and Philadelphia until Newark took the whole state in 1853, and the new diocese holds the entire Jersey coast from Sandy Hook to Cape May Point.

The first Mass in its territory was said at Woodbridge about 1672, and Trenton itself gained its first congregation and church in 1814. Its first bishop was Michael Joseph O'Farrell, born at Limerick in 1832, a Sulpician ordained in 1855 who had taught dogmatic theology at Montreal before coming to New Jersey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tucson:
A diocese, suffragan of Santa Fe, covering Arizona and the southernmost counties of New Mexico across 131,212 square miles, mostly desert. Its Catholic population is about 48,500, mostly Mexicans, served by 43 priests in 27 parishes, with 43 missions, 100 stations, 7 academies, 10 parochial schools and 5 hospitals.

Arizona belonged to the Mexican Diocese of Durango until the Gadsden Purchase of 1853, joined Santa Fe in 1859, became a vicariate in 1868 and a diocese in 1897. Its first vicars, Salpointe and Bourgade, both died as archbishops of Santa Fe, and Bishop Henry Granjon, consecrated at Baltimore in 1900, succeeded them. The mission was founded by French missionaries and stayed mostly in French hands, helped by Franciscan Fathers and several orders of sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
The University of Avignon, lasting from 1303 to 1792, grew from the city's existing schools and was formally set up in 1303 by a bull from Boniface VIII. Beside Boniface, King Charles II of Naples stands among its first great protectors and benefactors. The law faculty, both civil and ecclesiastical, existed almost alone at first and always stayed the university's most important department.

Pope John XXIII erected a faculty of theology in 1413, though its students stayed few for a long time. The faculty of arts never gained great weight, and medicine developed notably only in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The Bishop, from 1475 the Archbishop, of Avignon served as chancellor, while the vice-legate, usually a bishop, stood for the civil power. The entry closes with the university's decline and suppression in the Revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-christoph:
Christopher Buxton was a priest and martyr born in Derbyshire, who died at Canterbury on 1 October 1588. A pupil of Nicholas Garlick at Tideswell grammar school in the Peak District, he trained for the priesthood at Reims and Rome and took ordination in 1586. He left Rome a year later, and soon after reaching England he was seized and condemned to death for his priesthood.

He suffered at Oaten Hill, Canterbury, with Robert Wilcox and Edward Campion. Because he was so young, his captors hoped the sight of his companions' brutal killing might shake him, and they offered him life if he would conform to the new religion. He answered bravely that he would not buy a corruptible life at such a price, and that with a hundred lives he would gladly give them all for his faith.

Christopher Robinson was born at Woodside near Westward in Cumberland at an unknown date and executed at Carlisle on 19 August 1598. He entered the English College at Reims in 1589, was ordained priest, and was sent on the mission in 1592. Two years later he witnessed the condemnation and execution of the martyr John Boste at Durham and wrote a vivid account of it.

That account survives in print from a seventeenth-century transcript in the Catholic Record Society's first volume, pages 85 to 92. His labours lay mainly in Cumberland and Westmoreland, though nothing is known of their details. Arrested at last and jailed at Carlisle, he faced Bishop Robinson, perhaps a kinsman, who pressed him to conform and save his life. He refused and suffered under the statute against priests.

Christopher Wharton was born at Middleton in Yorkshire before 1546 and martyred at York on 28 March 1600. Second son of Henry Wharton and Agnes Warcop, he was younger brother of Thomas, first Lord Wharton. He studied at Trinity College, Oxford, graduating Master of Arts on 3 February 1564 and becoming a fellow. In 1583 he entered the English College at Reims for the priesthood.

Ordained priest on 31 March the next year, he kept studying until 1586, when on 21 May he left Reims with Edward Burden. No details of his mission work survive, though at his trial Judge Savile remarked that he had known Wharton at Oxford some years after 1596. Arrested in 1599 at the house of Eleanor Hunt, a widow seized with him, he was tried at York and suffered for his priesthood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edward-os:
Edward Osbaldeston was an English martyr born about 1560, hanged, drawn, and quartered at York on 16 November 1594. Son of Thomas Osbaldeston and nephew to Edward Osbaldeston of Osbaldeston Hall near Blackburn, he went to the English College of Douai, then at Reims. There he was ordained deacon in December 1583 and priest on 21 September 1585. He was sent on the mission on 27 April 1589.

Seized at night through an apostate priest named Thomas Clark at an inn in Tollerton, Yorkshire, on St Jerome's day, 30 September 1594, he was taken to York the next day. He had said his first Mass on St Jerome's feast and therefore held great devotion to the saint. Tried at the next assizes, he was attainted of high treason for being a priest, and suffered at York.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edward-wa:
Edward Waterson was born in London and martyred at Newcastle-on-Tyne on 7 January 1594, in old style 1593. His youth holds a romantic episode: journeying to Turkey with English merchants, he drew the eye of a wealthy Turk, who promised his daughter's hand if Waterson embraced Islam. Rejecting the offer with horror, Waterson travelled west through Italy and at Rome was reconciled to the Catholic Church by Richard Smith, later Bishop of Chalcedon.

The English College pilgrim book records his stay at Rome from 29 November to 11 December 1588. He then went to Reims for the priesthood, arriving on 24 January 1589. He took tonsure and minor orders in August 1590, subdiaconate in September 1591, diaconate in February 1592, and the priesthood later that year. Sent to England, he laboured in the north until his arrest and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-brit: Bede Camm's Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells of John Britton, also called Bretton, a layman and martyr from an old Bretton family near Barnsley, Yorkshire. Ardent in his Catholic faith, he was often parted from wife and family by persecution for his faith. Advanced in years, he was wrongly accused of treasonous speeches against the queen, refused to renounce his faith and was executed at York on 1 April 1598.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-marie-de-:
Marie de l'Incarnation, in the world Marie Guyard, was the first superior of the Ursulines of Quebec. She was born at Tours in France on 28 October 1599 and died at Quebec on 30 April 1672. Her father was a bourgeois by birth, and her mother was kin to the illustrious house of Barbon de la Bourdaisière. From infancy Marie showed great piety and detachment from the world.

At seventeen, obeying her parents, she married Martin, a silk manufacturer, and gave herself wholly to the duties of a Christian wife. The union brought trials, and its only consolation was the birth of a son. He later became the Benedictine Dom Claude, wrote his mother's life, and died in the odour of sanctity. Widowed after two years of marriage, she heard a call to the Ursulines, and the entry follows her voyage to Quebec and her schools for French and native girls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-robert-an:
Robert Anderton was an English priest and martyr born in the Isle of Wight about 1560, who died on 25 April 1586. He matriculated at Brasenose College, Oxford, in 1578. Afterwards he went abroad, was converted, and entered the college at Reims in 1580. There he and Marsden began a companionship unbroken even by death.

Having finished their course, they sailed for England but a storm overwhelmed them. They prayed to die on land rather than at sea, and their prayer was granted. Washed ashore, they were at once seized and shortly after tried and condemned. They pleaded that they had not broken the statute, having been cast ashore by force. Summoned to London, they faced the celebrated bloody question: would they fight against the pope, even if the pope sent an army? They suffered together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-robert-mo:
Robert Morton was an English priest and martyr born at Bawtry in Yorkshire about 1548, executed in Lincoln's Inn Fields, London, on Wednesday, 28 August 1588. A catalogue probably compiled by Father John Gerard and printed by Father Pollen gives 30 August for the deaths of Morton, Moor, Holford, Claxton, and Felton, but that date seems an error. Morton was the son of Robert Morton and nephew of Dr Nicholas Morton.

Ordained deacon at Rome and priest at Reims in 1587, he was condemned at Newgate on 26 August merely for being a priest, contrary to 27 Elizabeth, chapter 2. At the same time and place suffered Hugh Moor, a layman aged twenty-five of Grantham and Gray's Inn, for having been reconciled to the church by Father Thomas Stephenson. On the same day others suffered at Mile End and elsewhere, the entry notes, in the Armada summer's harvest of martyrs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-roger-ash:
Roger Ashton was a martyr, third son of Richard Ashton of Croston in Lancashire, hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn on 23 June 1592. His indictment is not preserved. Challoner gives the cause as a Roman dispensation sought to marry his second cousin. Later evidence, while confirming that charge, shows it was not the only cause.

Ashton had left in 1585 to campaign in the Low Countries with the Earl of Leicester against Spain. Sir William Stanley, placed on guard over Deventer, which had revolted from Spain, gave the town back to Spain with Ashton's help. He went over to the Spanish side on 29 January 1587. Cardinal Allen published a Defence of that act as a letter to one R.A., whose own letter is prefixed, and under those initials the entry recognizes Ashton himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-at:
Thomas Atkinson was a Yorkshire priest who served English Catholics in secret for nearly thirty years before his death at York in 1616. Born in the East Riding, he trained at Reims and returned home in 1588. He visited his flock on foot, with special care for the poor, until a broken leg forced him to ride.

So well known was he that daylight travel grew unsafe, and at seventy he was betrayed and carried to York with his host and members of the household. A pair of beads and a printed indulgence found on him sealed his fate. Condemned to be hanged, drawn, and quartered, he bore the sentence, in the entry's words, with wonderful patience, courage, and constancy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-be:
Thomas Belson was an Oxfordshire layman put to death at Oxford in 1589 for helping Catholic priests. Born at Brill, he had studied at the English college at Reims in 1584. Five years later he was seized at the Catherine Wheel Inn near Balliol College, together with his confessor George Nicols, priest Richard Yaxley, and a servant named Prichard.

Taken to London, the men were questioned before Secretary Walsingham and tortured in Bridewell and the Tower, then sent back to Oxford for trial. Belson was convicted of felony for assisting priests. He suffered after the priests, kissing their dead bodies and asking their prayers that he might match their courage and constancy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-p:
William Patenson, also spelled Paterson, was an English priest executed at Tyburn in January 1592. Born in Yorkshire or Durham, he entered the English College at Reims in 1584, was ordained in 1587, and returned to the English mission early in 1589.

On the third Sunday of Advent 1591 he said Mass at a house in Clerkenwell, and while dining with priest James Young the priest-catchers burst in. Young hid, but Patenson was taken and condemned at the Old Bailey after Christmas. In prison he converted fellow condemned men, reconciling thieves before their deaths, and, by one account, six of seven felons sharing his cell on his last night. For that reason, the entry says, he was cut down while still conscious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-r:
William Richardson, alias Anderson, was the last martyr of Elizabeth's reign, executed at Tyburn in February 1603. He reached Reims in 1592, moved to Valladolid, then to Seville, where he was ordained. Betrayed by a trusted friend to the Lord Chief Justice, he was tried with unseemly haste at the Old Bailey for being a priest who had entered the realm.

Sources differ on whether he was seized at Clement's Inn or had already spent a week as a close prisoner in Newgate before his condemnation on 15 February. At his execution on 17 February he showed great courage and constancy, dying most cheerfully, to the edification of onlookers. One of his last utterances was a prayer for the queen herself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-rob:
Robert Sutton was a priest executed at Stafford in July 1587, not to be confused with a namesake companion of William Hartley. Born at Burton-on-Trent, he took his M. A. from Christ Church, Oxford, in 1567 and became rector of Lutterworth in 1571, but was converted by his younger brother William, later a Jesuit.

With another brother, Abraham, he reached Douai in 1576, and both were ordained priests the following February after saying their first Masses. They left for England in March 1578. Robert was arrested at Stafford and condemned merely for being a priest, and was cut down alive. A year later Catholics recovered one of his quarters, and found thumb and forefinger intact; Abraham gave the thumb to Father John Gerard, and it is now at Stonyhurst College.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-wil:
William Harrington was an English martyr executed at Tyburn in February 1594. Born in 1566, the youngest son of a family that had entertained Edmund Campion at Mount St John in 1581, he never forgot Campion's example. He studied at Reims and with the Jesuits at Tournai. Ill health kept him home for six or seven years before he returned to Reims, was ordained, and came back to England in mid-1592.

Seized the following May, he suffered nine months later after showing unusual constancy in prison, at the bar, and on the scaffold. The entry devotes much space to clearing his name: an apostate named Friswood, or Fid Williams, later claimed he had fathered a child before priesthood. Father Morris showed that her other charges against clergy and Catholics were baseless, so the claim against Harrington is entirely rejected, the only such accusation on record against an English martyr.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-baron:
Vincent Baron was a French Dominican theologian and preacher who lived from 1604 to 1674. Born at Martres in Haute-Garonne, he moved at seventeen from the Jesuit college at Toulouse to the Dominican convent of St Thomas there, professed in 1622, studied and taught philosophy and theology. By 1634 was first professor in his convent and conventual doctor at Toulouse university.

Rare learning, depth of thought, and clarity of exposition made him one of France's leading theologians. While teaching he preached Lenten courses in Toulouse, Avignon, Bordeaux, and other southern cities. For ten years, at the Languedoc bishops' invitation, he preached through their dioceses, reviving Catholic faith, raising morals, and debating Calvinist ministers, sometimes in their own synods. His controversies were abridged as Heresy Convinced in 1668, and his Paris sermons of 1658 and 1659 survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-conte:
Vincent Contenson was a French Dominican theologian and preacher who died at Creil in 1674, aged only thirty-three. Born at Altivillare in 1641, his epitaph called him in years a youth, mature in wisdom and venerable in virtue. He entered the Order of Preachers at seventeen, taught philosophy at Albi and theology at Toulouse. Then began a preaching career as brilliant as it was brief, struck down in the pulpit at Creil while giving a mission.

His reputation rests on Theology of Mind and Heart, published posthumously at Lyons in nine volumes in 1681, with a second edition in 1687. Its peculiar merit lay in moving away from dry scholastic reasoning while keeping its accuracy and solidity. Clothing arguments with illustrations and images from the Fathers that appeal to heart as well as mind, a compilation the entry says still holds value for students and preachers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-virtue-of-rel:
The virtue of religion is the virtue by which we render God the worship due to him as source of all being and principle of all government of things. Its name, on the derivation favoured by Lactantius and Augustine, comes from religare, to bind, the bond joining man to God. Aquinas treats it in the Summa, second part of the second part, question 81.

It is a distinct virtue, not merely a phase of another, marked off by its object, offering Almighty God the homage his singular excellence demands. It is not a theological virtue, because its immediate object is not God himself but the reverence owed him. Theologians place it among moral virtues as part of justice, giving God his due, and Aquinas ranks it first among moral virtues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-hilton:
Walter Hilton was an Augustinian mystic who died on 24 March 1396. Little is known of his life beyond his headship of a house of Augustinian Canons at Thurgarton near Newark in Nottinghamshire. His close touch with the Carthusians, though he never joined their order. A man of great holiness, his spiritual writings were widely influential in fifteenth-century England.

Most famous is the Ladder of Perfection, in two books, first printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1494. A guidebook for the journey to the spiritual Jerusalem, defined as contemplation in perfect love of God. The soul is reformed to God's image, first in faith only, then in faith and feeling, speeded by humility and love through the mystical dark night. A withdrawing of thought and soul from earthly things by yearning to love, see, and feel Jesus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-odingt:
Walter of Odington, also called Walter of Evesham and sometimes confused with Walter of Eynsham fifty years earlier, was an English Benedictine who died not earlier than 1330. Stationed first at Evesham and later at Oxford, he pursued astronomical and mathematical work as early as 1316, writing chiefly on scientific subjects.

His most valuable work, On the Speculation of Music, first published complete in Coussemaker's Scriptores, was written at Evesham, certainly before 1316 and, by Riemann's dating, before 1300. It gathers practically all contemporary knowledge of music theory and adds considerations of his own. Riemann credits him with establishing, on theoretical grounds before the thirteenth century's close, the consonance of minor and major thirds. Other works, in manuscript only, include a treatise on alchemy and one on the eighth sphere's motion. Others include one on the multiplication of species in vision, a metrical art, a geometry by numbers, and an Evesham calendar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-of-cha:
Walter of Châtillon, also Gautier de Lille, was a poet of the second half of the twelfth century. Born at Lille and dying of plague, probably at Amiens, early in the thirteenth century. He studied at Paris under Etienne of Beauvais, settled at Châtillon, changing his name from de Insulis to de Castillione, ran its schools, studied law at Bologna.

Returned to serve as secretary to Henry, Archbishop of Reims, and then to his successor William, archbishop from 1176 to 1201. At William's request Walter wrote his Alexandreid, dedicated to the archbishop, a Latin poem of 5,464 hexameters in ten books on Alexander the Great, based on Curtius's account. It shows great familiarity with Virgil and later Latin poets but abounds in anachronisms, most startlingly treating Christ's Passion as already past in Alexander's time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-of-mer:
Walter of Merton was Bishop of Rochester and founder of Merton College, Oxford, dying on 27 October 1277. He was already a clerk in holy orders.

Preferment came steadily: livings across the country by 1241, agent for Durham's bishop in a lawsuit in 1256, prothonotary of the chancery in 1258. Prebendary of St Paul's in 1259, chancellor under Henry III in 1261, and prebendary of Exeter and canon of Wells in 1262. In 1261 he set aside two Surrey manors for Merton priory to support scholars residing at the schools, the seed of Merton College. Statutes of 1264 founded a house of Merton scholars at Malden, transferred to Oxford ten years later, the earliest example of collegiate life at Oxford. A common corporate life under a warden, without vows, since scholars entering a religious order forfeited their scholarships.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wellington:
Wellington is a New Zealand diocese originally part of the Vicariate of Western Oceania erected in 1835. In 1836 Gregory XVI entrusted New Zealand and the western Pacific islands to the newly founded Society of Mary, and. Owing to communication difficulties across the vicariate's many islands, New Zealand was made a separate vicariate in 1842 under Mgr Pompallier, titular Bishop of Amasia.

British colonists soon arrived in great numbers: the first body landed on 22 January 1840 and founded Wellington town, Queen Victoria's sovereignty was proclaimed days later. The Treaty of Waitangi ceded sovereignty to the queen while securing chiefs' territorial rights. New Zealand, first a dependency of New South Wales, became a separate colony in May 1841. In 1843 the colony was divided into two vicariates, Auckland province forming one and the remainder, including Wellington, the other, whose history the entry follows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-allis: William Allison was one of the English priests who fell victim to the plots of 1679 and 1680, and he died a prisoner in York Castle about that time. John Joseph A'Becket's Catholic Encyclopedia entry preserves his name among those sufferers, a priest whose imprisonment ended in death in custody. No birthplace, ordination or trial is given for him there; his story stands as a brief witness to persecution ending in a York prison cell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-cally:
William Callyhan Robinson was an American jurist and teacher who built Catholic legal education in Washington. Born at Norwich, Connecticut, in 1834, he died at Washington in 1911. He graduated from Dartmouth in 1854, trained for the Episcopal ministry, served parishes in Pennsylvania, entered the Catholic Church in 1863, and joined the bar in 1864. Yale kept him as law lecturer and teacher from 1869 to 1895, with spells as a New Haven judge.

Robinson also sat in the state legislature in 1874. In 1895 the Catholic University of America called him to teach, where he set up the School of Social Sciences and served as law dean until his death. His books range from Notes of Elementary Law and Elementary Law through a three-volume Law of Patents to Forensic Oratory and Elements of American Jurisprudence. Colleagues prized his thorough grasp of law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-caxto:
William Caxton was the first English printer and the man who brought printing into England. Born in the Weald of Kent about 1422, he died at Westminster in 1491. Little is known of his early life beyond his own prefaces. Apprenticed to the London mercer Robert Large in 1438, he became a merchant at Bruges about 1446, prospered, and in 1465 governed the Merchant Adventurers there, handling delicate trade talks with skill.

About 1470 he left trade for the service of Margaret, Duchess of Burgundy, and finished his translation of the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye in 1471. Copying could not meet demand for it, so he learned printing, likely at Cologne, and printed the Recuyell at Bruges in 1474. Returning in 1476, he set up his Westminster press, issuing ninety-six books, including Chaucer, Gower, and Malory's Morte d'Arthur.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-errin:
William Errington was an English priest who founded Sedgley Park School after three failed starts. Born in 1716, he died on 28 September 1768. Son of Mark Errington of Wiltshire, he went to Douai in 1737, swore the mission oath in 1741, and took orders in December 1747. He reached London in March 1748 and lodged with Bishop Challoner, then coadjutor to Bishop Petre, who prized him as a zealous missioner and a shrewd man of business.

Challoner urged him to build a good middle-class school, and Errington tried Buckinghamshire, Wales, and Betley near Newcastle-under-Lyne without success. On Lady Day 1763 he opened Sedgley Park near Wolverhampton with twelve boys in Park Hall, once Lord Ward's home. Parliament attacked the venture, but Lord Dudley defended it, and the school served the Church for over a century, living on today as Saint Wilfrid's College, Oakmoor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-gasto:
William Gaston was a North Carolina jurist who won Catholics the vote in his state. Born at Newbern in 1778, he died at Raleigh in 1844. His father, a Presbyterian Irish surgeon in the British navy, was killed by British troops during the Revolution, leaving his Catholic English mother Margaret Sharpe to school him. He entered Georgetown College in 1791, graduated first in his class at Princeton in 1796, and joined the bar in 1798.

In August 1800 Gaston won a state senate seat despite a constitution barring Catholics from office. He served in Congress in 1813 and 1815 as a Federalist leader, then returned to law and joined the North Carolina supreme court bench in 1833 for life. At the 1835 convention he drove repeal of the clause that kept Catholics from office, and his gifts always served his faith and his fellow Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-habin:
William Habington was a Worcestershire poet and historian of the Caroline age, praised for pure and seemly verse. Born at Hindlip in 1605, he died in 1654. Son of the antiquarian Thomas Habington, he studied at Saint Omer and Paris. A tale that he fled England to dodge Jesuit pressure to join their order rests only on a vague claim by the ex-Jesuit Wadsworth.

Habington married Lucy Herbert, daughter of Baron Powis, and in 1634 issued Castara, love poems chiefly to his wife, enlarged in 1635 and 1640 with sonnets and prose characters. His verse is skilful, tuneful, and touched by the metaphysical fashion of his day, yet marked by strict decency of thought and tongue. In 1640 he also staged the romantic tragedy Queen of Arragon and published a History of Edward IV, followed in 1641 by reflective Observations upon History.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-harri:
William Harrison was the third and last archpriest of England, who worked to heal the breach between secular priests and Jesuits. Born in Derbyshire in 1553, he died on 11 May 1621. He studied at Douai from 1575 to 1577, went to Rome as a deacon, took orders, and swore the mission oath at the new English College in April 1579. He laboured in England from 1581 to 1587, then read civil and canon law at Paris.

Harrison ran Father Persons's small school at Eu in Normandy from 1591 until war broke it up in 1593. He served as procurator at Reims, and taught theology at Douai after his 1597 doctorate. Five years in Rome gave him wide church experience. Back in England in 1609, he succeeded Archpriest Birkhead in 1615, backed Kellison against Jesuit sway at Douai, and pushed for restored bishops, dying just as Rome's envoy set out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-henry:
William Henry Anderdon was an English Jesuit writer whose Catholic tales and sharp controversial pamphlets sold in thousands. Born in London in 1816, he died in 1890. After King's College, London, and Balliol, Oxford, he took his degree in 1840, served as an Anglican vicar at Withyam and Leicester, and entered the Catholic Church at Paris in 1850. Ordained at Oscott in 1853, he taught at Ushaw, preached in Dublin, and served Cardinal Manning as secretary until joining the Jesuits in 1872.

From 1875 to 1889 he lived at Manchester as preacher, guide, and writer. His tales, Bonneval, Owen Evans the Catholic Crusoe, Afternoons with the Saints, and In the Snow, ran to nine or ten editions each and spread into German and French. His controversial best sellers probed Luther, ritualism, and what Catholics truly believe, aiming to understand opponents rather than caricature them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-hough:
William Houghton was a Dominican scholar-statesman who became Archbishop of Dublin and brokered peace between France and England. His birth date and place are unknown; he died at Dijon in 1298. He took the Dominican habit in England, studied and lectured at Saint James in Paris, and was chosen provincial of England at the Vienna chapter of 1282. He governed five years with a charm that won love and respect.

Recalled to Paris lectures, favoured by Philip IV, then provincial again for seven years, Houghton became a favourite of Edward I. The king sent him to Rome in 1289 to seek aid for Holy Land Christians. Edward pressed Boniface VIII to name him to Dublin, and he was consecrated at Ghent in 1297. His mediation sealed a two-year Anglo-French peace, and he died at Dijon while carrying news of it to the pope, his body brought to London for burial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-seton:
William Seton was a New York author and soldier, grandson of Saint Elizabeth Ann Seton. Born in New York in 1835, he died there in 1905. His father, a navy captain, was Elizabeth Ann's son, and his mother was Emily Prime. Burke's Peerage of 1900 named him head of the Parbroath Setons, cadets of the Earls of Winton. He studied at Fordham, Mount Saint Mary's, and Bonn, travelled widely, and joined a New York law office.

Answering Lincoln's first call in 1861, Seton fought as captain of the Forty-first New York at Antietam, where two wounds disabled him for a time. He then returned as captain of the Sixteenth Artillery in Grant's Richmond campaign. After the war he turned to letters: novels Romance of the Charter Oak and Pride of Lexington, the poem The Pioneer, Rachel's Fate, and science writing for the Catholic World. He also worked finding jobs for the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-the-w:
William the Walloon was an eleventh-century abbot caught between pope, archbishop, and emperor. His birth date is unknown; he died probably on 22 December 1089. He became Abbot of Saint Arnoul at Metz in 1050, kept his predecessor Warin's good rule, and spent leisure on Jerome and Augustine. In June 1073 Gregory VII scolded Archbishop Manasses of Reims for abusing Saint-Remi monks and ordered a fit abbot chosen; William won election but found the post untenable.

Manasses kept persecuting him despite papal letters, so late in 1073 William went to Rome seeking leave to resign Saint-Remi. The pope prized him and wished him to keep both abbeys, but Manasses seized his crosier and installed Henry of Hoimblière without consulting him. Back at Metz, William weakly let Henry IV intrude him into the Metz bishopric in 1085 after driving out Bishop Herimann, then publicly resigned at Gorze in 1086 and regained Saint Arnoul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-westo:
William Weston was an English Jesuit missioner whose exorcisms and Wisbech prison quarrels divided Elizabethan Catholics. Born at Maidstone in 1550, he died at Valladolid in 1615. Schooled at Oxford, Paris, and Douai, he walked to Rome and joined the Jesuits in November 1575, giving all he owned to Douai College. After novitiate and work in Spain, he reached England in September 1584, when no Jesuit stood free, and received Philip Howard, Earl of Arundel, into the Church.

Weston's exorcisms, aided by other priests, impressed many for a year, though modern reading sees hysteria, then called mother, rather than possession. Persecution ended the movement, and Weston was seized in August 1586 and held at Wisbech from 1588. He was drawn into the 1595 split over common rules, twenty of thirty-three priests backing his call for order against Bagshaw's minority. Arbitrators settled a compromise rule in November 1595, and Weston later wrote his mission autobiography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilmington:
Wilmington is the Delaware diocese erected on 3 March 1868 across the Delmarva Peninsula. It covers Delaware, nine Maryland counties, and two Virginia counties east of Chesapeake Bay. Jesuits founded the peninsula's first Catholic mission at Bohemia Manor, Maryland, in 1704 and remained its only priests until Patrick Kenny settled at Coffee Run, Delaware, in 1808. That year Wilmington's first church, Saint Peter's, now the cathedral, opened.

First bishop Thomas Becker, a Richmond priest, found only eight priests and fourteen churches, most little more than sheds, a Catholic flock under five thousand, and schools in Sisters of Charity hands. By tireless work amid poverty he raised churches to twenty-six and clergy to twenty-one, and brought Benedictines, Franciscans, and Visitation sisters. He founded a boys' orphan asylum, and grew the flock to about eighteen thousand before his 1886 transfer to Savannah. His successor Alfred Curtis then cleared debts and added thirteen churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-yukon:
Yukon is the Canadian prefecture covering the far northwest, from 54 degrees north to the Arctic Ocean and the Rockies' crest to 141 degrees west, about 312,000 square miles. It joins Yukon Territory with northern British Columbia, once split between Mackenzie River vicariate and New Westminster diocese. The prefecture arose on 9 March 1908 under Oblate Fathers of Mary Immaculate, with Father Bunoz as first prefect that April. Nine Oblate missionaries served it over five churches, twenty-two chapels, and six mission stations.

Twelve Sisters of Saint Ann run its school and hospital for some five thousand Catholics. Dawson gained its first church and hospital as log buildings in 1907 and 1908 from Jesuit Father Judge, who died there in 1899. A 1902 Yukon law guaranteed separate schools under the British North America Act. Prince Rupert, founded June 1909, holds the prefect's headquarters, and Stuart's Lake serves two thousand Indian missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zabulon:
Zabulon was one of Jacob's twelve sons and father of the Israelite tribe bearing his name. Scripture knows nothing of the man beyond his sons Sered, Elon, and Jahleel, heads of three tribal families. The name is of doubtful sense, with a wordplay on zebed, gift: Leah says God gifted her, and this time her husband will honour her, for she bore six sons.

At Sinai's census Zabulon counted 57,400 fighting men under Eliab, camping east of the tabernacle with Judah and Issachar. At Shittim a second census gave 60,500. Elisaphan son of Parnach shared the land division for them. Under the judges they shone: Deborah's song praises Zabulon for risking life at Merom, and they joined Gideon against Midian. They gave judge Elon for ten years, and sent fifty thousand warriors to crown David at Hebron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zambesi-missi:
Zambesi Mission is the Jesuit prefecture covering Rhodesia north and south of the Zambesi and northern Bechuanaland. British rule governs the whole field. Founded in 1877 under the English Jesuit province, its bounds were fixed by Propaganda in 1879, when Father Henry Depelchin's first party left Grahamstown for a thousand-mile trek to Bulawayo.

No railways eased that road, prices ran enormous, and fever and want killed many. The Matabele, under King Lobengula, were unready for Christianity, and Depelchin's push north past the Zambesi failed, as did Law's eastward venture to the Portuguese border. After the Company broke Lobengula in 1893, stations multiplied, Dominican sisters took hospitals and settler schools, and railways cut the old obstacle. Progress stayed slow, since adult pagan customs, above all polygamy, blocked converts, so hopes rest on schooling children. The mission now counts thirty-two Jesuits, twenty-two lay brothers, and Mariannhill priests and brothers.
complete-project-gutenberg-collection-of:
Three memoir collections by various insiders of Napoleon's court fill this large Project Gutenberg gathering. Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne, Napoleon's private secretary and school friend from Brienne, anchors the volume. His memoirs, edited by R. W. Phipps, show the emperor at work and at home. Bourrienne claims impartial aim, praising and blaming his old master in turn.

Constant, the emperor's premier valet de chambre, adds Recollections of the Private Life of Napoleon in Walter Clark's translation. Stewarton's Memoirs of the Court of St. Cloud close the set as secret letters from Paris to London. Together the three give campaigns, councils, dress, temper, and table talk from men who stood in the room. Editors extended Bourrienne past the Elba abdication through Waterloo to the death at St. Helena. Napoleon readers who want the private man behind the battles, in slippers as much as in uniform, start with these witnesses.
concept-great-power-mattison:
Ages of the world roll past in a short apocalypse from the Nag Hammadi codices. The Concept of Our Great Power, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that vision in English. The power of the title is the high God, whose plan the seer lays bare.

The text moves from creation through the flood and the age of flesh to fire and final rest. It tells how the savior comes, how the rulers fail, and how the saved are known. The sweep is vast for so brief a book. Mattison's free rendering lets readers trace that sweep in one sitting.

country-life-in-canada-fifty-years-ago-p:
Canniff Haight's Country Life in Canada Fifty Years Ago gathers the personal recollections of a sexagenarian looking back on pioneer Ontario. Haight dedicates the book to the young men of Canada, on whose integrity and energy, he writes, the future of their great heritage rests.

The recollections cover clearing land, building homes, travelling rough roads, worship, school and neighbourly life in a colony still close to the forest. Haight writes as a man who lived the changes he describes, contrasting the hardships of early settlement with the settled country of his old age. Readers interested in Canadian social history will find here a first-hand, unpretentious account of how ordinary settlers actually lived.
criticism-and-fiction:
William Dean Howells argued the case for literary realism in Criticism and Fiction, a collection of his critical essays. Howells asks whether any lasting standard of taste exists. Quoting John Addington Symonds, he answers that fashion changes but truth endures. What is simple, natural, and honest in art, he argues, stays beautiful. Fantastic and artificial work pleases briefly, then fades.

Essays take up fiction's aims, the role of the editor, and the faults of romantic storytelling. Howells praises novels that study ordinary life honestly. He attacks false sentiment and stagey plots. His manner is conversational, full of asides about dress, furniture, and painting. Readers get the clearest statement of the realist creed that shaped Howells's own novels and his editing of a generation of American writers.

dombey-and-son:
Charles Dickens builds Dombey and Son around a shipping merchant whose firm name states his whole ambition: a son to inherit both. Paul Dombey arrives, frail and strange, while his sister Florence is dismissed as merely a girl. The contents trace Paul's christening, schooling, and decline, and the wooden midshipman at Sol Gills's shop.

Paul dies, the firm falters, and Dombey's proud second marriage to Edith collapses into recrimination, as the middle chapters' confrontation between Edith and her mother shows. Florence's steadfast love finally redeems her broken father. Dickens planned this novel more tightly than its predecessors, and its railway scenes, sea imagery, and study of pride made it a turning point in his art.
drusilla-with-a-million:
Elizabeth Cooper's Drusilla With a Million opens in an old ladies' home, where little Drusilla Doane sits darning a tablecloth in the sun. Two men arrive in the parlour asking for her by name, news so wonderful that every other woman stops her work to stare.

From that comic, touching opening Cooper builds a story about an elderly woman whose life is changed by sudden fortune. It asks what money can and cannot do for a person long used to plain living. Drusilla's birdlike neighbours, her modest habits and her good sense carry the tale. Readers who enjoy stories of late-life surprises, told with warmth and humour, will take to Drusilla at once.
eight-years-wanderings-in-ceylon:
Samuel White Baker's Eight Years' Wanderings in Ceylon records his life as a planter and elephant hunter in the island's highlands from 1847. His contents begin with Colombo's dullness, cinnamon gardens, jungle fever, and the hill station Newera Ellia that Governor Barnes's energy created. Baker bought land at Nuwara Eliya and imported English stock, dogs, and settlers.

Chapters mix settlement disasters, eccentric grooms, insubordinate servants, and the sagacity of elephants with hunting of elk, hog, and leopard. His hounds, once in jungle, become their own masters, he warns, and training them is a study in itself. Baker later became famous as an African explorer; this first book shows the sportsman-planter learning his trade.
epictetus-discourses-enchiridion-matheso:
Epictetus, a Greek slave in Rome who won his freedom and taught philosophy, left no writings of his own. His pupil Arrian took notes on his talks, which became the Discourses, and boiled the teaching into the Enchiridion, or Handbook. P. E. Matheson's 1916 translation covers both, the four books of Discourses and the short Handbook.

Epictetus teaches that some things are up to us and others are not, and peace lies in knowing the split. Wealth, health, and fame sit outside our power; our judgments and choices sit inside it. His voice is blunt, funny, and practical. The Handbook became a pocket guide carried by soldiers and emperors alike.
erewhon:
Samuel Butler, an English writer with a sharp wit, wrote this satire of a made up land in 1872. Erewhon is 'nowhere' spelled near back to front, a hint of the game he plays. Butler had lived in New Zealand, and the land of his book owes much to that stay.

In Erewhon, machines are banned as a risk to man, and sick men are tried as rogues. Health is a crime and crime is a disease to be cured, in a world turned on its head. The mirror shows Victorian England its own face, and the joke still cuts deep.
fanny-campbell-the-female-pirate-captain: Fanny Campbell, the Female Pirate Captain, a tale of the Revolution. The lady pirate. This book preserves that adventure. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
five-lectures-on-reincarnation:
Swami Abhedananda's Five Lectures on Reincarnation presents Vedanta thought for Western readers. Abhedananda, author of India and Her People and How to Be a Yogi, argues that all we see in the world follows the law of cause and effect.

What we see is the effect, he explains, while the cause stays unseen, as a falling apple shows the unseen pull of gravity. Talks treat rebirth itself, birth traits, growth of life forms, and which is more sound, rising from the dead or rebirth, closing with the old view of souls passing on. Readers keen on Hindu thought, or on the Vedanta drive in America, will find these talks clear and plain.
from-the-earth-to-the-moon-and-round-the:
Jules Verne wrote From the Earth to the Moon in 1865 and its sequel, Round the Moon, in 1870, and the hosted text joins the two novels in one volume. The tale begins with the Baltimore Gun Club, masters of cannon left idle after the American Civil War. Their president, Barbicane, proposes a bold new target: fire a shell at the Moon from a giant gun dug into the Florida ground.

A daring Frenchman, Michel Ardan, talks the club into building a hollow shell with room for passengers. Barbicane, Ardan, and Captain Nicholl ride it together. The second novel follows their flight, as a stray asteroid pulls them around the Moon instead of onto it, and they fall back to a splash in the Pacific. Verne loads the fun with real figures and star lore.
gardening-without-irrigation:
Steve Solomon's Gardening Without Irrigation belongs to his Cascadia Gardening Series for the Pacific Northwest. Solomon moved from Michigan to Lorane, Oregon, in 1978 to homestead five acres. His well faltered just as his first garden needed water. That failure set him asking how pioneers gardened through rainless summers.

Chapters explain predictably dry summers and the science of water-wise gardening. He shows how wide spacing, deep soil, and timing help plants need less irrigation. A long chapter treats crops one by one, from A to Z. His own garden plan and backyard notes close the book. Solomon writes for maritime Northwest growers whose summers bring eight to twelve dry weeks. The method promises a lush vegetable garden on little or no pumped water.
garuda-purana-basu-edition:
